        Edison stayed behind to buy time, fending off the attackers while his companions escaped.

        “That boy is slippery; he’ll be fine alone. Don’t worry,” Galileo said calmly. “Our priority now is to find the Headmaster and report our discovery of the machinas.”

        “Let’s hurry and find him!” Nicole eagerly ran toward the central hall.  As she looked out through the large windows, she saw that the barriers, which had disappeared due to the compromised security system, were now reactivated, sealing all the demons away from the institute.

        Still, the atmosphere in the hall remained heavy and oppressive.

        On a raised platform, Headmaster  Michelangelo stood beside a tall, muscular man—Zeus, the King of the Holy Gods, who was holding a bolt of lightning, his eyes gleaming with overpowering authority. All the scientists in the room wore complicated expressions, but none dared speak.

        Furrowing her brow, Galileo immediately spoke up, “Headmaster, what are the god soldiers doing here?”

        “...Galileo,” Michelangelo slowly raised his gaze and spoke, as if struggling with his words. “The gods saved us from the demons, and to repay their kindness, I’ve decided to form an alliance with the gods.”

        “That’s ridiculous!” Galileo shouted. “The gods turned a blind eye to the tragedies they caused for humanity in the past, and now they want to form an alliance with us? They’re definitely plotting something else! Once an agreement is signed, humans will become their vassals; we’ll never be able to break free from their chains!”

        “Enough!” Michelangelo’s voice reverberated through the hall. “The Lomond Manor is found to ensure the survival of humanity and bring peace to this land. Forming an alliance with the gods is the only way we survive!”

        “That’s not the only way!” Einstein stepped forward, pushing Descartes into view.  His tone was firm. “Headmaster, we’ve found the key to change our fate: if we awaken the machinas from the slumber beneath the earth, we can turn the tide for humanity!”

        Zeus scoffed at Einstein’s words, his voice like thunder as he spoke,  “The machinas? You mean those metal monsters that once hid underground? They tried to claim the land’s power for themselves, only to seal themselves away after their failure. Now, you want to awaken them? What’s your true motive?”

        Michelangelo’s face darkened. He coldly stared at Einstein and the others. “So you seek to provoke conflict between the gods and humans for your own selfish reasons… Men! Seize these traitors!”

        In an instant, Einstein and his group were surrounded by swarms of scientists and god soldiers. A heavy, fraught silence fell over the entire hall.

        “Wait,” Zeus spoke again. Casting his gaze downward, he pointed at Descartes, who stood beside Einstein, and coldly demanded, “We, gods, are kind. We will forgive you if you hand over that wicked creature.”

        [i]‘No! I won’t let my people suffer any longer!’[/i] Schrödinger’s voice rang out in Einstein’s mind. Feeling the rage in his teacher’s voice, he inwardly reassured him, “Teacher, I’ll handle it. I will protect everyone.”

        Einstein took a deep breath and responded coldly, “I will not hand him over! Nor will I be captured without a fight!”

        Einstein summoned his power before his words had fully left his mouth. A burst of deep blue radiance exploded from his body, sending waves of energy capable of bending time and space through the hall. Zeus swung his lightning bolt down to block the attack, only to be repelled by the unknown force. Blood trickled from the corner of his mouth.

        Meanwhile, everyone in the hall was plunged into chaos as the dazzling light temporarily stripped them of their sight.

        “Run!”  Einstein shouted, grabbing Descartes and breaking through the encirclement. Galileo quickly pulled Nicole along and stayed close behind. They managed to escape the central hall and made their way to the garden outside, but the pursuers were relentless; a single misstep would turn them into birds trapped in a cage.

        “The exit is just ahead! Hurry!” Galileo shouted. Everyone immediately shook off their fatigue and sprinted toward the exit as fast as they could. However, an alarm blared as they neared the door, and the heavy steel gate in front of it began to sink.

        “Oh no! They’re closing the gate!” Nicole cried out in panic. To their surprise, a pair of powerful metal arms lifted the gate just as it was about to close completely.

        “Darwin!” Galileo gasped as she recognized the figure.

        “We’ll explain everything after we’re out of here. Hurry!” A young man appeared. It was Newton, one of the new scientists. The gate slowly rose as he pressed a button at the side.

        “But Edison is still underground—” Einstein said anxiously. 

        “I found him,” a familiar voice interrupted Einstein. It was Marie Curie, walking in from the other side while supporting the battered Edison.

        “Hey! Great to see you again,” said Edison with a grin, throwing Einstein a wink.

        “Ah! They’re catching up!” Nicole whispered urgently.

        The group quickened their pace and finally broke through the door. Once everyone was safely outside, Darwin released the gate and stepped out after them. Together, they climbed into the large transport vehicle that Darwin had prepared and drove off into the blinding sunlight, leaving the Lomond Manor behind.

        Later, Mary told everyone about Socrates’ betrayal and the fact that Michelangelo had fallen into the gods’ control. The news brought complex expressions to everyone’s face.

        “That explains why Michelangelo’s attitude changed so suddenly. He couldn’t tolerate the arrogant gods, which is why he hastened to explore the underground, looking for a new opportunity...” Galileo remarked.

        “So, what do we do now? Should we go back and tell everyone the truth?” Nicole asked.

        “Too risky,” Newton said. “Going back now would likely get us silenced.”

        The group, troubled by the current predicament and the unknown future, fell into silence until Einstein spoke, “Since the Lomond Manor is now compromised, we must find another way. We’ll create a new organization... a place that truly belongs to humans.”

        Darwin nodded in agreement. “Yeah. One day, we will tell the truth if we gather more evidence. We’ll show the world that the gods are not protectors, but predators trying to build a cage for their prey.”

        “Exactly,”  Edison said with a calculating smile. “Let creativity and knowledge light up this darkened night.”

        While the sun slowly set, Einstein’s gaze remained as resolute as ever, as if he could see the stars of the future, knowing that his journey was far from over…
STORY_2951:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 5

        It was with the help of Darwin that Newton, the young scientist, broke through the demons’ encirclement and reached the northern wing of the Lomond Manor headquarters. When the heavy doors slammed shut with a thunderous boom, sealing off the raging battle and roars outside, Newton pressed his back against the icy surface. His chest heaved as he drew a deep breath, trying to calm his racing heartbeat.

        [i]‘I don’t have much time to waste. I have to repair the defensive barriers as soon as possible,’[/i] he reminded himself.

        Months earlier, Newton had received an invitation from the Lomond Manor, a scientific organization, to join them as a scientist. Unexpectedly, he was attacked by unknown assailants and knocked unconscious upon his arrival—but in truth, it had all been a test created by the Lomond Manor for newcomers. It was after a series of difficult trials that Newton became one of the qualified candidates, eventually earning a place on the subterranean exploration team.

        Today was supposed to be the day of their departure. Yet the unexpected struck—the institute’s security system had been compromised, and the demons, who had long been watching from the shadows, seized the opening of the disappearing defensive barriers and mounted a full-scale invasion. To secure the progress of the subterranean exploration, Darwin volunteered to lead most of the scientists in repelling the demons.

        However, the demons’ assault came in relentless waves. The number of scientists in the facility alone was never going to be enough to fight off an entire army. Knowing that only by reactivating the barriers could they have a slim chance of survival, Darwin fought his way through the demons’ siege with Newton to the northern wing, where the security system was housed. After sending Newton inside the building, he stood valiantly before the doors, vowing not to let a single demon break through.

        Newton understood all too well that the time Darwin could buy with his life was limited. He had to move—now.  He hurriedly raced down the spiral staircase, level by level, until he reached the heart of the security systems at the bottom. 

        The door there had long broken down, revealing what was behind it—a meticulous network of metal conduits filled with flowing elemental energy. But the device now bore a gaping hole with flames and white smoke pouring from several severed conduits.

        ‘It’s so badly damaged…’ Newton’s expression darkened. He crouched to inspect it, his fingers flying over each fracture while his mind raced through possible repair methods.

        “Good, at least the core is still intact. If I reconnect the circuits, I can force-reactivate the barriers. A full repair can wait.” Newton let out a breath of relief, then sprang into action, pulling tools and spare parts from his backpack.

        His hands began to move with speed and precision, slipping every component and conduit back in place, as though he had already simulated the process a thousand times in his head.

        Suddenly, an ominous disturbance rippled through the air. A shadow crept silently out from the corner of a wall. Almost by reflex, Newton twisted his body and swung his longsword—

        Clang! Sparks exploded into the air as two weapons met with a piercing shriek.

        “Nice reflexes.” A low, cold voice resonated as a burly man stepped in from another entrance.

        “Socrates… so it was you who destroyed the device…” Newton demanded coldly, “Why did you betray us?”

        “It was the Lomond Manor, humans, who betrayed me first.”  Socrates, a silver scientist, spoke calmly. “Leave now, and I’ll pretend I never saw you—”

        Newton ended his speech with a flash of his sword. Yet, Socrates, who came well-prepared, dodged it with ease. His gaze hardened as he said, “Since you insist on being stubborn, then don’t blame me for this.” 

        His legs tensed like steel springs. With a powerful kick, he hurled himself at Newton, who raised his sword to block the attack, only to be sent flying by the sheer force. He slammed into the wall, sliding down amid a deafening crash.

        “Cough!” A searing pain tore through Newton’s chest, forcing violent coughs—even blood—from his throat. Through blurred vision, he saw Socrates draw a dagger and walk toward the device. It was clear that the man intended to destroy it completely and erase any chance of repair.

        [i]‘No… I can’t let him succeed… if I can’t reactivate the barriers… Darwin… everyone will die under the demons’ hands…’[/i] Clenching his teeth, Newton endured the agony and propped himself up with his sword. Then, he threw himself forward just as Socrates brought the dagger down—

        Thud! The blade pierced Newton’s shoulder, stopping just short of the device and stopping its destruction as well.

        “You…” Shock flickered across Socrates’ face before quickly turning into a complex expression mixed with admiration and resignation.  In the end, it dissolved into a long sigh and an apology: “I’m sorry.”

        Socrates yanked the dagger free and raised it high. Just as he was about to deliver the final blow, a hazy, intoxicating fragrance suddenly filled the room.

        “This is… a paralytic gas! Marie…” Socrates understood the danger in that instant, but the realization came too late. The paralytic gas had already filled his lungs, and with a strangled breath, he crumpled to the floor, unconscious, revealing the woman who stood not far behind him.

        Newton saw her. Both of her sleeves had been cut open, exposing the unique patterns on her arms. They were actually painted with a special kind of paralytic agent that she used to paralyze Socrates and render him unconscious.

        “Marie… Curie…” Newton murmured, his vision growing hazy; he, too, had inhaled the paralytic agent.

        “Here, take a deep breath. This is the antidote.” Marie walked to Newton’s side and held a vial beneath his nose. It was not until several deep inhales that the fog finally lifted from his mind.

        But then, Marie’s strength failed her. As she tumbled forward, Newton rushed to catch her regardless of the pain in his shoulder. He gently lowered her to the ground, anxiously checking her condition.

        “I’m fine. It’s just exhaustion,” she said with a faint smile. “Socrates imprisoned me, and I haven’t eaten properly for days. Releasing that gas took what little strength I had left. Don’t worry about me. Go—repair the device and reactivate the barriers.” 

        “…All right. Rest here.”

        Newton turned back to the device and resumed the repair. Despite his injury, his movements did not falter. Moments later, he connected the final circuit and pressed the activation switch.

        The machinery roared to life as powerful, prismatic light flowed into the core. The intricate mechanisms responded with solid barriers rising from the ground until they enclosed all of the Lomond Manor.

        Newton strenuously staggered out of the control room. When he stepped outside the building, he saw demon corpses strewn across the ground while Darwin lay slumped against the wall, his body covered in soil and blood from the brutal fight. His face was pale, his eyes tightly shut, seemingly lifeless as Newton saw him.

        “Darwin!” Newton rushed to his side.

        “Oh… you’re back…” Darwin slowly opened his eyes. Seeing the anxious look on the young scientist’s face, he offered a reassuring smile and said, “I’m fine. Just a bit tired.”

        With his worries laid to rest, Newton managed a joke. “Tired already? Looks like you’re getting old.”

        “Haha, can’t deny that,” Darwin gave a hearty laugh as he reached out to ruffle Newton’s hair. “You’ve outdone an old man; you did well this time, my boy.”

        “Humph. Anyone could’ve handled something like that.”  Newton muttered as he turned his face away awkwardly.

        “We really owe this one to you.” Darwin stood and extended a hand.  “Let’s head back. Though the barriers have kept away the demons’ reinforcements, we still need to take care of those already inside the facility.”

        “Yeah.” Newton took his hand and stood.

        The two then hurried back to the central building, only to find that every invader had already been annihilated. All scientists were kneeling on one knee before a man bathed in golden light—Zeus, the King of the Holy Gods.

        “Great gods, we thank you for your timely salvation,” said Michelangelo, one of the headmasters of the Lomond Manor, bowing respectfully. Yet his eyes were strangely distant, hollow in a way beyond description. 

        [i]‘I’ve got a bad feeling about this…’[/i] Newton frowned deeply as he stared at the unsettling scene before him.
STORY_2952:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 4

        In the central hall of the Lomond Manor headquarters, Darwin stood perfectly straight as he watched Galileo lead the subterranean exploration team past the heavy doors that descended into the depths below.

        Several months earlier, Darwin had been assigned as a member of the first subterranean exploration. Though he had made it back alive, part of his body had been mechanicalized; the transformation almost cost his life. Even so, neither he nor the other scientists withdrew from the mission in fear. On the contrary, their resolve only hardened. They reworked the plan. To recruit more promising teammates, they even created a covert test—simulated crises designed to force candidates to unleash their latent potential under extreme pressure.  In the end, only four had passed, earning their places on this expedition.
  
        Originally, the second exploration should have followed immediately, but it was delayed as one of Lomond Manor’s headmasters, Copernicus, had attempted to shatter the boundary between realms using elemental forces. Numerous scientists joined forces to stop Copernicus’s ambition, and the incident, at last, ended with the headmaster’s death. It was after countless hours and resources lost to the aftermath that they were finally able to continue their exploration.

        Yet the unexpected struck.

        Just before their departure, they discovered that the institute’s security system had been compromised. As the defensive barriers disappeared, the demons seized the opportunity to attack. Michelangelo, as one of the headmasters, attempted to call off the expedition, but under Galileo’s insistence—and at Darwin’s suggestion—they agreed to split their forces.

        While Galileo led Einstein, Nicole, and Edison into the depths for the second subterranean exploration, Darwin remained behind to repel the demons’ invasion with the other scientists.

        The doors slowly closed. Though Galileo and her group vanished into the darkness below, her relentless resolve still lingered in the air.  Darwin withdrew his gaze and turned around, only to see Newton standing there, his brows tightly knit in a grave frown.

        “Newton, my boy, what’s with the long face? It’s not the end of the world,” Darwin said, patting the young scientist’s shoulder. His smile was bright and reassuring. “Don’t worry. You have me here—and the other scientists. They’re all people you can trust.”

        Newton pressed his lips and gave a quiet nod.

        Darwin said no more. He tightened his grip on his weapon and turned toward the other scientists standing on alert throughout the hall. Everyone’s nerves had been stretched to their limit as they heard explosions and screams coming from outside. The air grew heavy, taut with dread, and all of their faces bore the unmistakable shadow of unease.

        “Everyone, listen to me. The demons have broken through our outer defenses!” Darwin’s voice thundered through the oppressive air and silenced all the whispers. “Now follow me, and we shall drive those invaders back!”

        With the weapon clenched in his hand, Darwin strode forward, shoving the doors open as he led the charge. An overpowering stench of blood and gunpowder greeted him the moment he stepped outside. The other scientists followed close behind. All of a sudden, flames, lightning, and frost erupted as they met the invaders head-on. Elemental energy crackled in the air as weapons clashed. The smell of blood and fire thickened, spreading across the battlefield amidst the cacophony of roars and screams.

        After a brief engagement, the scientists managed to clear the enemies around the institute’s main building. Darwin, seizing the moment, leapt onto one of the walls to survey the situation from above. Yet, all he saw was a grim reality: a demon army—their ranks thicker and more numerous than ever—surging toward the Lomond Manor like a black flood.

        [i]‘This won’t work. The demons will wear us down… Oh, I got it! If we can repair the security system and bring back the defensive barriers, we can completely seal the defensive line and cut off the demons’ advance.’[/i]
 
        With that thought in his mind, Darwin immediately spun around, his voice low but resolute as he asked, “Newton, my boy, how well do you understand the institute’s security system?”

        “Headmaster Bacon dismantled it once before,” Newton replied. “If we have the parts… I should be able to reassemble it.”

        “Good. Then the task of repairing the system is yours.”

        “Me? Alone?” Newton froze.

        “I’ll be right beside you.” Darwin leapt down from the wall, his eyes already locked on the route toward the northern wing where the security system was located. “Now move, follow me!”

        The two dove into the chaos of the battlefield. Alerted by their movement, the demons prowling near the northern sector lunged toward them with furious howls.

        Darwin simply raised his left arm. The test tubes mounted on the metal rotary disk flared to life, glowing brilliantly as he absorbed the elements around him. Power concentrated in his legs, wrapping his muscles like chains. In the next instant, his body shot forward like a bolt of lightning, crashing into the charging demons. Several demons were sent flying away as he tore open a path. 

        “Go!” Darwin shouted.

        Gripping his weapon tightly, Newton followed close behind and watched as Darwin carved a safe road for him. They were nearly surrounded several times, but each time Darwin scooped the young scientist up without hesitation, carrying him through shattered ruins and seas of flame.

        Newton could hear his own heartbeat, intertwined with Darwin’s steady, powerful breathing. In such an apocalyptic predicament, he almost had a strange illusion that they were bound in a desperate communion of survival.

        At last, the northern wing came into view—but the demons had completely sealed off the final corridor leading to the security system. Darwin drew a deep breath. His eyes burned with a fiery resolve as he spoke in a low voice. “Hold tight.”

        BOOM! Darwin unleashed his power once more. Elements ignited as he accelerated, charging straight into the enemies.

        The clash sent numbing shocks through Newton’s arms, yet not once did he loosen his grip. Like an unyielding shield, Darwin endured every collision and cleaved through raging waves, blocking every attack head-on.

        At the end of the corridor, the thick doors of the control room stood right before them.

        Darwin set Newton down and shoved him forward, shouting, “Now! Get inside!”

        Newton unhesitantly dashed into the room, and the heavy doors slammed shut behind him.

        Once Newton safely entered the control room, Darwin turned back to face the surging horde of demons.

        A fierce wind whipped his tattered white coat. The test tubes on his metal arm flickered with an eerie glow. Darwin grinned and said, “Heh. Not a single one of you shall take another step forward!”

        The demons roared and charged at him. Still, he stood like an immovable bulwark, unmoved—not even the slightest—as wave after wave of enemies crashed against him…
STORY_2953:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 7

        “Thank you for saving my life. My name is Descartes. I’m a newly born machina.”

        “Machina?” Even the usually imperturbable Edison paused, surprised by the unfamiliar term. He stared at Descartes, a boy made of metal who only came up to his chest in height.

        Months earlier, Edison had received an invitation from the Lomond Manor, a scientific organization, to join them as a scientist. However, on the day of his arrival, he was attacked and knocked unconscious by unknown assailants. When he woke up, he found himself faced with a series of difficult challenges. 

        Only until afterwards did he learn that it had all been a test created by the Lomond Manor for newcomers. Nevertheless, his brilliant mind made him one of the qualified candidates, and eventually earned him a place on the subterranean exploration team.

        Today was supposed to be the day of their departure. Yet the unexpected struck—the institute’s security system had been compromised, and the demons, who had long been watching from the shadows, seized the opening of the disappearing defensive barriers and mounted a full-scale invasion. 

        To secure the progress of the subterranean exploration, Darwin, one of the golden scientists, volunteered to lead most of the other scientists in repelling the demons. Meanwhile, Galileo, another golden scientist and the exploration team leader, led Einstein, Edison, and Nicole into the underground to continue the mission.

        Following Nicole, the four scientists successfully avoided the mad beast, Behemoth, guarding the first level, and arrived at a ceremonial site on the second floor, where they heard cries the moment they stepped in.

        Edison, unafraid of the ghostly rumors, followed the calls to the pile of rubble and eventually rescued Descartes, a boy who had been buried beneath.

        “Yes, I’m a newly born machina. My name is Descartes.” Descartes said proudly, puffing up his small chest. His eyes shone with excitement.

        “Machina… to think I’d reunite with one again…” A clear and bright voice, filled with both nostalgia and excitement, suddenly spoke.

        Nicole looked at Einstein’s glowing chest in disbelief. “What... what is happening? Stein, why is your chest glowing? And it’s speaking too?”

        “That’s my teacher… Schrödinger. He saved my life in the past,” Einstein replied softly, his expression gentle as he looked down at the silver-blue glow emanating from his chest.

        “Schrödinger? The Schrödinger who founded the Lomond Manor?” Edison asked, wide-eyed.

        “Yes, I met him by accident years ago after he had left the Lomand Manor, and he became my teacher. But Copernicus sent assassins after him when he decided to return to the Lomond Manor. One of the assassins drove his blade through my heart, so Schrödinger transplanted his kinetic core into my body to save me,” Einstein explained.

        “The kinetic core!” Descartes emotionally interrupted, “So is that Schrödinger you mentioned a machina? Zana said that only the machinas have kinetic cores, and that the core is the heart of a machina; we die if it’s destroyed.”

        “That’s right. I am one of you,” Schrödinger’s voice echoed in the space.

        “Wait!” Galileo hastily broke into the reunion of the two machinas; her innate wariness left her unable to resist probing the intentions of this stranger. “Why did you found the Lomond Manor if you’re not a human? What is your true intention?”

        “My teacher has no ulterior motives. He founded the Lomond Manor simply to save his people and to preserve the peace of this land,” Einstein clarified.

        “Yes! This world will be a mess if Monesis is taken!” Descartes hurriedly nodded in agreement. He opened his bag and poured out a pile of complex metal circuits. “These are memory metals I’ve collected from all over this place. They hold the history of this underground city.”

        Edison picked up one of the circuits and examined it carefully. Only after a long moment did he murmur, “It requires special methods to activate it.”

        “Leave it to me. I’ll activate these circuits,” Schrödinger’s voice responded.

        Edison, Nicole, and Galileo quietly exchanged glances. Finally, Galileo, as the leader, nodded and handed the circuits to Einstein.

        Einstein held the circuits up to his glowing chest. As if guided by an invisible force, the circuits spread open and floated in midair. Countless fine threads made of elemental power extended from his chest, connecting to each circuit. As the circuits pulsed with brilliant light, several projections appeared, showing images of the past.

        From the fragmented memories, the scientists glimpsed the history of this underground city; they learned the mysterious existence of Monesis, the source of all things, another ominous power that lurked in the dark, and what sacrifices the machinas had made to protect the peace.

        “Ugh… What happened to the machinas was so sad…” Nicole, touched by the pain and sacrifice, burst into tears. Einstein gently patted her back to comfort her.

        “Well, there was no other way to keep Monesis safe and prevent  the terrifying power from awakening,” Edison said, sucking on his lollipop. He turned to Galileo and asked, “Dear Captain, what should we do next? Judging from these memories, it seems we don’t have a reason to continue our exploration.”

        “…Only by awakening the slumbering machinas can we turn the tide of this chaotic war,” Galileo said. After a brief moment of thought, she made up her mind and continued, “Let’s return to the surface and inform the Headmaster and everyone.”

        “Do you think they can resist the demons’ attack?” Nicole asked, concerned.

        “Don’t worry,” Galileo replied confidently. “Darwin is there, with our fellow scientists. They won’t lose to those vile demons.”

        Thus, the group began their journey back to the surface, with Descartes now part of the team. Thanks to Nicole’s abilities, they once again avoided the maddened Behemoth.

        Just as they neared the exit, Edison, who had been through countless perilous situations, felt a sudden premonition. As he expected, he soon spotted a faint flash of light in the distance. On high alert, he shouted, “Stop!”

        Everyone reflexively froze in place, and the next moment, a massive explosion occurred in front of them, leaving a deep crater in the ground ahead. Had Edison not called out, they might have been seriously injured or worse.

        “Ha, of course, such little tricks were not enough to kill the elite scientists of the Lomond Manor like you,” a voice sneered as the smoke cleared. Three cloaked figures appeared. The leader was a man whose eyes gleamed with patronizing admiration, his tone dripping with obvious condescension.

        “You’re… the Ashes of Life!” Galileo instantly recognized the emblem on the cloaks of the intruders.

        ‘I can’t believe it’s them…’  Shock flickered across Edison’s face before giving way to a sinister smile, one filled with anger and murderous intent. [i]‘I couldn’t protect the ones I cherished in the past, but now I’ve become stronger. I won’t let tragedy strike again’[/i]

        “Galileo, time is running out. Take the others and go! I’ll deal with them!” Edison shouted with a fierce look.

        “…Alright,” Galileo quickly assessed the situation and nodded. “Be careful!”

        Galileo decisively took Einstein and the others back toward the surface. The three intruders attempted to stop them, only to be blocked by a powerful electrical current that surged through the air.

        Edison took the lollipop out of his mouth and pointed the stick at the intruders. Golden lightning wrapped around his body as he declared in a commanding tone, “Ashes of Life… I, Edison, will be the one who crushes your schemes!”
STORY_2954:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 3

        When dawn broke over the Lomond Manor, the headquarters stood in brooding silence, as though even the air itself had frozen. The first light of morning fell over the institute like a veil of gauze, sliding across the ancient stone walls. It slipped past the carved window frames and gently streamed into one of the dormitories, setting the dust motes aglow in the quiet air.

        Within that gentle glow, a scientist, Galileo, stood before her desk, methodically gathering her belongings. Today marked the departure of the subterranean exploration mission. As the leader, she understood better than anyone that even the smallest oversight could determine the result of their mission.

        Several months earlier, she had been assigned to lead the first subterranean exploration. Though she had made it back alive, part of her body had been mechanicalized; the transformation almost cost her life. Even so, neither she nor the other scientists withdrew from the mission in fear. On the contrary, their resolve only hardened. They reworked the plan. To recruit more promising teammates, they even created a covert test—simulated crises designed to force candidates to unleash their latent potential under extreme pressure.  In the end, only four had passed, earning their places on this expedition.

        Originally, the second exploration should have followed immediately, but it was delayed as one of Lomond Manor’s headmasters, Copernicus, had attempted to shatter the boundary between realms using elemental forces. Numerous scientists joined forces to stop Copernicus’s ambition, and the incident, at last, ended with the headmaster’s death. It was after countless hours and resources lost to the aftermath that they were finally able to continue their exploration.

        When Galileo was about to leave with her meticulously checked backpack, her gaze caught on a photo frame atop her desk. She paused, turned back, and picked it up. The edges of the photograph, yellowed and curled, bore proof of time. The image showed a man in worn clothing. His brows held stubborn determination, and behind his smile lay an exhaustion he could not conceal.

        He was Galileo’s father—a man who had devoted his entire life to becoming a scientist capable of changing the world. Yet, he had failed due to a lack of talent, and in the end, he had chosen to end his life.

        In Galileo’s memories, her father was always bent over his desk or standing in the garden, gazing up at the stars while speaking of unreachable truths. His obsession with ideals pushed him into an abyss he could not climb out of, leaving him condemned and scorned by countless others, even long after his death.

        “Father…” Galileo murmured, her fingertips tracing the outline of his face. “I won’t follow your path. I will achieve something great, something brilliant.”

        She set the frame down and strode into the central hall, where more than a dozen scientists were already assembled. Under her direction, they then began checking instruments and protective equipment.

        “Headmaster, all preparations are complete,” Galileo reported to the man standing at the center of the hall. He was Michelangelo, one of the three headmasters managing the Lomond Manor. He stood in an upright posture, but his eyes somehow seemed lost—distracted, absent-minded. The faint haze in his gaze made Galileo’s heart tighten, her brow creasing into a frown.

        “Headmaster?” she called in puzzlement. Michelangelo blinked, seemingly startled, then asked, “What is it?”

        “We’re ready for depar—”

        Boom!

        An explosion cut her off. All in an instant, the hall was plunged into chaos: the floor trembled violently; instruments collided, shrieking as metal scraped against metal. It felt as though the air itself had been torn apart. Faces blanched as panic rippled through the room. 

        A scientist covered in dust staggered in, his breath coming in broken bursts, terror plain in his eyes.

        “The demons… The demons are here!”

        “That’s impossible!” Galileo said, her brow furrowing. “The institute is surrounded by defensive barriers. They can’t have breached them!”

        “The system’s been destroyed!” the scientist cried, his voice shaking. “They’ve already broken through the outer defenses!” 

        Everything fell apart in an instant. Some swore under their breath, others instinctively stepped back, and a few clutched their weapons.

        Michelangelo raised his voice to quell the chaos. “I now call off the subterranean exploration! Repel the demons. Guard our institute. This is our only priority!”

        “No!” Galileo’s voice was sharp as a blade. “Now that the demons are coming for us, delaying the exploration will only leave our future even more precarious!”

        “We still have another option,” Michelangelo said solemnly. “We seek aid from the gods. They have approached me before and are willing to offer us support.”

        All of a sudden, the hall broke into hushed whispers. Galileo was stunned. As far as she recalled, Michelangelo had always been the most distrustful of those aloof, high-handed gods.

        “Even so, we cannot rely entirely on the gods,”  Galileo countered calmly. “We must become stronger. Only then can we defend our dignity.”

        “And for that dignity, you’re willing to wager the entire institute—the lives of all the scientists here—on the unknown?” Michelangelo questioned.

        “I…” Galileo clenched her teeth. She had no hesitation to put her own life at risk, but she also knew it was not her place to decide for everyone else.

        “Then we do both,” said Darwin, a golden scientist, his voice brimming with confidence. “We’ll split into two teams: one goes underground with Galileo, the other follows me to repel the demons.”

        “Agree.” Edison, a newly recruited scientist, grinned casually with a lollipop between his lips. “We’re all once-in-a-generation geniuses here. So why not just take everything we want?”

        “I’m fine as long as I get to be with Stein!” said Nicole, another new scientist, holding onto Einstein’s arm.

        “Then Einstein, Nicole, and Edison, you’re coming with me on the subterranean exploration,” Galileo decisively said, then she turned to Michelangelo and asked, “Would that be okay, Headmaster?”

        Although her words came dressed as a question, her voice brooked no refusal. Michelangelo fell silent. Beside them, Socrates, finding the atmosphere unbearingly strained, decided to speak up, “Headmaster, time is short. You need to make a decision.”

        Pressed by Socrates, Michelangelo finally spoke. “…Very well. Go.”

        Galileo cast Michelangelo a meaningful glance. Without saying a word, she turned and led her group to the underground entrance, once again stepping into that strange and uncanny land of eternal darkness.

        As Galileo stared at the path ahead, one from which there was no turning back, a cold flame ignited within her chest.

        [i]‘This time, I will find it—the key to change the fate of humanity!’[/i]
STORY_2955:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 1

        “Marie, congratulations on your promotion to Silver Scientist.” A researcher looked at Marie Curie, who had just entered the room, a smile spreading across his face as he congratulated her. The other researchers followed suit, praising her achievements. Yet, Marie felt no joy in their words. Instead, she felt a nagging sense of frustration, a feeling she couldn’t quite name. Still, her upbringing had taught her never to wear her heart on her sleeve. So, she suppressed her feelings and thanked them politely before walking over to her desk.

        There, resting on the desk, was a fine brocade box. Inside of which rested a silver badge, a symbol of her new rank—a silver scientist. But as Marie held it in her hand, the badge felt heavy, like a weighty chunk of lead that pressed down on her chest with unanswered questions and anger.

        She still remembered vividly what happened in that “promotion test”.

        Months ago, Marie, as a bronze scientist, had been tasked with arranging an orientation session for the new scientists. However, someone ambushed the group and knocked all of them unconscious. When they awoke, they found themselves in a strange laboratory. There, she met Edison, one of the newcomers, and Socrates, the silver scientist.

        Together, the three of them had navigated a series of difficult trials, only to discover, at the end, that the entire ordeal had been a setup. Socrates and the other scientists had known it was all a test—except for her, for the whole event had been designed for her promotion.

        And so, she somehow ended up becoming a silver scientist. However, the promotion didn’t bring her joy, but only an inexplicable rage, and that anger finally erupted when she looked at the badge.

        [i]“I didn’t earn this... I have to return it!”[/i]

        With that thought, Marie stood abruptly. She strode out of the room, headed straight for Michelangelo’s office. When she arrived, she caught sight of a scene that shocked her through the crack in the door—

        Michelangelo lay slumped over his desk, weak and barely conscious. Socrates stood beside him, his hand outstretched. The back of his hand glowed with a brilliant golden light that exuded an almost palpable force. Marie immediately sensed the danger in the air. Without thinking, she grabbed the small knife she carried for self-defense and threw it at Socrates.

        The blade whizzed through the air, but Socrates dodged it effortlessly. Still, the attack forced him back a step, temporarily easing Michelangelo’s crisis.

        “Marie...” Socrates turned around to see her standing at the door. A look of embarrassment and regret crossed his face, but it quickly disappeared.

        “Socrates, what are you doing?” Marie asked, her voice sharp and demanding.

        Only after a long pause did Socrates finally speak. “As you can see… I have to control Michelangelo to seek justice for myself.” 

        “Why?” Marie’s voice trembled with disbelief. “This isn’t who you are!”

        “I just never had the chance before,” Socrates said, looking Marie straight in the eye. Even in her wrath, she remained the one who moved his heart. He then continued, “Everyone lives for themselves and for those they care about, Marie. Only by breaking the rule can I get what I want.”

        “Don’t try to justify your actions! This is betrayal!”  Marie retorted sharply. “Socrates, if you stop now, I can still plead for you.”

        “No. It’s too late now. There was no going back from the moment I agreed to work with him.” Socrates’s voice was calm, resolute. “For me, it’s either everything through victory—or nothing in death.”

        “No,” Marie said coldly. “I’ll stop you. And you’ll pay for what you’ve done in prison.”

        With those words, Marie drew her knife and sliced open her sleeve. She channeled her power to activate a refined paralytic agent in her skin that could freeze anyone through the air.

        Socrates, realizing her plan, immediately held his breath. He stepped forward in an attempt to subdue her. But he hesitated; his reluctance to harm her slowed him down. 

        Time slipped away in the space of his hesitation. Having held his breath for too long, Socrates felt his strength beginning to fail, and Marie took advantage of his pause. She sent him crashing to the floor with a swift sweep of her leg.

        But as she prepared to strike the final blow, a brilliant light flared from the back of Socrates’s hand. A translucent figure appeared before her. His commanding godly power pressed down on her, locking her in place.

        “You’re... a god…” Marie gasped, struggling to speak.

        “Foolish mortal,” the translucent figure—Zeus, the King of the Holy Gods—spoke. “How dare you try to sabotage my plan!”

        “So... you and him... You’ve sided with the gods?” Marie asked, her voice shaking with disbelief as she looked at Socrates. But the man stood silent, his head lowered in shame, avoiding her gaze.

        “Yes,” Zeus said. “He became one of us, to claim unimaginable power.”

        “Hah, such a beautiful way of putting it,” Marie spat, her disdain for the gods apparent in every syllable. “He’s nothing more than your lapdog.”

        “How dare you, mortal! To speak so arrogantly before me!” Zeus roared. With his godly power pulsing, he raised his hand as if to strike her.

        “Stop! Don’t hurt her!” Socrates shouted, rushing forward to intervene.

        “For the sake of our partnership, I will spare her life. But I will not allow her to disrupt our plans again.” Zeus declared, his hand raised high as he summoned his power. Although Marie resisted with every ounce of her will, she began to feel her strength ebbing away. Zeus’s presence bore down on her, completely suppressing her resistance.

        [i]‘Damn it… I can’t give up... I have to expose their scheme…’[/i]

        Unfortunately, the force proved too overwhelming for her to endure, and soon, her body gave way under the weight of his power. Her vision faded to black as she sank into unconsciousness…
STORY_2956:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 2

        Inside the brightly lit conference room at the Lomond Manor headquarters, Socrates, a silver scientist, sat among more than a dozen scientists around the long table. He looked calm, yet his gaze unconsciously drifted to the empty seat that should have belonged to Marie Curie.

        Just then, a tall woman entered the room. Her name was Galileo, a golden scientist, and the leader of this operation. She switched on a magic projector, and an incomplete map shimmered into view on the wall, showing the destination of their mission: a mysterious world hidden deep beneath the earth.

        Several months earlier, the Lomond Manor had issued invitations far and wide, seeking scientists with exceptional potential. Through a rigorous test, four outstanding candidates had been selected to join this exploration.

        Galileo began outlining the tactical deployment and objectives, carefully briefing each scientist on the risks and points of attention. When the meeting concluded, she deliberately asked Socrates to stay behind. 

        “Is something wrong?” Socrates asked. A flicker of caution passed through his eyes, gone almost as soon as it appeared.

        With a note of concern, Galileo asked,  “Is Marie still unwell?”

        “Yes. She’s still running a high fever. She’ll need a few more days to rest.”

        “I see…” A small frown betrayed Galileo’s disappointment. Still, she nodded understandingly. “That’s unfortunate. She was supposed to join this operation. We would’ve set out long ago if it weren’t for what happened with Copernicus… Just take good care of her.”

        “Don’t worry. I will,” Socrates replied. He turned and left the meeting room, his footsteps steady as he made his way to the dormitory, where he stopped in front of Marie Curie’s door. He placed his hand against it and began channeling his power. A magic circle that symbolized a barrier spell appeared beneath his palm, then shattered into fragments.

        He gently pushed open the door. The room was dim, unlit. The air was unnaturally still, cold in a way as though no one lived there. He turned his gaze to the large bed at the center of the room, on which Marie—whom he had just claimed was bedridden with a fever—lay, her wrists and ankles bound by chains. The metal bore intricate runes designed to suppress her magic power.

        Not long ago, Socrates had yielded to the temptation of Zeus, the King of Holy Gods, and agreed to be his spy. He had acted on Zeus’s order, trying to brainwash Michelangelo, one of Lomond Manor’s headmasters, only to be caught by Marie at the very moment he struck.

        Despite Marie’s effort to stop him, she had been subdued by Zeus’s godly power. And to prevent Zeus from harming her further, Socrates had no choice but to imprison her in her room with a magic barrier spell that cut off all sound and contact.

        Though Marie looked weak, her eyes were sharp as blades, fearless as she looked at him directly. She asked coldly, “Are you going to kill me?”

        “No. I won’t kill you; I will never hurt you.”

        “And this is what you mean by not hurting me? Tying me and locking me up in my room?”

        “Zeus will not spare you if you get in his way again,” he said.

        “Heh.” Marie let out a quiet, scornful laugh. “And you think obeying every word he says will earn you mercy and trust? Don’t be naïve. He’s just using you; you’re nothing more than a convenient tool to him.”

        “I know,” Socrates replied, his voice calm and steady, tinged with a bitterness so faint it was almost imperceptible. “I’ve always known.” 

        Marie froze, unable to understand the despair underlying his words.

        Instead of explaining his reason, Socrates walked to the window and gazed at the distant, flickering light. They reminded him of the bonfires during festivals in his homeland—brilliant, alive, full of warmth. Yet, those days would never return, for his homeland had already been reduced to scorched earth.

        Alone. Forsaken. Without reason.

        Only after a long silence did he finally speak, “I… I never dreamed of being a hero. Nor did I want to be a traitor. But this world has long since strayed from reason… Justice, truth, knowledge—they’ve all become tools of power.” 

        “That’s the reason why you betray everything and let the gods decide our fate?”Marie growled through her clenched teeth. “Your plan won’t succeed! Galileo and the others will expose you. They’ll stop you, and you will fail!”

        A complicated emotion flickered through Socrates’ eyes. He looked at her quietly. A faint smile touched his lips as he replied calmly, “If that is how it ends, then so be it. At least I won’t have to keep hiding anymore.”

        “You…” His answer left Marie momentarily speechless.

        “In this game of chess, I’m nothing more than a puppet worked by fate,” he murmured.         “If I’m exposed, perhaps I’ll finally be free… free to reunite with my people.”

        With those cryptic words, Socrates turned and left. Back in his room, memories of his homeland came flooding back, again and again. That night, he sat in his chair, dwelling in the past, until the faintest trace of dawn appeared on the horizon. Only then did he rise and walk out of the dormitory.

        He passed through the northern corridor and entered the north wing. Past the heavy doors, a spiral staircase carried him down to the heart of the security systems at the bottom.

        He placed his silver scientist badge against the identification panel. [i]Beep.[/i] The door unlocked, revealing a network of metal conduits filled with flowing elemental energy that sustained the Lomond Manor’s defensive barrier. He raised his hand and gathered his power, aiming at the device—

        Boom!

        A thunderous crack resonated outside the institute as the device was destroyed. Like shattering glass, the translucent barrier around the Lomond Manor collapsed in an instant, leaving it completely vulnerable.

        Suddenly, the mark on the back of Socrates’ hand released a brilliant burst of golden light.

        A figure with divine authority far beyond that of mortals emerged from the radiance. It was Zeus, King of the Holy Gods.

        “Well done, Socrates,” Zeus said, his tone laced with patronizing praise. “The demons will not miss this opening, and when they come with dire threats, we gods shall descend in the name of salvation. All humans will kneel before us, weeping with gratitude.”

        Zeus laughed, as though victory were already in his grasp.

        Socrates merely stood there in silence, like a detached observer.

        His future had been shrouded in despair and darkness the moment he learned that his homeland lay in ruins. He had lost his home. All the hope he once held had shattered into a thousand pieces.

        To him, this deal with Zeus was nothing more than a desperate gamble. Even if he were to be remembered as a traitor, he would see it through to the end, hoping that, somewhere along the way, this world would give him an answer to the unreasonable destruction of his innocent homeland…
STORY_2957:
Finale of Gifted Scientists - Ch. 6

        A party of four, two men and two women, slowly made their way through a vast underground space by the light of the flickering lanterns. Their footsteps echoed clearly through the silence. Among the ground, a red-haired girl surveyed her surroundings with curiosity and excitement. Finally, her awe broke through as she exclaimed, “Wow! This place is amazing! So it’s true… the mysterious civilization beneath the earth exists!”

        “Quiet,” the purple-haired woman walking ahead snapped, her voice cold as she shot daggers at the redhead, “We are not here for sightseeing. We bear the hope of humanity, here to find a way to defeat the demons.”

        Yet, the girl paid it no mind. Dismissing it with a mischievous smile, she suddenly wrapped her arms around the purple-haired woman’s and said with excitement, “Oh, I know, I know! But Gali, you’re always so serious—aren’t you tired of that?”

        The red-haired girl’s name was Nicole. Months earlier, she had received an invitation from the Lomond Manor, a scientific organization, to join them as a scientist. However, on the day of her arrival,  she was attacked and knocked unconscious by unknown assailants—but in truth, it had all been a test created by the Lomond Manor for newcomers. It was after a series of difficult trials that Nicole became one of the qualified candidates, eventually earning a place on the subterranean exploration team.

        Today was supposed to be the day of their departure. Yet the unexpected struck—the institute’s security system had been compromised, and the demons, who had long been watching from the shadows, seized the opening of the disappearing defensive barriers and mounted a full-scale invasion. To secure the progress of the subterranean exploration, Darwin, one of the golden scientists, volunteered to lead most of the other scientists in repelling the demons, while Galileo, the purple-haired woman—a golden scientist and the leader of the expedition—led Einstein, Edison, and Nicole into the underground to continue the mission.

        “Yeah, who knows how long will this exploration take us. You’ll have to relax at some point. Here, have a candy!” The brown-haired scientist, Edison, took out a piece of candy from his pocket and offered it to Galileo, only to be completely ignored.

        With a solemn expression, Galileo scanned the three new scientists.

        “Don’t underestimate this place. It’s far more dangerous than you think,” she warned, rolling up her sleeve to reveal an arm now made of metal. “The last time we came down here, we encountered a mad beast and nearly lost our lives. So keep your wits about you unless you want to end up like me!”

        “Ugh! I don’t want to turn into metal!” Nicole gasped in horror. She quickly pulled out a pair of mechanical glasses from her bag and put them on. Then, she pressed her hands to the ground and said earnestly, “I’ll find us a way out! We won’t run into that mad beast!”

        Closing her eyes, Nicole began channeling her power to let her mind resonate with the elements. Behind her eyelids, the darkness shimmered with flowing hues, constructing a network of layered signals. However, the subterranean world housed such abundant elements that the information was far more than her thoughts could contain. A splitting headache overtook her as soon as she made the connection, and a warm, nauseous liquid began to seep from her nostrils.

        “Nicole!” Einstein, the white-haired boy, cried out in alarm as he saw her nose bleed.

        “I... I can do it!” Nicole gritted her teeth, enduring the pain as she kept probing. Finally, she found a safe path just before her mind almost broke down.

        “I found it!” Nicole exclaimed, lifting her head with joy as she cut off the connection. Someone offered a handkerchief to her.

        It was Galileo, her tone surprisingly gentle as she said, “Well done. Here, wipe your nose.”

        “Th-thank you...” Nicole, flattered and surprised, took the handkerchief and wiped the blood from her nose before leading the way forward. They navigated through several forks, carefully avoiding the slumbering mad beast Behemoth, until they finally found the staircase leading deeper underground and entered the next floor.

        “This place… It seems like a place for ceremonies…” said Einstein as he looked around, his voice filled with uncertainty.

        “Shh!” Suddenly, Galileo raised a finger to her lips, signaling for silence. She closed her eyes and tilted her head slightly to listen more closely. After a moment, she opened her eyes and whispered, “The calls are coming from the left.”

        “I-is it a ghost?” Nicole’s face instantly turned pale. She grabbed Einstein’s arm and shrieked, “Stein! Protect me!”

        “Uh... Okay.” Einstein said resignedly, patting Nicole’s hand to calm her nerves.

        “You’re all making too much of a fuss,” Edison said with a nonchalant shrug. “I’m not scared of ghosts; living people are far scarier.”

        With his hands in his pockets, he followed the sound of the calls and soon arrived before a pile of rubble. Gathering elemental power in his right foot, he kicked it with all his might.

        Boom! His kick blasted away the heavy debris, revealing a figure buried beneath—a boy entirely made of metal, the one who made all the calls.

        “Phew...” Small stones and sand fell from the boy as he sat up and said, “Thank you for saving my life. My name is Descartes. I’m a newly born machina.”
STORY_2958:
Dusk in the abandoned district always arrived in gray. The sky looked forever powdered with dust, and even the wind carried a sour breath of rust and rot.

        In one of the narrow, filthy alleyways, a small girl, like a little explorer setting foot in unknown lands, wandered through shards of broken glass and soggy cardboard with a giant fly in her arms. Curiosity glimmered in her bright eyes.

        The girl’s name was Beelzebub. She had been abandoned by her parents and left to starve until a boy named Abadon found her and pulled her back from the brink of death. From that day on, Beelzebub clung to Abadon like a stubborn little shadow, and as days passed, the two became each other’s only family, struggling side by side to survive in this barren realm.

        Today, the two had split up to search for food, and it was not after an entire morning of scavenging that Beelzebub finally found something.

        “Oh, something’s over there… something shiny!” She exclaimed, pointing at a glass bottle sticking out from behind a broken barrel. She darted toward it and picked it up. Lifting it into the light, she squinted to look at what was inside—a liquid, glimmering softly like molten gold.

        The giant fly circled the bottle excitedly and began buzzing, “It smells so good! Feels like we could drink it!”

        “No!” Beelzebub hugged the bottle tightly to her chest. “We have to wait for Brother. Beelzebub wants to drink it together with Brother.”

        Her eyes shone with pure satisfaction; she had never found anything that felt this much like a treasure since she had started scavenging.

        When she returned to their shabby house, Abadon still hadn’t come back. She carefully set the bottle atop a pile of rubble, wiped the dust from its surface, then plopped down on the floor and stared at the giant fly.

        “Brother will definitely be happy when he sees this…” she said, smiling to herself.

        “But it smells so good…” the fly whined, licking at the corner of its mouth. “Are you sure you don’t want to take a little sip?”

        Beelzebub scrunched up her nose. “No! Not until Brother comes back—”

        However, before she could finish, the giant fly lunged forward and popped the cork. Its fuzzy legs fumbled for a grip but failed. The bottle slipped. The golden content spilled out in a sudden rush, splashing all over Beelzebub and soaking her clothes.

        “Waaah— You big dumb bug!”

        She frantically tried to wipe it off, but the stain only smeared further. A faint sweetness rose from her skin and slipped into her nose. Then, an unusual heat pooled in her throat and began spreading through her entire body. She blinked, only to find the world slowly swaying.

        Just then, footsteps sounded outside.

        It was Abadon. A wave of humid, fermented sweetness hit him in the face as he pushed open the door. He frowned and looked toward Beelzebub to see her drenched. Worry tightened his voice as he asked, “Beelzebub, why are you all wet? You’ll catch a cold.”

        Hearing him, Beelzebub slowly lifted her head. Her cheeks were flushed, her eyes unfocused.

        “Brother… you’re back…” Her voice melted into a whisper. She took a shaky step forward and collapsed straight into his arms.

        “Careful…” Abadon steadied her. Sensing something was wrong, he hurriedly asked, “Did you drink something?”

        “No… Beelzebub didn’t drink anything… ” She murmured and nuzzled into his chest. Her breath was thick with fruity sweetness. “I just… feel hot… and Brother… your body is so cool…”

        Abadon froze. He should have pushed her away, but he couldn’t. Her warmth seeped through his clothes, straight into his chest, burning in a way he didn’t understand.

        “You stupid girl…” he muttered under his breath.

        Beelzebub lifted her head. Her eyes sparkled as she gazed up at him. “Brother… do you hate Beelzebub?”

        “Of course not.”

        “Then… can you give me another hug?”

        Abadon’s throat tightened. His heartbeat grew loud in his ears. A strange, unfamiliar urge stirred inside him, prompting him to get a little closer. Yet, he swallowed hard and forced it down, simply wrapping his arms around her.

        While the wind was howling outside, the house was so quiet that only their breathing could be heard. The giant fly had long since curled up in the corner, snoring softly.

        After a while, Beelzebub shifted in his arms and murmured, “Brother… you smell nice… Umm, comfy…”

        Her words trailed off as she fell asleep against his chest.

        Abadon looked down at her, his gaze filled with immense tenderness. He gently brushed her hair aside, but didn’t dare to give another touch.

        “You really are impossible…” he murmured, a helpless smile tugging at his lips. Gently, he lifted her into his arms and laid her on the bed of tattered cloth.

        Night deepened. The wind in the abandoned district continued its endless wail.

        Abadon sat beside Beelzebub. As he watched her peaceful sleeping face, something stirred quietly in his chest, something he couldn’t say in words. In the end, he only let out a resigned sigh and buried those feelings deep in silence…
STORY_2959:
The night slowly deepened. Wind poured down from the distant mountains into the forested depths, brushing through Ursula’s hair as she and Novalis followed the moss-laced road in silence, walking one behind the other. Neither spoke a word, and in that hush, the humming of Dracospirits echoed all the more clearly through the night.

        Ursula and Novalis were both victims of a horrible experiment that made children into vessels to house the ethereal dragons’ powers. Ursula used to live with other children inside a camp built by wizards. But one day, Novalis broke into the camp in a frenzy, intent on tearing everything apart. Ursula stepped forward to stop him from hurting her friends—and in doing so, saved him from the chaos consuming his mind. Afterward, they decided to travel together, setting out to trace the footsteps of the primordial dragons…

        One day, they departed before the sky had fully changed color. Partway along the path, Novalis suddenly stopped and stared ahead, where a mother bird with a broken wing lay beneath the gnarled roots of a withered tree. Blood stained her feathers, and in her dying eyes was a hollow reflection of the vast, cloudless sky.

        Following his gaze, Ursula gasped, “The bird must have fallen from the tree!”

        “She won’t survive.” Novalis’s voice was calm as he raised a hand, dark elements gathering in his palm. “At least… I can end her pain.”

        “No! Don’t kill her!” Ursula rushed in front of him. A pale blue glow spread from her hands as water elements flowed between her fingers, seeping gently into the mother bird’s wounds. The bird’s breathing gradually steadied, but her wings still drooped.

        “You’re only prolonging her suffering,” Novalis said coldly.

        “Ma-maybe… but at least…” Ursula lowered her eyes, her voice soft yet resolute. “At least I’m here to stay with her.”

        Gold eyes met crimson. Two beliefs collided in a silent standoff. At last, Novalis lowered his hand and turned away.

        “You’re too naive, Ursula. The world isn’t as good as you think.”

        The days slowly passed as they remained in the forest. Every day, Ursula used elements to heal the mother bird’s wounds and fed her flower nectar. She slowed their journey—only to guard that fragile, fading breath.

        Novalis always watched from a short distance. He watched her cradle what little life remained in her hands; he watched her hum a gentle tune at night to soothe that weakened soul. 

        He saw Ursula cradle what little life remained in her hands. He saw her hum softly at night, soothing the weakened soul. Finally, he couldn’t help but ask, “Why are you so persistent?”

        “Because she still wants to live,” Ursula replied.

        “No,” Novalis said. “It’s you who refuses to let her die.”

        Ursula didn’t argue. She simply continued feeding the bird, her fingers trembling.

        Yet the mother bird’s breath grew weaker by the day. She stopped eating. Even elemental power could no longer sustain her life. Tears welled in Ursula’s eyes as she stroked the frail bird.

        Suddenly, a clear, piercing birdcall rang out from the sky.

        Ursula abruptly looked up to see a male bird dive down from the clouds. His cry cut through the forest, filled with worry and joy.

        The mother bird struggled to get up. Yet, her broken wings could no longer lift her into the air. With the last of her strength, she lunged upward, only to fall back to the ground. Still, she chirped softly, again and again, calling to her counterpart.

        The male bird landed beside her. Pressing against each other, the two love birds rubbed their beaks and feathers. Their cries intertwined, as if singing out the joy of reunion.

        Ursula watched, breath caught in her throat as tears shimmered in her eyes. “She… she’s smiling.”

        However, that fragile joy did not last until morning. When the male bird’s mournful cries echoed in the silent forest, Ursula jolted awake and ran toward the sound. Still, it was too late. The mother bird was dead. There she lay quietly, wings neatly folded, the corners of her beak curved faintly upward, as though she were wearing a smile.

        Ursula burst into tears, still clutching the unused herbs in her hand.

        Novalis stepped to her side, his voice low as he said, “See? Your kindness didn’t change the outcome.”

        “No.” Ursula slowly lifted her head. Tears filled her eyes, but so did light. “At least she saw the one she loved. She didn’t die alone.”  

        “You’re just seeking comfort for yourself.”

        “But that comfort,” Ursula said softly, “is the meaning of life.”

        The wind passed between the two, scattering loose feathers across the ground.  After burying the mother bird, Ursula watched as the male bird spread his wings and flew into the sky. While she stood there for a long time, Novalis remained silent, standing behind her. It was the only way he knew to offer what little comfort he could.

        After that, they simply resumed their journey in silence. There was no more argument. When night fell, moonlight stretched their shadows long across the ground.

        Walking at the back, Ursula looked at the boy’s figure and murmured inwardly:

        [i]‘Someday, I’ll make you understand the meaning of life. Death is not only an end; it is also proof of love. If even sorrow is deemed meaningless, then what value does living hold at all?’[/i]
STORY_2960:
At the first light of dawn, a girl of fifteen or sixteen walked quietly up to the school gates. She glanced left, then right. Only after making sure no one was around did she dart out from the shadows, moving quickly and quietly across the campus like a skillful ninja. Light on her feet, she made her way down to an underground classroom, pausing at the door to check inside before slipping in.


        [i]‘Third row, fourth seat… this is it!’[/i]

        Her eyes moved across the desks, counting under her breath. When she finally found her target, she let out a small breath of relief and hurried over. A faint blush spread across her fair cheeks as she opened the drawer and carefully placed a beautifully wrapped box inside. Then she turned and quickly left the room, waiting in a hidden corner nearby.

        [i]‘I wonder what kind of face Enoch will make when he sees it…’[/i]

        Anticipation bubbled in her chest as she waited. But time passed slowly, too slowly. Between the long wait and how early she’d woken up, her eyelids began to droop. Before she knew it, she had curled up against the wall and fallen asleep.

        As a witch of Kremier, Ingrid had known her fate since childhood. Her life was meant for one purpose—to die for someone. And that person was a student at this school, Enoch.

        When Ingrid first learned of her destiny, she couldn’t accept it. She refused to become some offering to fate. At one point, she had even tried to kill him, hoping to break the prophecy. But she failed. And ironically, Enoch was the one who saved her.

        That moment changed her mind. She stopped trying to kill him. Instead, she began watching him.

        Sometimes, love comes in the least expected way. At first, it was just curiosity. And somewhere along the way, it became something else. Before Ingrid realized it, she had found herself drawn to this somewhat clumsy but kind boy. With the feelings growing day by day, she had decided to sneak into school this very day—on Valentine’s Day—to tell him how she felt with a box of chocolate.

        “Enoch! You’re late today!” A loud voice jolted Ingrid awake.

        “I overslept,” a gentle voice replied. “I was up studying magic last night.”

        [i]‘Enoch! He’s here!’[/i] Now fully awake, Ingrid quickly peeked out from her hiding spot. There, she saw Enoch walk into the classroom. He went straight to his seat and began sorting through his drawer like it was any other day.

        Ingrid held her breath, her heart racing with excitement as she waited for Enoch to find her gift. But the reaction she expected didn’t come. Enoch simply sat down. Just as confusion crept in, someone voiced the question.

        “Hey, Enoch,” the boy sitting next to Enoch shouted. “It’s Valentine’s Day. Did you get any chocolate?”

        “Oh, it’s today? That explains why everyone’s acting so differently.” Enoch blinked in realization. Then he shook his head and said, “No. I didn’t get any.”

        [i]‘WHAT? Where’s my box of chocolate?’[/i] Ingrid’s eyes widened in disbelief. The shock quickly gave way to anger. [i]‘Someone must’ve taken it while I was asleep… I will find out who did it!’[/i]

        She untied the ribbon from her hair—what was left after she’d used it on the gift—and drew her wand. With a soft whisper, she cast a spell. Light gathered in front of her, forming into a butterfly that flew toward the forest with a gentle flutter.

        Ingrid followed it. Deep among the trees, she found the culprit: a small rabbit spirit lay curled up in the grass, fast asleep. Around it were the torn remains of her gift box. Smears of chocolate stained its mouth. There was no room for doubt.

        “Mm…?” The rabbit stirred as Ingrid approached. It blinked sleepily, rubbing its sticky eyes before looking up at her in confusion. “W-Who are you…?”

        “So it was you who stole my chocolate…” Ingrid crossed her arms, glaring down at the confused rabbit. Her voice tightened with restrained irritation. “It seems you need someone to teach you a lesson!”

        Ingrid grabbed both the rabbit’s cheeks and pulled. She pulled so hard that the rabbit gave a grimace of pain. With tears brimming in its eyes, it flailed and begged for mercy: “Ow—ow! I-I’m sorry! I’m sorry!”

        Ingrid huffed. It was after a moment longer that she finally released her grip. The rabbit sniffled miserably as it clutched its reddened cheeks. But Ingrid, standing firm as stone, simply demanded, “Why did you take my chocolate?”

        “I-I was hungry…” the rabbit whimpered. Its voice broke with guilt as it started crying again. “And it smelled really good… I couldn’t help it… I’m sorry…”

        Ingrid let out a long sigh; all her anger had faded when she saw the tears. She gave its head a small, awkward pat, looking away as she spoke, “W-well… My chocolate’s already gone, and getting mad won’t fix anything. But if you help me make another one… I’ll let it go.”

        “R-Really?” The rabbit stopped crying, its eyes shining as it looked up at her. 

        “Yeah,” Ingrid said, trying to keep a stern face. “So stop crying and come with me. We don’t have time to waste.”

“Okay!”

        And so, the two of them worked together to make a new batch of chocolate. Although it took a while, eventually, they finished and carefully wrapped it in another box. At lunchtime, the rabbit slipped into the classroom and quietly placed the chocolate into Enoch’s drawer while no one was paying attention, just as Ingrid had instructed.

        Afternoon classes were about to begin. When Enoch reached into his drawer for his book, he paused. His fingers hit something hard. He pulled it out to see a box neatly wrapped in paper, through which he detected the sweet scent of chocolate.

        “Whoa! Valentine’s chocolate!” The boy next to him slammed his hands on the desk and leaned over, eyes wide. His voice was so filled with excitement that his words came almost like a shout: “Enoch, you actually got some? That’s unbelievable! Who’s it from?”

        Startled, Enoch leaned back slightly. He opened the box. Inside was chocolate—and nothing else.

        “Well… I don’t know,” he said. “There’s no note.”

        “Huh? Who leaves Valentine’s chocolate without a note?” His classmate slumped back into his seat, disappointed.

        “But I actually find it quite amusing,” Enoch said with a shy smile, his voice soft and sincere. “Although I don’t know who it’s from… I’m really happy that I got it.”

        A quiet laugh slipped out of Ingrid’s lips as she eavesdropped on the whole conversation with magic in her hiding spot. Those simple words brought a soft smile that lit her face.

        Beside her, the rabbit tilted its head, confused. After a moment, it finally asked: “Why didn’t you tell him it was from you?”

        The question pulled Ingrid out of her happy bubbles. Her smile faded. With a complicated expression, she said, “…Because I haven’t found a way to change my fate yet.”

        “Huh?” The rabbit blinked, not fully understanding. Nevertheless, it gave her its earnest wishes. “Well… Then I hope you find it soon.”

        Unfortunately, Ingrid never found that answer. Even so, she decided to face the boy she loved, quietly waiting on a miracle…
STORY_2961:
Deep within a fungal forest, where the canopy swallowed most of the sunlight, a young woman made her way along the shadowed path with a three-tailed tuxedo cat nestled comfortably in her arms.

        “Once we cross that little stream up ahead, we’ll be at the Kerales’ village, meow,” said the cat, Panther, a Kerales. He sounded immensely pleased with himself, as though bringing his master into his home was the greatest achievement imaginable.

        “But is it really all right for you to bring a stranger into your village?” Ingrid lowered her gaze toward him. There was a hint of hesitation in her voice. As a witch of Kremier, she knew better than to walk uninvited into another person’s home, let alone a hidden village like the Kerales’. After all, every clan had its own rules.

        The moment she finished speaking, Panther shot back in fierce protest.

        “What stranger? You’re not a stranger, meow!” Panther snapped his head up, his eyes wide with pure outrage, looking as if he had just suffered the greatest injustice of his life. “You’re the master I chose myself, meow!”

        Panther had wanted nothing to do with becoming a witch’s companion, but he changed his mind and chose Ingrid as his master during a recent crisis that pushed him to the brink. Through their contract, he gained the strength they needed to survive. And once a Kerales found a master, they were expected to leave the village and follow them. Yet, Panther had one request before leaving with Ingrid: he wanted to say goodbye to his closest friend, Dannie—and that was why he brought Ingrid back to the village.

        “Anyway, if I say it’s fine, then it’s fine, meow.” With that, Panther nuzzled back against Ingrid’s chest. He closed his eyes in comfort, refusing to hear another word of it.

        Seeing how firmly he insisted, Ingrid said no more. She followed his directions toward the village, and before long, a cluster of buildings appeared among the giant fungi. But as she approached with Panther in her arms, she quickly sensed that something was wrong.

        A strange tension hung over the entire village. Scores of Kerales had gathered before the largest house in the village—the chief’s home. Their faces were grim, their voices low. Ingrid could almost feel the unease and worry prickling in the air.

        A bad feeling rose in Panther’s chest. He jumped down from Ingrid’s arms and darted straight to the chief’s house. Catching the nearest Kerales by the shoulder, he asked, “Hey! What happened?”

        “Dannie was badly hurt. The chief is treating her now, but… it doesn’t look good.”

        “WHAT?” Panther cried out in panic. He plunged into the crowd, squeezing through with all his strength until he reached the chief’s door. Then he rushed inside, straight toward the room heavy with the smell of medicine.

        Inside, a weak, barely conscious calico cat lay on the bed. Her waist and belly were wrapped in thick bandages, but even the layers of gauze could not fully hide how deep the wound was. The cat was none other than Dannie, Panther’s closest friend.

        “Dannie!” Panther called, his voice tight with worry. At the familiar voice, Dannie struggled to open her eyes. She managed a faint smile and said, “Panther... You’re back...”

        “You... How did this happen?” Panther anxiously turned to the village chief. “What happened to Dannie?”

        “Her belly was nearly ripped open. Lucky for her, it missed anything vital. Otherwise, even I wouldn’t have been able to save her.” The chief shook his head with a weary frown. “She’ll need at least two months of proper rest.” 

        “It’s... that bad...” Panther’s paws involuntarily trembled in anger as he shouted, “WHO did this? Who dared hurt you like this, meow?”

        Dannie was silent for a moment. Then she whispered the truth: “My master...”

        “WHAT?”

        Not long ago, Dannie had set out on an adventure with her master. But when they ran into a powerful monster, her master used her as a decoy and fled, leaving her to face the monster alone. Somehow, Dannie survived. She fought her way free and dragged herself back toward the village until a Kerales found her and rushed her to the chief’s house.

        “That rotten coward...!” Panther gritted his teeth. “She’s not getting away with this!”

        “Don’t... Panther...” Dannie said weakly. “She’s powerful... You can’t beat her alone...”

        “She’s right. Know your place; you’re no match for me.” A sweet, mocking voice came from the doorway. It was a red-haired woman, strikingly beautiful and dressed—she was a witch, unmistakably.
