        “Master...” Dannie whispered. Her body reflexively trembled as fear gripped her.

        “Here you are, my dear companion. You managed to crawl home alive even against a monster like that,” the red-haired witch said with a pleased nod. There was no warmth in her voice, only cold satisfaction, as though she were praising a tool that had proved more useful than expected. “Very good. Now come back with me.”

        All color drained from Dannie’s face. She looked at Panther, then forced herself to meet the witch’s eyes. Clenching her teeth, she said, “No... I’m not going back with you. I want to end our contract.”

        “That is not your choice.”

        The witch stepped into the room, her staff raised to control Dannie with magic. But before she could cast the spell, a massive shadow slammed into her and sent her flying out of the house with a thunderous crash.

        “You don’t get to boss her around anymore, meow!” Panther roared in his true form with one of his huge paws pinning the witch to the ground. His tails whipped through the fungi around them, each furious sweep making the air feel heavier. “Dannie isn’t your shield. She isn’t your tool, meow!”

        “Humph! You think you can stand in my way?” the witch sneered. As she confidently swung her staff, vines burst from the earth and wrapped around Panther’s limbs and throat, suspending him in midair.

        “L-let me go!” While Panther thrashed to break free from the unexpectedly tight vines, the witch climbed to her feet and raised her staff again. Light gathered at its tip, condensing into a glowing sphere that shot toward the Kerales with threatening power—

        Clang! A translucent shield flashed into place and blocked the attack.

        “Who did that?” the witch screamed in flustered rage. “Who dares stand in my way?” 

        “His master. Ingrid, a witch of Kremier,” Ingrid arrived just in time. With one clean sweep of her staff, she freed Panther from the vines.

        “Master! You came!” Panther rushed to Ingrid’s back the moment he regained freedom. His eyes lit up as if he had seen a lifesaver, and the fury and panic from moments before gave way to absolute trust. 

        “I heard what happened from the other Kerales.” Ingrid rested a gentle hand on Panther’s head. Then she looked at the red-haired witch, and the warmth disappeared from her gaze. 

        “You abandoned your companion in a crisis and used her as bait. Then you had the audacity to come here and take her back.” Her voice turned cold with disdain. “You’re shameless. And as a witch, I’m embarrassed to even look at you.

        The red-haired witch flinched under Ingrid’s stare. For a second, fear broke through her confidence, but she quickly forced a defiant glare and said, “T-this has nothing to do with you! Stay out of it!”

        “It has everything to do with me.” Magic surged into Ingrid’s staff as she aimed it at the red-haired witch. “You hurt my companion’s friend. Then you attacked my companion. That gives me every reason to teach you a lesson. ”

        “N-no, wait. Please, I—” The red-haired witch tried to beg the moment she realized how overwhelming Ingrid’s power was, but it was too late. 

        “Feel the pain you caused!” 

        “Aaaah!” The spell struck, and the witch let out a shrill scream. A moment later, her cry broke off as she crumpled to the ground. 
        Afterward, under Ingrid and Panther’s watch, the witch reluctantly ended her contract with Dannie and returned her freedom. The moment it was done, she fled the village in a panic. 
        Dannie watched her former master disappear into the fungal forest. Mixed emotions surfaced in her eyes—fear, relief, and the uncertainty of one who did not yet know what to do with her newfound freedom.
        “This is great! You’re free from that villain now, meow!” Panther, simple and straightforward as ever, cheered without noticing the complicated look on his friend’s face. 

        Dannie looked at him, then at Ingrid beside him. Her eyes held a little envy, but also genuine happiness for her friend. 

        “You really do have better eyes than me,” she said. “You found yourself a good master.”

        Panther’s mouth twitched at the compliment. He tried to hold back his smile, but failed almost immediately. All he could do was turn his face aside and pretend to be calm, though his gently swaying tails betrayed him completely.

        “O-of course I did, meow!” he said, trying his best to sound proud and composed. Even so, he could not quite hide the joy in his voice.  “Just watch. I’m going to get stronger. So strong that no one will ever hurt you again, meow!”

        At his bold declaration, Dannie gave him a weak but genuine smile.
        “All right. I’ll be waiting for you to come back.”
        Beside them, Ingrid watched in silence with a faint smile gracing her lips.
STORY_2962:
Under the guidance of Jiang Ziya, the general of the Heavenly Kingdom, Daji, the once-feared nine-tailed vixen, had finally left her violent past behind. She no longer slaughtered without reason, but devoted herself to practicing asceticism. Sensing the change in her heart, the elements gathered their power and created an illusion—a vision of the fate she might have faced had she chosen a different path…

        It was late at night, yet one particular residence in the Heavenly Kingdom senior Xians’ neighborhood remained softly lit.

        Beneath the flickering candlelight, Daji lounged on her bed, her hair cascading over the sheets. Though sleep pulled at her eyelids, she refused its call, brushing her tails lazily against the bedside to keep herself awake.

        Suddenly, she perked her ears. Her eyes lit up, and every trace of sleepiness vanished within a second as she slipped off her bed and hurried to the door. She opened it just before the person outside could.

        “Jiang Shang! You’re back!”

        Surprised by her warm welcome, Jiang Ziya paused for a moment before returning a gentle smile. He nodded and said, “I’m back. What are you doing up so late at night?”

        “I couldn’t sleep. Tomorrow’s your day off, remember? I already planned where we’re going. First, we’ll—” Daji chattered excitedly. Yet, a subtle change in Jiang Ziya’s expression caught her attention, and so she wrapped herself around his arm and asked, “Is something wrong?”

        “I’m sorry,” Jiang Ziya let out a quiet sigh. “There’s been a last-minute meeting tomorrow. I’m afraid we might need to cancel our plan.”

        “You—” Daji bristled at Jiang Ziya’s answer. With her hands on her hips, she was ready to snap. Then she saw the exhaustion beneath his eyes, and all her anger went out with a hiss, like a flame hit with cold water.

        [i]‘I’m still upset with him for breaking our promise… but I know better than anyone that he isn’t doing this because he wants to. He’s given so much to keep this world at peace. I shouldn’t take it out on him.’[/i] she thought.

        “…It’s fine. I knew what kind of man you were from the beginning.” She turned away with a huff and crossed her arms. Then her eyes made a sly little turn as an idea came to her. She then said, “Well, if you can’t skip the meeting, then I’ll go with you.”

        Jiang Ziya blinked, then laughed softly under his breath. He never did know how to refuse her.

        The next day, the meeting began as scheduled, and as agreed, Jiang Ziya took Daji with him.

        The moment they entered the hall, people—Xians and monsters—gathered around Jiang Ziya, swarming him with unresolved disputes and requests, anything small or big that they wanted him to settle.

        Curiosity kept Daji listening for a time, but the endless conversations soon dulled her interest. Her tails gently swayed behind her as she rested against a pillar, and slowly she drifted off. It was not until a sudden burst of laughter that she was finally awake and found the banquet had already started. Even then, Jiang Ziya was still trapped among the crowd.

        “No, really, I shouldn’t drink any more,” he said politely.


        “Oh, come on, General Jiang! A man with your bearing must be able to handle a few more cups. Don’t be shy! Bottoms up!” Another representative proposed a toast to Jiang Ziya.

        Before he could refuse again, more wine was poured into his cup. Several rounds later, even his cheeks had begun to flush faintly red.

        “Here, General Jiang! Another!” A pig monster came with an enormous jar of wine. Just as he poured a cup for Jiang Ziya, a slender hand claimed it before it reached him.

        “He’s done drinking. I’ll take this one.” Daji said. She tipped the cup and finished the wine in one gulp. Her bold gesture won her admiring looks from the nearby monsters.

        “Aha! General Jiang’s partner, heh? Impressive! Impressive!” The pig let out a hearty laugh and said, “Here! Take another!”

        And just like that, the drinks originally meant for Jiang Ziya somehow all ended up down Daji’s throat. At first, she drank simply to rescue him from the relentless toasts, but the crowd’s cheers stirred her competitive spirit. Before she realized it, one cup turned into several, and little did she know that a hand had slipped something into one of the cups.

        A moment later, a strange heat spread through her body. An unusual flush swiftly bloomed across her fair skin. Her eyes became unfocused as something violent, twisted inside her chest grew stronger with every breath. Seeing her sway, Jiang Ziya immediately caught her and sensed that something was wrong.

        “Daji? Are you feeling unwell?” he asked.

        “N-no… Stay away from me… hurry… Stay away!” Daji muttered, struggling to suppress the savage impulse tearing through her mind. Yet, it only grew worse, and eventually, it went out of her control.

        Overwhelmed by the violent urges, Daji lost all reason and reverted to her true form. Her nine tails lashed out wildly, sweeping away every Xian and monster around her—including Jiang Ziya, who had been right beside her. 

        “What…What’s happening?”
        “It’s Daji! General Jiang’s partner! She’s lost control!”
        “I knew the vixen could never change!”

        The hall descended into chaos. Some Xians even drew their weapons, ready to strike Daji down, but a rain of talismans stopped them in their tracks.

        “No one touches her!” Jiang Ziya’s voice cut through the chaos.

        One Xian protested, “General Jiang, it is not our intention, but if we don’t stop her now—”

        “There’s nothing to worry about! I, Jiang Shang, guarantee with my life that she won’t harm anyone. So long as I’m here, none of you is to hurt her.” Jiang Ziya shouted. Then, he closed his eyes and channeled his powers, casting a shimmering protective spell before rushing toward the rampaging vixen.

        Instinct took over Daji the moment she sensed someone approaching. With a furious snarl, she lunged forward and dug her claws into the assailant’s skin—

        Swish!

        Blood splashed, but Jiang Ziya stood firm. Ignoring the deep wounds across his chest, he grabbed hold of her foreleg. The scent of blood briefly dispersed the haze clouding her mind, granting her a fleeting moment of clarity. Her heart ached as her eyes fell on the gash she had left.

        “K-kill me… I don’t want to hurt you… Jiang Shang… please…” Daji pleaded hoarsely with tears shimmering in her almond-shaped eyes. She could feel herself slipping further into madness with every passing second. Soon, she would be lost entirely, and the first to meet her claws would be the man she loved.

        “No… I would never kill you… I will save you!” Jiang Ziya whispered, cupping her face with bloodstained hands. He rested his forehead against hers as his consciousness entered her mind. There, hidden deep within her head, he found the source of the corruption—a field of strange flowers blooming in grotesque abundance.

        [i]‘This is a gu poison! Someone must have slipped the gu inside Daji’s cup during the toast…’[/i] Anger flared up in Jiang Ziya’s eyes.

        [i]‘First, let me get rid of this gu poison.’[/i] Closing his eyes, he pressed two fingers together to form the sword-finger seal. As he drew a line across the air, golden talismans materialized around him. They coalesced into arcs of heavenly lightning that rained down on the flower field. The blossoms shrieked as they writhed. From their petals came a swarm of venomous bees, rushing toward him, only to be sliced apart by a sweep of his hand.

        [i]‘You’ve picked the wrong enemy!’[/i]  White flames flared in Jiang Ziya’s palm. He then hurled them toward the flowers. The fire spread instantly. In moments, the field lay in ashes, and at its heart remained only a charred seed.

        Jiang Ziya picked up the seed and withdrew from Daji’s consciousness. When he opened his eyes, she had already returned to human form, her breath calm, her aura cleansed. Her eyes reddened as soon as she noticed the blood seeping through his robes.

        “It’s nothing serious,” Jiang Ziya reassured her softly. “You’re safe, and that’s enough.”

        “It’s all my fault… I let my guard down…” Daji murmured. Guilt gnawed at her, but from it rose a fire of rage. Her eyes blazed as she said, “I’m going to find whoever did this!”

        She took the charred seed from Jiang Ziya’s hand and breathed gently against it. The moment her powers wrapped around the seed, a wisp of smoke rose from its surface, slowly taking the shape of a tiny nine-tailed fox. The fox leapt into the crowd and tugged at the sleeve of a young woman standing within.

        “Ha! Found you!” With a chilling laugh, Daji unleashed her power and swept toward the young woman like a gust of wind.

        The girl spun to run, but Daji was faster. A blow to her ribs sent her crashing into a tree, and she crumpled to the ground, trembling.

        Daji descended a few steps away and looked down at her.

        “Young girl, you’ve got a lot of nerve,” she said coolly. “Poisoning me right under my nose.”

        “…So what if I did?” the woman shot back bitterly, unfurling three fox tails behind her to reveal her identity—she was also a vixen. Then she said, “We’re both vixens. Why are you the only one allowed to stand beside General Jiang?”

        “Because I’m better than you,” Daji gave a quiet scoff and replied. “Cultivation aside, what could you possibly rival me in? Certainly not body, or looks.”

        “So what? No matter how beautiful you look, you and Jiang Ziya can’t stay together forever. Those stubborn old Xians will never accept a nine-tailed vixen like you. Jiang Ziya will surely abandon you to save his name one day!” The three-tailed vixen gritted her teeth.

        “I won’t,” Jiang Ziya stepped forward and said, his voice unwavering. “I, Jiang Ziya, am in love with Daji, and I’ve made a life-long promise that I will never fail her in both sickness and in health, not even until death do us part.”

        “Jiang Shang…” Daji called softly, her voice overflowing with tenderness. Hearing Jiang Ziya’s words, she felt her eyes sting faintly. Emotion swelled quietly in her chest, deeper than anything she had ever felt before.

        In the end, the three-tailed vixen’s cultivation was stripped as punishment for poisoning Daji. Meanwhile, Jiang Ziya’s injuries bought him three days of respite from his duty in the Heavenly Kingdom. And so, at long last, Daji had what she wanted: three quiet days with the man she loved…

        [i]“I love him, but I’m still me. Loving someone does not mean losing myself in the process.”[/i]

STORY_2964:
As one of the Holy Gods, Chessia had been sent by Khaos to capture a descendant of the Ancient Gods. After many twists and turns, however, she ended up falling for her very target: Mesopotamia, the kingdom’s “prince” who was actually a girl. Following her feelings, Chessia turned her back on her kin and chose to remain by Mesopotamia’s side.

        And on this day, as always, Chessia slipped quietly into the palace and crept up to Mesopotamia’s bedchamber.

        [i]‘Hehe. She should still be asleep now. Let me wake her with a little scare,’[/i] Chessia thought. Mischief sparkled in the corners of her eyes as she covered her mouth to stifle a giggle. Carefully, she pushed open the window, hopped through it, then tiptoed to Mesopotamia’s bed. With a dramatic leap, she pounced—

        “Rise and shine, my prince… Huh? Where is she?” Chessia shouted excitedly, only to find that there was no one in the bed aside from the blanket and pillows. 

        “Tut! She must have gone off to train at dawn again.” Chessia’s mood soured as her prank failed. Pouting, she folded her arms and kicked the bedframe with the tip of her shoe. Then she growled, “Oh, I’ll find you. Just watch me.”

        A heartbeat later, flames flared in Chessia’s palm. With the flames unfurling like wings, she flew into the air and shot through the morning mist beyond the window. Soaring above the palace, she scanned the city walls, the training grounds, and the distant hills until she spotted a familiar figure on a lonely peak far away.

        “Found you!” Her eyes lit up. She flew toward the mountain with a smile, but that smile froze the moment she drew near.

        [i]‘Is she… crying?’[/i]

        There, Chessia saw Mesopotamia. She was not training, but kneeling before a headstone, her shoulders trembling as she wept. Her sobs were quiet, broken, almost restrained, yet Chessia heard every unsteady breath—as well as the unbearable grief hidden within—through the wind. Tears slipped down her face and fell onto the monument, each drop leaving a dark mark on the cold stone.

        [i]‘I’ve never seen her cry like this… She didn’t even frown when I stabbed her. But now…’[/i]

        Chessia stopped in midair. Her chest tightened as if an invisible hand had closed around it. She wanted to go to Mesopotamia. She wanted to laugh, tease her, and annoy her the way she usually did, but she couldn’t. A strange hesitation, or perhaps fear, held her in place.

        [i]‘If I go to her now… will I upset her?’[/i] she thought.

        For the first time, Chessia chose to run away. She returned to the palace, but the playful spark in her eyes that morning was gone. Her expression tightened with an inexplicable defiance as she clenched her teeth and thought to herself: [i]‘What was she crying about? I need to find out!’[/i]

        Then, she snapped her fingers. Fire engulfed her body, and in the blink of an eye, she turned into an ordinary maid. She stepped into the corridor,  stopped another servant, and asked, “Hey. Do you know where Meso… where did the prince go? His Majesty is looking for him.”

        “The prince…?” The maid blinked. “Oh. Today is the day of General Argo’s passing. He must have gone to pay his respects.”

        “General Argo?” Chessia narrowed her eyes and asked, “What was he to the prince?”

        “General Argo was the prince’s teacher. He taught him swordsmanship, and they were very close… Sadly, he died in a battle against the demons a few years ago.” The maid suddenly paused as suspicion crept into her expression. “Wait. How do you not know— 

        Before the maid could finish, fire flashed—and Chessia was gone. She was back in the empty bedchamber, but this time, she was in no mood for pranks. Her brows drew tight as she sat on the bed, chewing at her nails.

        “Her teacher, huh…” she murmured. “Then he must be the one who taught Meso that ‘the eyes are the windows to the soul’ nonsense… But she wouldn’t cry like that if he were just a teacher to her…”
　
        Irritated by the thought, Chessia grabbed a pillow and hurled it against the wall. Then she kicked over a nearby chair before dropping to the floor with a shout, “Urgh! This is so annoying! Why do I care so much?”

        Even Chessia did not know the answer. All she knew was that her chest felt tight, as if something was pressing down on her. As she fumed, a thin object came loose from the bookshelf and fell lightly to the floor.

        “…Hm? What’s this?” Chessia picked it up with a frown.

        It was a painting with delicate brushwork and steady lines—a portrait of a man standing with a sword in hand, his gaze calm, firm, and fearless.

        “So this is Argo…” Chessia’s grip unknowingly tightened as she stared at the painting. “She painted this. She loved him…”

        It was more than a simple portrait. There was warmth in every stroke, and every line revealed how deeply she had cared for him.

        For a moment, Chessia forgot how to breathe. She pressed a hand to her chest. There was no wound, but it ached.

        “…Why?”  she whispered. “I’m not hurt… But why does this feel so painful? I hate this!”

        Chessia abruptly raised the painting high, ready to smash it into pieces, but she stopped at the last second.

        “…Damn it.” She glared at the man in the painting. A flicker of complicated emotions passed through her eyes as she continued, “It’s you… You’re the reason she’s so sad… I would never make her cry like that if it were me; I’d make her smile!”

        For the first time, Chessia’s eyes held something other than selfishness and mischief: a clumsy, genuine determination.

        Soon, the night fell. When the cold wind swept across the desolate peak, the grief-stricken sobs from the day had long quieted, and only faint, uneven breaths remained.

        Mesopotamia lay before the cold gravestone, her forehead resting lightly against it. Her tears had finally run out, and exhaustion had carried her into sleep.

        Moonlight spilled quietly over the grave. Then, someone appeared beside her without a sound. He slowly crouched and reached out. His fingers hesitated for a moment before brushing gently against her cheek. His touch was careful and tender, as if handling something fragile and precious.

        Mesopotamia trembled. Her lashes fluttered as she slowly opened her eyes. Her pupils shrank when she saw the man before her.

        “Teach…er?” Her voice shook in disbelief, as though she was still caught in the dream. “Am I… dreaming?”

        In the moonlight, she saw the man whose silhouette looked painfully familiar to her. It was Argo, smiling, his face as gentle as she remembered.

        “No, Meso.” His voice was low and steady. “This is real. I’ve come back.”

        Those words seemed to open a crack in time, and through it came every memory she had tried to bury.

        Mesopotamia’s breaths faltered. In the next instant, she found herself in a familiar embrace, warm and firm, exactly as it had been in her memories.

        “I will always be by your side and keep you safe,” he said.

        “Mr. Argo!” Mesopotamia’s restraint finally broke. She wrapped her arms tightly around him and buried her face in his shoulder. Her body trembled like a child who had finally found her home.

        Argo gently placed a hand on her back. Yet in the shadow beyond her gaze, his eyes flickered with hesitation and uncertainty.

        For one brief moment, time seemed to stop.

        Then, all at once, Mesopotamia pushed Argo away. She took a step back and lifted her head. Tears still shimmered in her eyes, but the haze had cleared.

        “Thank you,” Mesopotamia said softly. “But that’s enough, Chessia.”

        “...I can stay like this forever if you want.”

        But Mesopotamia simply shook her head and said,

        “No one can be a replacement for another person.”

        In the next second, Argo’s body vanished in a flash of flame, and Chessia appeared in his place.

        Standing there, she bit down on her lower lip, her brows drawn tight. The mischief and confidence that usually lit her eyes were gone, replaced by unease and frustration. 

        “Then what about me?”  Chessia blurted out, her voice sharper than usual. “What can I do to make you not cry?”

        She stepped forward, looking straight into Mesopotamia’s eyes as if demanding an answer.

        “What would make you happy? Tell me!”

        She had never asked anyone for something like this before. The words came out like a plea, clumsy and raw, though she herself did not seem to realize it.

        Mesopotamia looked at her in silence, then she gave a soft sigh.

        “I think you misunderstood what I meant,” she gently placed a hand on Chessia’s head as she explained, “No one is replaceable; no one can ever replace Mr. Argo, just like the way no one can ever replace you.”

        Chessia froze. Her expression went blank for an instant. The words seemed to echo somewhere deep inside her, and only then did a helpless blush begin to rise to her cheeks.

        “You just need to be yourself,” Mesopotamia said with a smile. “And stay by my side. I’m happy just the way you are.”

        “...Okay,” Chessia answered in a muffled voice and lowered her head, giving a nod so small it was almost invisible.

        The smile on Mesopotamia’s face deepened as she watched Chessia’s reaction. She then held out her hand and said, “All right. It’s getting late. Let’s go back.”

        Chessia took her hand, happiness shining plainly on her face. Together, they walked beneath the moonlight, their figures slowly fading into the night…
STORY_2965:
Ever since Pupuro became a hunter of lost things, her work had taken her to all kinds of places.

        The requests she received were always different, and so were the things people had lost. But she had come to believe that behind every “lost” item was a memory or a piece of someone they could not bear to lose.

        That was why she never treated her job lightly, no matter how small the reward. A few pieces of bread, a handful of dried fruit, even a simple thank-you spoken from the heart—if it mattered enough for someone to ask, it mattered enough for Pupuro to try her best.

        One afternoon, Pupuro and the little slug arrived at a small town by the sea.

        The streets smelled of salt and warm stone as the sea breeze drifted over the sunlit ground. Following the address she had been given, she came to an old house at the end of a narrow alley. Beside the door sat a clay bowl filled with fish scraps that still faintly smelled.

        An elderly woman with silver hair stepped slowly out of the house, leaning on a wooden cane.

        “Are you the one who called about the missing cat?” Pupuro asked. 

        “Yes…” The old woman’s voice trembled. “Please, find her for me. She hasn’t come home in days.”

        “Don’t worry, ma’am. My partner and I will do everything we can.”

        “Partner?” The old woman blinked.

        Pupuro smiled and pointed to her shoulder. “This is Little Slug. My partner.”

        Little slug gave a slow, wobbly sway, as if greeting her.

        Pupuro looked back at the old woman and continued, “What’s your cat’s name? What does she look like? Does she have any favorite places?”

        “Her name is Dusky. She’s a big girl, with black fur and golden eyes.” As the old woman recalled, her expression softened, though worry still lingered in her eyes. “Sometimes she goes up the mountain, but she also likes to hang near the docks sometimes.”

        Tears gathered in the old woman’s eyes as she continued:

        “She’s rather a moody girl, and she’s not much of a hugger… but she always comes home before nightfall. So I leave some fish out for her, and she always finishes them… But this time… she never came back…”

        Pupuro nodded. “Don’t worry. We’ll bring Dusky home.”

        After leaving the old woman’s house, Pupuro went to the docks first.

        The muddy ground was covered in different tracks—birds, cats, fishermen’s boots, and a few deep pawprints.

        Pupuro crouched down to examine them. She murmured, “These tracks… I don’t think they belong to an ordinary animal.”

        One of the fishermen nearby, noticing her search, called out to her: “Something big has been prowling up the mountains these past few days. Huge beast. Glowing eyes… It’s definitely not something usual. Could be a monster. So best stay away, whatever it is.”

        Pupuro did not go along with the fisherman’s advice right away. What first came to her mind was the old woman’s face when she spoke of Dusky. That wasn’t the look of someone talking about a mere pet; it was the look of someone waiting for their family to come home.

        On her shoulder, the little slug slightly lifted its head and turned toward the mountains behind the town. Following its gaze, Pupuro nodded and whispered, “You think she’s in the mountains too, huh? All right. Let’s take a look.”

        The forest grew colder the farther they climbed. Following the trail carefully, Pupuro noticed some small prints mixed among the large pawprints that continued up the slope.  

        “Big ones… and small ones… So the monster isn’t alone?”

        Before she could think further, the little slug suddenly trembled. Then she heard a faint sound somewhere ahead: “Mew…” She immediately pushed aside the grass, and the sight beyond it made her breath catch—

        There she saw several kittens huddled together, their backs arched as they cried weakly at the creature before them. It was an enormous monster with black fur, its golden eyes gleaming in the shade. 
It was enormous, covered in black fur, with golden eyes that glimmered in the shade.

        [i]‘Oh no! It’s trying to eat the kittens!’[/i]

        Pupuro’s eyes darted across the clearing and landed on a small lake behind the monster. She quickly exchanged a glance with the little slug. No words were needed. The little slug immediately opened its mouth and drew in the lake water. A moment later, its body shifted into a raincloud that hovered close to the ground, turning the air into a damp mist to create the perfect environment for Pupuro to strike.

        “Stop!” Channeling her powers, she dashed bravely out of the bushes and swung her magnifying glass. The water in the air quickly gathered into several sharp arrows that struck the ground in front of the monster.

        With a loud splash, water sprayed everywhere.

        The monster leapt back with a startled growl. The kittens squeaked and pressed closer together in fear.

        Pupuro planted herself between them and the monster. Though her knees were a little shaky, she  puffed out her chest and said, “You’re not hurting them!”

        The monster lowered its body, its fur bristling. The air was instantly charged—

        “Dusky! Dusky!” Suddenly, a familiar voice came from behind.

        Surprised, Pupuro turned to see the old woman who hired her walking toward them, breathless.

        “There you are… I knew I’d find you here,” the old woman said, her hands trembling as she approached the monster.

        To Pupuro’s astonishment, the fierce black monster didn’t bare its teeth at the old woman. Instead, it slowly stepped toward her, lowered its head, and let her stroke its fur.

        The old woman gently patted its head, her voice a mix of anger and delight as she said, “You troublemaker… How could you run off for so long…”

        With her eyes wide in disbelief, Pupuro stuttered, “W-what? This is your cat?”

        “That’s right.” The old woman nodded. “Dusky was always bigger than the other cats, even when she was little. Though she looks different as the years go by, she’s a good girl. She’s never hurt anyone. She’s a very sweet kitty.”

        [i]‘That is absolutely not a cat!’[/i] Pupuro couldn’t help but grumble inwardly. Keeping that thought to herself, she glanced at the kittens, now tumbling happily over one another, and asked, “Then… where did these kittens come from?”

        The old woman paused for a moment until the truth dawned on her, and she murmured, “Oh… I see. So Dusky wasn’t lost at all. She went off to have her babies.”

        Only then did Pupuro understand.

        Dusky had not been stolen nor caught in an accident. She had come to the mountain to give birth, and the kittens were her children—she wasn’t trying to “eat” them; she was protecting them.

        Feeling a flush of embarrassment at her misunderstanding, Pupuro muttered, “I thought you were going to eat them…”

        Dusky gave her a long look, then huffed softly through her nose. It sounded a little like she intended to hold a grudge. Their interactions made the old woman laugh.

        After that, Pupuro helped the old woman place the kittens into a basket one by one.

        At first, the kittens wriggled and cried, but Duskly walked beside the basket the whole time, brushing it now and then with her tail. Little by little, the kittens settled down. The old woman moved slowly, but her smile made her look more lively than she had all afternoon. As they prepared to leave, she kept murmuring to herself about what she would need at home: more bowls, more fish, and the old blanket from the cupboard to make a warm corner for the kittens to rest.

        Pupuro quickly said, “Take care of yourself, too.”

        The old woman responded with a chuckle.

        On the way down the mountain, the little slug curiously stretched its body over Pupuro’s shoulder to peer into the basket. One bold kitten stared back and even bapped the little slug right on the head with its tiny paw. The little slug immediately shrank back in fright.
 
        Pupuro couldn’t help but chuckle and tease it: “So there are things even you’re scared of.”

        The old woman looked back at Pupuro, her eyes warm with gratitude as she said,

        “Thank you so much, Miss Hunter.”

        “It was nothing. Besides, I almost made a terrible mistake,” Pupuro replied.

        Pupuro looked ahead at Dusky, who walked with slow, proud steps down the mountain path. Then she glanced at the basket, where the kittens curled together. Though this request had not led her to a priceless treasure or some long-lost heirloom, she felt a quiet warmth settle inside her.

        Sometimes, what is lost is not a thing at all. Sometimes, it is a person you’ve waited days to see. Sometimes, it is a bond that has never been broken. And sometimes, it is a home waiting for you.
STORY_2966:
Long after the street had gone dark, a workshop at the end was still lit. Clear notes drifted through the quiet night as a brass wind chime swayed gently above the door.

        Inside the workshop was a woman, Patra. A few strands of golden hair had slipped loose from the ponytail at the back of her head as she bent over her workbench and carefully channeled her magic power into a metal gear no larger than a fingernail. The forge left the workshop stiflingly hot, but she barely noticed, her full attention fixed on the delicate machine in her hands.

        Three measured knocks at the door broke the silence, each separated by almost the same interval.

        Without even glancing toward the door, Patra replied, “We’re closed. Come back tomorrow.”

        No answer came, and she simply kept working until fitting the final piece into place. On her way to the table for a drink, she noticed a small metal case sitting just outside the workshop. Inside was a rolled blueprint, a pouch of advance payment, and a letter.

        “Commission request. Improve the enclosed design. When the work is complete, leave the finished item on the third floor of the western clock tower.” Patra raised an eyebrow as she read the letter. “No signature, huh? That’s not suspicious at all.”

        Patra had decided the commission was more trouble than it was worth until her eyes fell on the blueprint.

        It took only one look for her to know how sophisticated and brilliant the design was. Whoever had drafted it possessed not only remarkable technical skill but an imagination unlike anything she had seen before. Drawn in by the details, she leaned closer until she was nearly sprawled across the table.

        “They didn’t use a drive shaft here? They’re using elemental energy to build water pressure instead… No, this angle would waste too much power. If the structure were split into two layers, it could improve efficiency by at least thirty percent.” Her eyes raced across the blueprint. Any trace of caution faded as a delighted smile tugged at her lips. “This is fascinating... absolutely fascinating!”

        Seven days later, Patra placed the finished product under a black cloth quietly beside the window on the third floor of the western clock tower.

        [i]‘I wonder… What kind of person came up with such an ingenious design?’[/i] Patra thought as she waited in the shadows nearby with her arms folded.

        At last, she got her answer just as the sun dipped below the horizon. A young man pushed open the door and stepped inside. He was wrapped in an oversized gray cloak, his hood pulled low, leaving half his face hidden in shadow. It seemed he didn’t want to be recognized.

        “So it was you.” Patra stepped out of the shadows and blocked his path. The young man faltered, surprised to find her waiting.

        “The finished piece is over there.” She pulled the cloth away, revealing a circular platinum device. “I made a few changes to your original design. It was solid, but you played it too safe.”

        The young man picked up the device and carefully examined it for so long that Patra began to wonder whether she had overstepped.

        “The output is higher than my calculations predicted,” he finally said. His voice was young and unusually clear. “You also reduced the reaction time.”

        Petra let out a soft chuckle and said, “That sounds like a compliment.” 

        “It is,” he replied with a sincere tone. “You’re an exceptional alchemist.”

        His straightforward answer surprised Patra. Most of the people who came to her workshop haggled over prices or treated alchemists as little more than smiths who hammered metal into shape. Rarely did anyone speak of her craft with such genuine admiration.

        The young man set another pouch of gold on the table beside a new blueprint.

        “If you’re willing,” he said, “I’d like to commission you again.”

        Patra didn’t reach for the gold. Instead, she picked up the blueprint. The moment she unrolled it, she found herself captivated once again by the brilliance of its design. It was only then that she noticed that the new one was also a tool designed simply to make people's lives a little easier, just like the one she had built.

        “I’ll take the job,” she nodded with a smile. “But on one condition.”

        “...What is it?”

        “Tell me your name.” She rolled the blueprint back up and said, “I don’t like working for strangers.”

        The young man remained silent for a long moment before finally giving a small nod.

        “Schrödinger,” he answered at last. “My name is Schrödinger.”

        From that day on, Schrödinger became a regular at Patra’s workshop.

        He always arrived at dusk or on rainy evenings, wrapped in the same oversized gray cloak. His hood never left his head, and his visits never lasted long.

        Yet each time he came, he brought another set of blueprints that surpassed the last. His inventions were all ingenious and thoughtful. None of them was made to impress people, but to make life a little easier for someone who needed it.

        Before long, Patra found herself looking forward to those three knocks at the door. Whenever Schrödinger came to collect a finished product, she would deliberately keep him a little longer with one question after another. He often took his time before answering, but he never gave her anything less than a mindful reply.

        “I need funding.”

        “What for?”

        “...Research.”

        “What kind of research?”

        Schrödinger looked out the window, through which the last rays of the setting sun caught in his eyes beneath the shadow of his hood. His voice carried a quiet sadness as he said, “I want to restore what was lost.”

        [i]‘He looks... like he’s in so much pain… I wish I could do something for him.’[/i]

        As much as Patra wished that she could ease some of the pain he carried, she held back. They barely knew each other, and she had no right to cross that distance.

        [i]‘He wouldn't even let me see his face... How could he ever let me touch him?’[/i]

        Then, something changed on one winter day.

        It was a snowy day, and everyone on the street scurried along with their shoulders hunched against the bitter wind.

        With the finished product in her arms, Patra hurried across the icy stone steps toward their meeting place. But she was moving too fast, and she slipped. Her body pitched backward, certain she was about to hit the steps.

        Unexpectedly, a hand caught her firmly around the waist.

        The man came to her rescue like a gray blur cutting through the snow. He moved so quickly that the wind caught his hood, tearing it back.

        When Patra looked up, she found herself staring at a young, handsome face. His eyes shone with an unusual light no human could possess, but metal along his face drew her attention even more. It ran down the side of his neck and disappeared beneath his collar, catching the dim light with a cold blue sheen.

        “S-Schrödinger?” She asked as she recognized the familiar cloak almost immediately.

        “...Yes.”

        “So… you’re not a human?”

        “...No.” Schrödinger's shoulders tightened, and his voice dropped almost to a whisper.

        He already knew what came next. He knew he should never have let her see him like this, and he was ready to disappear before she would scream in terror. But Patra didn’t. Instead, she grabbed his wrist, her eyes shining with barely contained excitement.

        “Where’s your kinetic core? There’s no way anyone could move that fast with muscle alone! And these lines on your skin... are they some kind of elemental conductor? This is incredible… I’ve never seen anything like this!”

        Schrödinger stared at her in disbelief. “You... don’t find me repulsive?” 

        “Why would I? I think you’re amazing.” Patra stepped closer, leaning in until her face was almost level with his chest. “Can I study you?”

        “...Study me?”

        “I won’t take you apart,” she added quickly, as serious as if she were swearing an oath. “At least… not at first.”

        For a moment, Schrödinger simply blinked.

        His reason told him to pull away at once, but the look in Patra’s eyes held him in place. There was no fear, no greed—only a pure, almost fervent curiosity, as though she were looking at a miraculous creation.

        A quiet laugh escaped his lips. It began as little more than a breath, then gradually grew into a genuine guffaw. In the pale light of the falling snow, the caution in his eyes slowly began to melt away.

        “At least not at first? What does that even mean?” he repeated.

        “It means if you’ll explain how everything works, I won’t need to take you apart,” Patra answered, utterly certain of her reasoning.

        Schrödinger looked at her. Deep within his chest, a strange, bright sensation pulsed through his core.

        He couldn’t remember the last time he’d laughed like that.

        Ever since his people had fallen into an endless sleep along with the sealed Mech City, he had been hiding himself beneath the cloak, living for one single purpose. He kept his distance from everyone. It kept him safe, but it also left him alone.

        Yet somehow, Patra had broken through all of those carefully built walls.

        “I’ll explain,” he said with a hint of childish smile in his eyes. “So you don’t have to take me apart.”

        “That depends,” Patra replied with a teasing grin. “You'll have to explain it well enough first.”

        Snow continued to fall as the city lights came on one by one. Schrödinger pulled up his cloak, but this time he didn’t hide his face in its shadow. Side by side, he and Patra walked back to the workshop. Somewhere deep within him, a circuit that had lain silent for years began to hum again, as though a single gentle spark had set the current flowing.

        He didn’t know it yet, but their encounter that had begun with a single commission would one day become the memory he treasured most—and the one he could never bear to lose...
STORY_2967:
The palace in the Dark Cove knew neither dawn nor night. Only a dim violet glow flowed through the cracks in its stone walls, casting the endless halls in an eerie half-light.

        Sasa was born beneath that glow.

        When she opened her eyes for the first time, she saw a tall man looking down at her.

        The darkness blurred the edges of his face, but his eyes were strikingly clear. They shone with the joy of someone who had recovered something precious he thought was lost forever—and with the fear that the miracle before him might vanish at any moment.

        His name was Loki. He had once served as the strategist of the Northern Alliance, until Odin granted him power beyond the limits of mortals and made him a god. But the death of his daughter, Hel, drove him to madness. Consumed by grief and vengeance, he rebelled against Odin again and again until the gods finally imprisoned him within the Dark Cove. 

        However, even endless confinement could not dull his longing for Hel. Alone in that cold, silent abyss, Loki turned to forbidden means. He poured his godly power and even his own soul into his work, creating imitation after imitation as he desperately tried to bring his dead daughter back to his side and fill the emptiness she had left behind.

        After countless failed attempts, at last, he succeeded.

        “My daughter... You’ve finally come back to me.” Loki reached toward Sasa, his fingertips trembling before they gently brushed her cheek. His voice was so soft, it was almost as though he feared he might wake her from a dream. “I’m your Daddy.” 

        Sasa had no idea what he meant by “come back.” She only knew that the person before her made her feel warm and safe, so she reached out with both arms and nestled against him.

        “Daddy?” she repeated innocently. That single word made Loki’s body freeze. For a long moment, he said nothing. Then a quiet laugh escaped him, and he pulled Sasa closer.

        “That’s right. I’m Daddy. And you’re Daddy’s most precious daughter.”

        From that day on, Sasa lived surrounded by Loki’s love.

        The Dark Cove was a cold and lifeless place, but Sasa never saw it that way. To her, it was a castle that belonged only to her and Daddy.

        Sometimes, Loki would conjure glowing black butterflies that stayed in her palms and shaped tiny flowers from dark elements to tuck into her hair. He would always smile and compliment her. Whenever she woke from sleep, she would find him sitting beside her bed, calling softly to her. “My daughter, my precious girl. Are you awake?”

        And every time, Sasa would beam and throw herself into his arms.

        She knew nothing of the world beyond the Dark Cove, nor did she understand the weight carried by words like imprisonment and hatred. All she knew was that Daddy held her when she wanted to be held, praised her when she did something well, and gently patted her head whenever she learned a new spell.

        “Well done,” Loki would always tell her.

        And so Sasa believed she was the happiest child in the whole world.

        One day, Loki was sitting in his study, writing in a notebook. Nearby, Sasa, with a little black cat he had made from dark elements in her arms, stood on her toes, trying to peek at what he was writing.

        “Daddy, what are you writing?”

        “Nothing interesting.” Loki closed the notebook and smiled as he lifted her onto his lap. “More importantly, where would you like to play today?”

        “The garden!”

        The “garden” was really just an open space deep within the palace, transformed by Loki’s magic. There was no sunlight and no real soil, but he had filled it with glowing flowers, singing vines, and an enormous black tree that would never wither.

        Sasa loved climbing that tree more than anything. She loved to sit among its branches while Loki told her stories.

        And that day was no different. She ran ahead of him, her laughter echoing through the empty halls.

        “Daddy, hurry!”

        “Slow down. You’ll fall.”

        “I won’t!”

        The words had barely left her mouth when her foot caught on a raised stone that sent her pitching forward. Her arm scraped against a sharp corner, leaving a red gash across her pale skin.

        The pain came so suddenly that Sasa froze. A moment later, her lower lip began to tremble, and tears welled in her eyes as she began to whimper, “D-Daddy… It hurts…”

        Loki walked toward her with an exasperated smile, his hands already reaching down to pick her up as he always did. But the moment his eyes fell upon the wound, he stopped.

        Blood trickled down Sasa’s pale arm. The cut wasn’t deep, but the red mark stood out clearly against her skin.

        Loki’s smile vanished.

        “...No.”

        Sasa looked up at him through her tears and asked, “Daddy?”

        “No... No, this isn’t right...” Loki seemed not to hear her. His eyes remained fixed on the wound, his breathing growing faster. “Hel... Hel didn’t have that scar! She didn’t! She didn’t!”

        Sasa stared at him, bewildered.

        She didn’t know who Hel was. She only knew that something had changed in Daddy’s eyes. The warmth inside them was gone. Now he was staring at her as though she were something that had broken—something flawed that needed to be fixed.

        “Daddy, I... I didn’t mean to...”
 
        “Hel didn’t have that scar!” Loki suddenly seized Sasa’s injured arm, gripping it so tightly that she cried out in pain. He didn’t seem to notice, but hysterically shouted, “It isn’t supposed to be here! It can’t stay there! It can’t!”

        Darkness gathered in his other hand and formed a small black knife, its edge gleaming coldly beneath the violet light.

        Sasa’s eyes widened as she watched the blade move closer to her wound. Fear rooted her to the spot. She could do nothing but tremble.

        “Daddy... don’t...”

        “I just have to remove it,” Loki murmured. His voice sounded almost soothing, as though he were comforting her—or perhaps convincing himself. “If I get rid of the mark, you’ll go back to how you were. Yes... That’s right. I just have to take it away...”

        The tip of the knife touched the edge of the wound and pressed into her skin. Fresh blood immediately flowed from the cut.

        “It hurts! Daddy! Sasa hurts!” Sasa’s scream finally broke through to him.

Loki’s hand stopped. The knife trembled in midair before dissolving into black mist.

        For a moment, he simply stared. Then it was as though he had woken from a nightmare. He looked down at Sasa’s tear-streaked face, then at the wound he had reopened with his own hands.

        “I...” His voice came out rough and broken.

        “Daddy...” Still sobbing, Sasa reached for his sleeve, but Loki recoiled and pushed her away as though her touch had burned him.

        Sasa lost her balance and fell back onto the ground. Confused and frightened, she watched Loki take one step away from her, then another. His face had gone pale, and she couldn’t tell whether the terror in his eyes was because of her or because of himself.

        “Don’t look at me,” he whispered.

        “Daddy?”

        “Don’t call me that!”

        Loki turned and fled the garden, disappearing down the corridor and leaving Sasa alone on the cold floor.

        The singing vines fell silent. Even the glowing flowers drooped their petals as though they, too, were scared.

        Sasa cradled her injured arm against her chest as tears fell one by one onto the stone.

        She didn’t understand what she had done wrong.

        “I’m sorry... Daddy...” she whispered, but no answer came. “Sasa didn’t mean to... Sasa will be good... Sasa won’t fall again...”

        The dark palace swallowed her words.

        Sasa looked down at the wound on her arm. The bleeding was already slowing, but somehow it hurt more than anywhere else. She covered the mark with her tiny hand, thinking that if Daddy couldn’t see it anymore, perhaps he would smile at her again.

        But hiding the wound couldn’t erase the look he had given her.

        Sasa drew her knees to her chest and cried until her voice gave out.

        “I’m sorry...” she repeated between sobs. “I’m sorry, Daddy... Sasa will be more like her... so please don’t hate Sasa...”

        And that was the day Sasa first learned that love and pain could come from the very same embrace.
STORY_2968:
At the farthest reaches of the realm of gods, Khaos, lord of all gods, devoted himself to creating an entirely new home for his people.

        The boundless elements sensed the strain he had placed upon himself. When exhaustion finally forced him to close his eyes for a brief rest, they gathered into shifting images until a dream took shape—one that revealed a different path fate might have followed.

        Somewhere in the vast universe, Khaos sat beside Aether, a fellow Holy God whom he trusted above all others. Before them, the galaxy stretched endlessly through the dark, its tides of starlight drifting in perfect silence.

        “Aether, you’ve always been skilled at reading the stars,” Khaos said. “Have they told you anything?” 

        “Lord Khaos, the stars merely reveal truths that already exist, but have yet to be discovered,” Aether replied with a respectful bow.

        “We gods have wandered for a thousand years, searching endlessly for a place to call our own...” Khaos said while looking toward the god soldiers resting in the distance. “Where is this place that can truly become our home?”

        Once, they had spoken eagerly of the paradise they would surely find. But after so many years of wandering, time and failure had worn that hope thin, leaving only exhaustion etched across their faces.

        [i]‘How much longer must we keep searching?’[/i] Khaos’s gaze darkened at the thought, a quiet ache settling over him. [i]‘The chief gods could endure this endless search a little longer. But what about the soldiers?’[/i]

        As he watched their young, weary faces, a new resolve slowly took hold. He turned to Aether and said, “If we cannot find a home, then I’ll create one myself—a world that belongs to us!”

        “Yes, my lord.” Aether lowered her head. Conviction burned brightly in her eyes.

        From that day forward, Khaos ended the gods’ long wandering through the cosmos.

        Guided by Aether, they found a quiet star system amid the endless sea of stars and began building a world of their own.

        Yet resources were scarce, and despite their best efforts, they could create little more than a barren, desolate planet.

        At first, the gods endured. They shared what little the land could provide and tried to live together in peace. But scarcity slowly turned patience into resentment. Disputes over resources and territory became more frequent, and among the proud, powerful Holy Gods, those conflicts grew especially bitter. 

        Khaos intervened whenever he could, mediating one quarrel after another, but the resentment beneath the surface never truly disappeared, and one day, it finally erupted.

        “Lord Khaos!”  Aether shouted as she hurried into the room, her expression grim. “Zeus and his followers attacked Gaia, and Erebus marched against Phanes after accusing him of taking his territory. Along the way, they also provoked Pontos, who governs the rivers. Now all three sides are locked in battle!”

        [i]‘This world has barely taken shape. It’s still too fragile to withstand a battle between the chief gods.’[/i] Khaos’s expression darkened. He looked down at the barren yet precious land beneath his feet and clenched his fist. Then he said, “We cannot let them destroy this place before it has even had the chance to live. We put an end to this madness now!”

        Khaos and Aether each gathered their soldiers and rushed toward the battlefield, determined to stop the disaster before it consumed their new home.

        What followed was a long and brutal battle. Khaos and Aether tried again and again to stop the fighting, but words were no longer enough. In the end, they were forced onto the battlefield themselves, subduing the enraged chief gods one by one until, at last, the conflict came to an end—

        —at the price of almost total annihilation.

        Bodies lay scattered across the battlefield, and the dull yellow earth was soaked red with blood.

        Then, with cruel irony, the barren world began to change. The blood and flesh of the Holy Gods nourished the lifeless soil. Tiny shoots pushed through the bloodstained earth. Rivers began to flow, and the wind carried the first signs of life across a land that had known only desolation.

        The world they had dreamed of was finally coming alive. But there was almost no one left to see it, except Khaos.

        Grievously wounded, Khaos knelt among the dead with Aether’s cold body cradled in his arms. He looked out over a world finally brimming with life, yet found only silence waiting for him. For a long time, he said nothing.

        Then a single crimson tear slipped from the corner of his eye.

        He had created this place with his own hands.  And with those same hands, he had buried everything he once tried to protect.

        [i]“We will never yield! Only the richest, most radiant land is worthy of bearing the glory and dignity of the Holy Hods!”[/i]

        As he watched their young, weary faces, a new resolve slowly took hold. He turned to Aether and said, “If we cannot find a home, then I’ll create one myself—a world that belongs to us!”

        “Yes, my lord.” Aether lowered her head. Conviction burned brightly in her eyes.

        From that day forward, Khaos ended the gods’ long wandering through the cosmos.

        Guided by Aether, they found a quiet star system amid the endless sea of stars and began building a world of their own.

        Yet resources were scarce, and despite their best efforts, they could create little more than a barren, desolate planet.

        At first, the gods endured. They shared what little the land could provide and tried to live together in peace. But scarcity slowly turned patience into resentment. Disputes over resources and territory became more frequent, and among the proud, powerful Holy Gods, those conflicts grew especially bitter. 

        Khaos intervened whenever he could, mediating one quarrel after another, but the resentment beneath the surface never truly disappeared, and one day, it finally erupted.

        “Lord Khaos!”  Aether shouted as she hurried into the room, her expression grim. “Zeus and his followers attacked Gaia, and Erebus marched against Phanes after accusing him of taking his territory. Along the way, they also provoked Pontos, who governs the rivers. Now all three sides are locked in battle!”

        [i]‘This world has barely taken shape. It’s still too fragile to withstand a battle between the chief gods.’[/i] Khaos’s expression darkened. He looked down at the barren yet precious land beneath his feet and clenched his fist. Then he said, “We cannot let them destroy this place before it has even had the chance to live. We put an end to this madness now!”

        Khaos and Aether each gathered their soldiers and rushed toward the battlefield, determined to stop the disaster before it consumed their new home.

        What followed was a long and brutal battle. Khaos and Aether tried again and again to stop the fighting, but words were no longer enough. In the end, they were forced onto the battlefield themselves, subduing the enraged chief gods one by one until, at last, the conflict came to an end—

        —at the price of almost total annihilation.

        Bodies lay scattered across the battlefield, and the dull yellow earth was soaked red with blood.

        Then, with cruel irony, the barren world began to change. The blood and flesh of the Holy Gods nourished the lifeless soil. Tiny shoots pushed through the bloodstained earth. Rivers began to flow, and the wind carried the first signs of life across a land that had known only desolation.

        The world they had dreamed of was finally coming alive. But there was almost no one left to see it, except Khaos.

        Grievously wounded, Khaos knelt among the dead with Aether’s cold body cradled in his arms. He looked out over a world finally brimming with life, yet found only silence waiting for him. For a long time, he said nothing.

        Then a single crimson tear slipped from the corner of his eye.

        He had created this place with his own hands.  And with those same hands, he had buried everything he once tried to protect.

        [i]“If there is no place in this world for us, then I will create one myself—a home for the Holy Hods.”[/i]
STORY_2970:
One evening, in a large house hidden deep within the forest, Li Ji prepared dinner for her sons. The smell of food filled the house as she worked at the stove in a plain dress and apron. She cleaned and prepared each ingredient with care, taking her time over the meal as she always did for the children she loved.

        The soup was simmering when a violent crash came from outside. Li Ji immediately put down the ladle and hurried to the door, only to find her thirteenth stumbling toward the house. His face was pale, and one arm was streaked with blood dripping between his fingers.

        “Thirteen!” Li Ji cried as she rushed over and caught him before he fell.

        “Mother…” He struggled to catch his breath. “I was gathering mushrooms on the mountain when a man with an axe suddenly attacked me. I waited until I saw an opening and pushed him away, and that’s how I managed to escape.”

        Li Ji’s heart sank. It wasn’t the first attack she had heard of. Just a week earlier, her eldest son had been ambushed by a shadowy figure on his way home. Her fifth son had been chased all the way to a stream and almost lost his footing, while her ninth son had been hit with a rock at the market. Though they had all escaped with only minor injuries, after what had happened to Thirteen, Li Ji could no longer treat any of it as coincidence.

        [i]‘Someone is doing this on purpose. Someone is trying to hurt my precious sons.’[/i]

        She pulled Thirteen into her arms. Her eyes burned with vengeance as she said, “How dare they come after my sons again and again… This is unforgivable! I’ll find whoever is behind this and make them pay!”

        Li Ji decided to lure the culprit out with a trap. She had Thirteen fetch water from the river alone, deliberately giving the attacker what looked like another easy opportunity while having the rest of her sons hide among the woods and wait for her signal. Li Ji herself stayed on higher ground, where she could keep eyes on every movement near the river.

        Sunlight glimmered across the river as Thirteen crouched at the water’s edge and lowered his wooden bucket into the current. Then heavy footsteps broke the quiet. They came fast through the trees, followed by a faint scrape of metal.

        [i]‘There you are…’[/i] Li Ji clenched her teeth.

        A man burst from the woods with an axe in his hands and charged toward Thirteen.

        “Stop!” Li Ji shouted. Her sons immediately sprang from their hiding places and surrounded the man before he could reach the river.

        “Tut! So it was a trap.” The man spat onto the ground. Li Ji frowned at the man’s crude gesture. There was something disturbingly familiar about it.

        “Who are you?” she demanded. “Why have you been attacking my sons?”

        The man slowly raised his head to reveal a face covered in old burns. His features twisted beneath layers of scar tissue. A malicious smile appeared in his eyes as he stared at Li Ji and said, “You really don’t recognize me?”

        The man’s answer made Li Ji’s stomach drop. She looked again at his burned face, searching past the scars this time. That hoarse voice, that venomous, leering gaze—piece by piece, they came together until she finally recognized the man standing before her.

        “It’s you!” Li Ji drew in a sharp breath. Her eyes widened as an old nightmare came back.

        This was the man who had kidnapped her and forced her to marry him. He had kept her trapped in that village all those years ago, and when she set the place on fire, she had believed everyone had died. But the man she hated most had survived.

        “You were supposed to die in that fire…” she whispered.

        “Hahaha… You’re the one who should have died!” he roared at her, his eyes filled with hatred. “You burned my village! You destroyed my home! Now I’m going to kill everyone you care about and make you suffer the way I did!”

        At his shout, footsteps sounded throughout the forest. Several men and women emerged from between the trees, their faces and bodies marked by the same old burns. Though some walked with hunched backs and damaged limbs, Li Ji recognized them. They were villagers who had survived the night she thought had killed them all, and they had come to take revenge, closing in around her and her sons.

        Li Ji stared at those familiar faces, and for a moment, she was back in that village. She remembered kneeling through a wedding she had never agreed to, the nights when she had been treated however he pleased, and the endless days of being kept prisoner with no one willing to help her. She heard her daughters crying as the villagers buried them, then felt the warmth draining from her son in her arms. One memory led straight into another until she could no longer separate the haunting past from what was happening in front of her.

        “No… Please… Don’t make me go through this again…” Li Ji pressed both hands over her ears. Her whole body trembled, and her eyes lost focus as the fear she had carried for years threatened to swallow her again.

        “Mother!” The cry came from all around her.

        It was her sons who rushed to her and placed themselves between her and the villagers. There was fear in their voices, but none of them backed away. Their calls pulled Li Ji’s attention away from the memories and back to reality.

        ‘No… I can’t give up like this. I spent all those years learning sorcery so I could protect my children… And this is when I use it!’ Her thoughts cleared, and the power within her awakened at once. 

        A strange blue light appeared in Li Ji’s eyes as she raised her arms. Mist gathered around her sleeves. Water rose from the river before gathering into several enormous spheres that hovered in the air. Cold light shimmered across their surfaces as Li Ji faced the villagers and shouted:

        “You took away my freedom. You took away my children… Now I’m going to make every one of you pay for what you did!”

        With a thrust of her hands, the water spheres flew toward the villagers. Their screams filled the forest as the spheres sent them crashing to the ground. At last, one massive sphere came down on one man—her former husband—driving him into the mud.

        Trapped beneath the crushing weight of water and earth, the man shouted desperately for help until his voice became a hoarse rasp. The arrogance on his face earlier was gone, and for the first time, Li Ji saw the same helplessness that he had once forced her to live with.

        “Mother!” Li Ji’s sons ran to her and gathered around her.

        Her expression softened immediately as she gently stroked their hair and spoke in a quiet, reassuring voice: “It’s okay now. As long as Mother is here, no one will hurt you.”

        Then she turned back toward the man and the villagers on the ground, her voice cold as ice as she said, “You locked me away and treated me however you pleased. You took away my children… Now it’s your turn to know what it feels like to lose your freedom.”

        At her command, her sons captured the villagers. They struggled and shouted in terror, but they had no strength left to flee.

        She watched them with a faint smile. There was still something motherly in her smile, but its warmth did not extend to the people at her feet.

        “You made me live in a cage,” she told them, her voice cold with revenge. “Now you can spend your time thinking about what that was like.”

        By nightfall, the forest had grown quiet again.

        Back inside the house, Li Ji sat with her sons gathered closely around her. She gently shook the bronze wind chime in her hand. Its clear notes carried through the hall as memories of the children she could not save mixed with the sight of those still beside her.

        [i]‘Whatever the world turns into, I’ll keep these children safe, now and always.’[/i]
STORY_2971:
The fading light of dusk painted the land red as an ornate carriage made its way along the cobblestone road. Its wheels sounded almost loud against the quiet of the empty streets. Three people sat inside the carriage—an old, wealthy art collector named Derry; his son, Derry Jr., a passionate young painter; and a strikingly beautiful girl seated across from them.

        Neither man could seem to look away from the girl. Her beauty was beyond compare, with a purity so sacred it felt almost untouchable. Her name was Eve, a daughter of one of the seven great noble houses of the Protodemons, who had come to Tarones in search of the elusive “true love.”

        [i]‘Mom, will Eve finally find it this time? The miraculous true love you told me about?’[/i] Filled with hope, Eve gently touched the rose pendant at her chest. It was the only keepsake her father had left her mother, a symbol of the promise they had once made to each other.

        Her mother had told her that true love was a miracle, something capable of overcoming any hardship and even saving a soul. Eve had held onto those words ever since, believing that somewhere in the world, such a pure and selfless love must truly exist.
        She dreamed that one day she, too, would meet a hero like her father, someone willing to love her with his very life.
        Yet, the way Derry and his son looked at her left her uncertain. There was no mistaking the fervent desire in their eyes, but was it really love? Or was it simply lust?

        Eve decided to put them to a small test. She lured a pack of vicious monsters to the carriage, curious to see what Derry and his son would do when their lives were truly at stake.

        More than anything, Eve hoped the test would finally show her the kind of true love she had always dreamed of.

        But once again, her hopes came to nothing that night.

        The moment the monsters closed in, Derry and Derry Jr. chose to save themselves and fled. Eve watched them disappear, and the answer she had been searching for became painfully clear.

        [i]‘So ordinary love really can’t overcome the fear of death. I suppose that’s what makes true love so precious... Mom, when will Eve ever find a miraculous love like yours?’[/i] Eve let out a quiet sigh and turned her attention back to the monsters gathering around her. Just as she was about to deal with them herself, a commanding shout cut through the street. Then, a squad of soldiers rushed in and quickly drove the monsters away.

        “Are you hurt?” The captain stepped forward to check on Eve, but his words caught in his throat the moment he saw her face. The rest of the soldiers had fallen just as quiet, captivated by her beauty.

        Eve pulled herself from her thoughts and gave the captain a faint smile. “I’m all right. Thank you for saving me.”

        “I-It was nothing. Really.” The captain cleared his throat, still visibly flustered. “Where are you headed? We’re of the Holy Gods. It’s dangerous around here; let us escort you.”

        “I... have nowhere to go.” Eve’s expression dimmed at the thought of Derry and his son. Almost unconsciously, she reached for the pendant at her chest, and the movement drew the captain’s attention.

        “Wait!” The captain’s face suddenly turned serious, and he asked, “Could I take a closer look at that pendant?”

        Though puzzled by his reaction, Eve let the pendant fall from her hand so he could see it clearly. 

        The captain stared at it for a long moment. Then his eyes widened when recognition dawned on his face. “I knew it... This is a token of the God of Pleasure!”

        Eve’s heart skipped at the name. For a moment, she heard nothing else.

        [i] ‘The God of Pleasure… Could that be Father? The miracle Mom protected with her life?’[/i]

        The thought filled Eve with sudden hope. She caught the captain by the arm and eagerly asked, “Does the God of Pleasure have a scar on his back? Where is he? Can you take me to him?”

        The captain blinked at her and said, “We’re only low-ranking soldiers. We’ve never had the honor of seeing the God of Pleasure himself, much less his sacred body... Are you a woman who spent a night with him?”

        Eve’s eyes widened, her breath catching in her throat.

        Taking her silence for confirmation, the captain lowered his voice and continued, “Listen, the God of Pleasure’s wives are not people you want to cross. They’re jealous, strong-willed, and not the forgiving sort—all five of them. I heard that the God of Pleasure used to chase women everywhere he went. He even got a mortal woman pregnant, and when his wives found out, they sent soldiers after her until she had nowhere left to run...  So whatever you’re planning, don’t do anything reckless.”

        The captain’s words shook everything Eve had believed about her mother.

        Her mother had known what carrying a child of god and demon would do to her body, yet she had still chosen to bring Eve into the world. Even as illness left her bedridden, she had refused to give herself to anyone else, though doing so might have saved her life. She had stayed true to her love for Eve’s father until the very end, never once doubting that he loved her in return.

        And yet, while her mother had sacrificed everything for that love, Eve’s father had gone on to build a life with five wives and children of his own. He even had other lovers, never once looking back at the woman he had left to die alone.

        [i]‘Mom… the love you gave your life to protect was nothing but a cruel, absurd lie...’[/i]

        Tears slipped silently down Eve’s face, her shoulders trembling as the truth sank in. The pain inside her felt endless, consuming everything she was.

        Seeing Eve in tears, the captain felt a surge of pity, along with an impulse he made no effort to suppress. He moved closer and lowered his voice. “Forget about the God of Pleasure. Come with me instead. At least for now, I can make you happy.”

        His fingers gently traced along Eve’s cheek before slowly moving downward, a gesture that suggested something far less innocent.

        Swish—

        Blood splashed through the air.

        A blade of dark magic gleamed in Eve’s hand. Her face was eerily calm as she watched the captain scream, clutching what remained of his arm.

        The other soldiers immediately drew their weapons and closed in around her.

        Eve stood with her head bowed, tears still running down her face. When she raised her eyes again, they burned with a cruel crimson light, her demonic blood fully revealed as fury rose beneath her grief.

        “You hypocrites... You deceived my mother… and made her whole life into a cruel joke…” Eve gave a cold, bitter laugh, her voice trembling with anger and grief. “Now you need to pay for every lie your wretched God of Pleasure told her!”

        The sky seemed to answer her. Thunder cracked, and rain began pouring down. Eve swept through the soldiers, her steps light and graceful even as her blade cut them down one after another. Before long, their screams were lost beneath the rain.

        When the last of them had fallen, Eve stood alone in the rain, drenched in blood. She staggered a few steps before sinking to her knees.

        [i]‘Mom… so this is how fragile true love really is… You gave your life for him... and he forgot you so easily.’[/i]

        Eve’s fingers closed around the rose pendant she had treasured for so long. With a quiet crack, it broke apart in her hand, as easily as the promise between her parents had.

        “Ah… If this is how fragile true love really is,” Eve gave a faint, broken laugh. “Does anything even last forever?”

        “Yes. Something does.” A young man’s clear voice came through the rain. Eve turned to see two men walking toward her: Baal, her “fiancé”, and a handsome young man she did not recognize.

        But Eve had no interest in who he was. She wanted only one thing from him—the answer he seemed so certain of. So she asked, “What is it?”

        The young man smiled as he stepped closer. He gestured toward Eve’s heart and said, “The love you have for yourself.”

        “My love...?”

        “If someone else’s love can’t fill that void inside you, then why not give yourself that love?” He continued, “That way, it will last forever.”

        “...Heh. I never thought of it that way.” Eve chuckled. “You’re interesting. I like you.”

        “I like you too, Eve.” Laplace, the ancient demon, extended his hand toward her. “Come join our plan.”

        Eve looked at the hand before her and took it without hesitation.
STORY_2972:
Hammer blows rang through the workshop. Several unfinished longswords lay scattered across the floor while Long Yangjun stood naked before the roaring forge, his eyes fixed entirely on the billet beneath his hammer. Turning the glowing steel between strikes, he corrected its shape little by little until he was finally satisfied. Only then did he put the blade into the heart of the forge for the next stage.

        Firelight danced in Long Yangjun’s eyes, and beads of sweat gathered at his brow as he watched the blade’s color change through the waves of heat. They ran down his face and muscular frame, but he never stepped away from the furnace. When the metal finally brightened to a fierce golden glow, he drew it from the fire and plunged it straight into the quenching bath.

        HISSS! Steam exploded in a thick white cloud. He watched for the slightest change as the metal cooled. Once the steam cleared, he lifted the sword and examined it from end to end. A moment later, he threw it onto the floor with a sharp clang.

        “Damn it! I failed again,” Long Yangjun cursed under his breath. He dropped into a nearby chair and leaned his head back, frustration plain across his face as he stared at the ceiling. 

        [i]‘I can’t make it without the Sea Pearl.’[/i]

        Long Yangjun had been working on the same sword for more than half a month, forging it again and again, yet every attempt still fell short of the perfection he demanded. His craftsmanship wasn’t the problem; he just needed one crucial material—a Sea Pearl. Without it, no amount of skill would give the blade the quality he was aiming for.
