        As the morning sunlight fell onto the bustling and elegant capital of music, Groove, the warm rays filtered through the curtains of a three-story house and gently roused a man from his slumber just as any usual day.

        The man, Haydn, calmly opened his eyes and began his daily routine—washing up, dressing, tidying his hair. Every movement was so perfect as though he were a pre-programmed machine. After smartening himself up, he opened the door and left his room. A small smile tugged at the corners of his lips as he detected a familiar scent—the smell of freshly brewed coffee drifting through the air, which brightened his mood and even made steps lighter.

        He went to the dining room and saw a woman placing two plates of hearty breakfast on the table. She turned to greet him upon hearing his footsteps, her captivating features brightened by a warm and affectionate smile.

        “Good morning, Haydn.”

        “Good morning, Paganini.” Haydn walked over and kissed her on the cheek before taking his seat. As usual, everything on the plate was his favorite: sourdough bread with cheese, a few rashers of crispy bacon on the side, and a steaming cup of freshly ground coffee.

        Paganini was Haydn’s lover. She always came to his home to share breakfast three days a week before they headed off for their usual orchestra rehearsals, and they would meet again for dinner at their usual restaurant at the end of the day.

        [i]What a perfectly stable and contented life.[/i]

        Haydn thought as he smiled and waved goodbye to Paganini before the auditorium. He then began another usual day as the conductor of the Chelidonian Winds Orchestra.

        Born from the seed of music, the Consonias held music in the highest regard, thus they had allocated a significant portion of social resources to support the operations of the Court of Music, a revered governing body formed by nine orchestras. While the court usually refrained from interfering in administrative affairs, it commanded absolute power when it came to major decisions.

        At the top of the Court of Music was Bach, the principal conductor of the Saint Fleur Orchestra, the Court’s first and most prestigious orchestra. Haydn, on the other hand, served as the conductor of the fourth orchestra, the Chelidonian Winds Orchestra. 

        Haydn assumed this day would be like any other—guiding young melodists, pointing out their mistakes, suggesting improvements, and eventually bringing his latest composition to life.

        However, something was different today.

        After the orchestra finished their first rehearsal of Haydn’s latest symphony, most of the melodists praised the beautiful and intricate composition, except for one who stood up, her unwavering gaze fixed on Haydn standing on the conductor’s podium.

        “Maestro Haydn, I find this new piece lacks a soul.” The bold critique came from a young and strikingly charming girl—Mozart. Her words sent a ripple of gasps and whispers through the hall.

        “Mozart… St-stop, okay?” a petite girl, younger than Mozart, timidly pleaded, tugging at her sleeve. It was Beethoven, trying to diffuse the tension. However, Mozart simply shook her hand off, undeterred as she continued, “The first to seventh measures of the violin section are identical to the twelve to eighteen measures of your sixth sonata. The eighth and twelfth measures resemble the thirty-six to forty-one measures of your twelfth symphony…”

        The sound of whispers gradually died down as Mozart gave her critique. Everyone was stunned by her photographic memory of Haydn’s works and her extraordinary ability to identify those similarities after hearing the latest piece just once.

        “...This isn’t a new composition at all,” Mozart concluded sharply. “It’s a patchwork of your previous works. It has no central theme, no soul—just emptiness!”

        Her conclusion plunged the entire hall into a dead silence in which one could have heard a pin drop, her words echoing around the room. No one dared say a word, fearing they might get caught in the invisible war between Mozart and Haydn. Meanwhile, Haydn, the subject of Mozart’s critique, remained silent, as though lost in thought.

        Finally, one melodist, finding Mozart’s statement rather unbearably audacious, broke the silence. “And so what? The music sounds good, and that’s all that matters! All you said was nothing but theoretical critique. Can you do something about it? You can’t, can you? ”

        “Can I do something about it?” Mozart repeated, finding the melodist’s question ridiculous. A smirk tugged at her lips, her tone dripping with sarcasm. “Let me show you.”

        She raised her violin and placed it gently on her shoulder. As she moved her arms, the bow touched the strings, and music began to flow in the hall. At first, no one understood her intention. However, it became clear after several measures—

        —Mozart was rewriting Haydn’s symphony on the spot!

        She restructured the symphony by removing redundant phrases and reordering the mismatched segments, strengthening the main melody with harmonies and deleting chaotic dissonance. Now with a more lively and dynamic rhythm, the music is infused with passion and energy. She had successfully recreated the piece and offered an innovative interpretation without losing Haydn’s signature style.

        Even those without a deep understanding of music could hear the stark contrast between the two versions; the Consonias, who revered music above all else, of course, could see the improvement. All melodists in the hall felt a rush of conflicting emotions—while they resented Mozart’s arrogance, they could not help but admire her unquestionable talent.


        Unable to confront their emotions, no one clapped when Mozart finished her performance and set down her violin. Silence reigned in the hall for a moment until someone clapped.

        Clap, clap, clap!

        To everyone’s astonishment, the applause came from the composer himself, Haydn. With a gentle smile, he gave Mozart genuine praise, “Bravo. Your performance was perfect, Mozart.”

        “We don’t have much time before next month’s performance,” Haydn said calmly. “Everyone, revise your scores according to Mozart’s version and we shall continue our rehearsal practicing afterward.”

        Haydn adopted Mozart’s version of the symphony, quietly diffusing the tension in the room. While some melodists felt the adoption was an imprudent decision, they had no grounds to judge or express their anger since the composer himself had said nothing against Mozart’s rearrangement. 

        The rehearsal ended uneventfully under a slightly awkward atmosphere. When Haydn pushed open the hall’s doors, Paganini, who had been waiting for him outside, approached him with a soft smile, “You’re late today. Was there a problem with your new composition?”

        “...Nothing. I’ve taken care of it,” Haydn replied with a smile, yet somehow he felt a void inside him. It was as if a layer of ice had formed around his heart, sealing his emotions, ever since Mozart had called his work soulless.

        He involuntarily shut down all his emotions to protect himself from falling apart. His mind seemed to have detached from his body. He watched himself joining Paganini at their usual restaurant and ordering their usual dishes, wearing a hollow smile throughout their conversation.

        Soon, their food arrived. The food was plated beautifully and tasted just as it always had.

        Delicious, yet devoid of surprise.

        Comforting, yet lacking excitement.

        Stable, yet uninspired.

        Everything that had once pleased him now felt bland, tasteless like wax.

        “The food here is just as delicious as it always is,” Paganini said cheerfully, oblivious to Haydn’s inner turmoil. Little did she know her words had struck a nerve with him.

        Everything they did was nothing but a re-experience of their past; nothing was new.

        ‘Everything is the same… same… A word that would be a compliment in other contexts perhaps—but in music, it’s an insult.’

        ‘Is this a reminder that I’ve lost my connection to music? That I’ve become an ordinary, uninspired musician?’

        ‘No… I won’t accept this… I can’t…’ Haydn struggled to breathe as the distressing realization dawned on him. It was as though he were drowning in an ocean, chased by a deadly wave called “despair.” He felt exposed, stripped bare like a man without armor, or perhaps like a fool, blissfully lost in the lie of happiness.

        ‘I’ve given my entire life to music. Without it, I’m nothing… And I can’t live without it!’

        Bang!

        Haydn’s suppressed frustration erupted as soon as he was back in his room. He slammed his fist into the mirror on the wall, causing cracks to spread across the surface.

        His distorted reflection stared back at him, red-rimmed eyes, clenching teeth—so pathetic, so foolish—an image that he desperately wanted to erase.

        From that day onward, Haydn, who realized the depths of his crisis, decisively threw himself entirely into music, locking himself away and devoting every waking moment to composing outside rehearsals. Yet music, cruelly unfair and indifferent, offered no rewards for his dedication. The more he tried, the deeper his despair grew, eventually turning into chains that held him down.

        ‘Why… why can’t I write something new?’
        ‘Mozart… She’s the real deal. She is who music has chosen…’
        ‘I can’t write anything… I’m nothing but a failure…’

        The more he failed to break through his creative block, the more he withdrew into isolation. The once well-groomed conductor became a haggard and unkempt man, living in frustration and self-doubt as days turned into weeks.

        One day, after yet another sleepless night spent agonizing over his compositions, Haydn finally collapsed into a restless slumber. When he awoke late in the afternoon, his weary gaze fell on the calendar. His mind, sluggish and clouded, suddenly found clarity.

        ‘Paganini… It’s her birthday today… I haven’t seen her in so long…’ The thought filled Haydn with guilt. For the first time in weeks, he set aside his creative struggles. He cleaned himself up, stepped out of his house, and bought a bouquet of fresh flowers, hoping to surprise his lover.

        He arrived at her house. Instead of ringing the doorbell, he used the spare key she had given him and entered quietly. It was dark in the living room, except for the glow of light spilling from the bedroom.

        ‘Could she already be asleep? But it’s barely dinnertime. She’s never gone to bed this early…’ A sense of foreboding crept up on Haydn as he approached the bedroom door. From within, he heard noises—breathy gasps, the rustling of sheets, and the unmistakable rhythm of bodies intertwining.

        The sounds struck him like an invisible thunderbolt, leaving him frozen in place. Trembling, he crept closer and peered through the crack only to witness a dreadful sight. On the bed, his lover, Paganini, lay entwined with a younger man, their naked bodies moving with wild passion. It was a side of her he had never seen—raw, untamed—which completely shattered his perception of her.

        Haydn knew he should have burst it, showed Paganini his fury, and demanded answers, but some invisible chains bound his legs when he tried to step forward. All the courage he had summoned evaporated in an instant, so he turned and fled. Yet, what he did not see, as he ran out of the house, was Paganini pulling away from the man. Her gaze, filled with both affection and sorrow, followed his figure into the night. 

        He stumbled into the streets, running aimlessly through the city. His breath came in short gasps as he collapsed onto the ground in exhaustion. His chest burned with anger and an icy despair. A storm of emotions raged within him, pouring on him like blades that tore his soul into pieces.

        ‘Why… Why would Paganini do this to me? Does she not love me anymore?’ Countless questions clawed at his mind. The pain and confusion crashed over him like relentless waves, driving him over the edge. Finally, he reached for the sigil on his skin. An ethereal piano materialized before him, floating in the air, and then he began to play, turning all those churning emotions into notes.

        Not a thought of harmony, structure, or melodic consistency came into Haydn’s mind in his spontaneous creation. Guided by emotion, he abandoned all the rules he had once lived by and played purely on instinct. It was a desperate cry for salvation through music, hoping it could become his anchor and ground him amidst the storm of anguish that threatened to drown him.

        Every note carried the weight of his emotions. Some were bold and thunderous, screaming with rage and frustration. Some were soft and mournful, whispering of heartbreak and sorrow. The melody rose and fell, laying bare his fury, despair, and grief for the world to hear.

        When Haydn finished the final note, he opened his eyes to find himself surrounded by a crowd, greeted with ripples of thunderous applause. It was nothing he had ever experienced before. Everyone clapped as they felt the storm of raw emotions through his music and resonated deeply with the pain he had poured into every sound.

        For so long, he had believed his inspiration had dried up, that his journey in music had come to an end. But now, in this moment of pain and despair, he realized: 

        [i]...Only through turmoil can I awaken my emotions and create something new…[/i]
STORY_10879:
According to the most ancient history, way back to the era when the primordial dragons created the universe, the lord of creation, Daoloth, used the power of constellations to create various instruments and played a requiem to save the lord of destruction, Azathoth, from the conflicting high-dimensional forces within its body.

        While they danced one last time to the requiem across the cosmos, Daoloth’s music—imbued with immense lifeforce—turned into countless seeds of life that scattered throughout space, and one seed took root on a star. Nourished by the emotions of the two transcendent beings, the seed quickly sprouted and came into bud. The buds, though vividly colored and radiant, were unable to bloom due to the leaden weight of their creator’s causality and destiny. It was not until the savior, Enoch, liberated the power of the origin that the buds were finally free from the shackles of fate and bloomed. From the blossoms a new life was formed: gods born in music, who were later known as the Consonias.

        From the moment of the Consonias’ birth, music had been everything to them; they expressed their emotions through songs and inspired creativity through melodies. Gradually, they cultivated their own culture and the unique legacy of melodists over the tides of time. The melodists saw creating harmonious music as their sole mission, vowing to praise the light and public virtues through their tune, and never play a note for individualism, darkness, and corruption.

        As time passed, the first generation of melodists eventually fell. New stars rose, and this is a story that unfolds among the younger generation…

        In the heart of Groove, the bustling capital, stood a magnificent building, the Saint Fleur Music Auditorium, and tonight the opulently designed grand hall was filled to capacity. Everyone waited with bated breath until the light came on. A stream of elegantly dressed men and women emerged from the backstage. They gracefully took their seats and summoned their instruments, ready to perform.

        In the front row, a boy no older than five or six craned his neck, eagerly scanning the stage. He turned to his mother, his voice filled with excitement as he asked, “Daddy? Where’s Daddy?”

        “Shh, keep your voice down,” she whispered, pointing to the right side of the stage, “Look, Daddy’s over there.”

        “Oh! I see him!” The boy covered his mouth. Still, it was not enough to muffle his excited exclaim. He waved enthusiastically at his father onstage.

        Despite the large crowd, the man onstage immediately noticed his son’s gesture. In response, he gave a subtle wave by lightly swaying the instrument in his hands without drawing unnecessary attention.

        “Daddy saw me!”

        “Yes, he did. Now sit down properly. The performance is about to start.”

        “Yes, ma’am!” The boy immediately straightened up in his chair, keeping a straight face. His overdramatic act made his mother let out a soft chuckle.

        Moments later, the concert began. The boy who had never attended a formal performance was overwhelmed by the performance. The music left him in a daze, lingering in his mind even after the performance ended.  It was not until he saw his father after the concert that he regained his senses.

        “Daddy, Daddy! You were amazing!” The boy darted into his father’s arms, his elfin face glowing with admiration. His eyes sparkled as he said, “I want to be a great melodist like you someday!”

        His father lifted him, a teasing smile on his face. “Well then, no more slacking off during practice, okay? Becoming a melodist isn’t easy.”

        “Um…” The boy hesitated, biting his lip. But after a moment, he clenched his tiny fists and nodded with determination, “Okay, I won’t slack off anymore!”

        “That’s my boy, Tchaikovsky! And Daddy will work hard too—maybe one day I can become a conductor and share the stage with you,” his father said wishfully.

        Unfortunately, that dream never came true.

        Years later, his father’s talent withered during dry spells, and he was reassigned as a tunesmith. Stripped of his place as a melodist of the orchestra, he could only watch from the shadows as his former peers continued to shine on stage. The weight of the bitter reality eventually crushed him. He resolutely resigned and opened a small restaurant in town to make ends meet.

        The loving father became a harsh and relentless man who pushed his lost dream onto his son, waking the boy before dawn every day to practice tirelessly until the stars emerged in the night sky.

        As his father wished, Tchaikovsky became a melodist. However, his father only grew even more controlling and oppressive, pushing him toward perfection through endless practices. He dictated everything—from the way Tchaikovsky expressed his music to the precise pressure of each finger on the instrument.

        Everything seemed to be a means to mold Tchaikovsky into his own image so that he could achieve the dream he could never realize.

        The family ties quickly deteriorated under his father’s twisted fixation. Arguments and fights became commonplace; the once warm and close-knit family lost its harmony. The deep-seated resentment against his father within Tchaikovsky slowly turned into hate for music which now only filled him with bitterness and rage.

        Music had brought him and his father pain and despair as much as the hope and joy they had felt in the past. It was a vicious cycle, an endless loop that left nothing but emptiness—like the inevitable end of all living things.

        One day, Tchaikovsky left home early. He wandered aimlessly on the streets and eventually ended up in a bar where he spent the night drinking and dancing until the early hours. Only then did he finally stumble back home reeking of alcohol and smoke.

        The moment he opened the door, he froze, startled by a shadowy figure standing in the doorway. He frantically fumbled for the light switch and reflexively shut his eyes at the bright light. When he finally adjusted to the brightness, he opened his eyes only to meet his father’s cold, expressionless gaze.

        “Ugh! Don’t stand there like that,” Tchaikovsky grumbled, rubbing his face and glaring at his father in annoyance. “You scared me! I thought some of those anti-Court thugs had broken into our home.”

        “Where have you been?” His father’s fury erupted at the sight of Tchaikovsky’s disheveled appearance. “You have a performance tomorrow, and yet you’ve been out all night! How do you expect to become a conductor like this?”

        “Enough!” Tchaikovsky snapped as he saw that familiar look of disappointment on his father’s face. A wave of frustration surged within him. His churning emotions turned into a helpless roar, “I’ve never wanted to be a conductor! That’s your dream!”

        At that moment, Tchaikovsky felt like his entire life was a cruel joke. He was nothing more than a tool to fulfill his father’s ambitions; he had no worth without the title of a melodist. The realization left him hollow, unsure what meaning his music—or his life—held. 

        Once, he had clung to the idea of love and family, but he had grown exhausted over the years. He now felt nothing but lethargic, and with a sudden burst of resolve, he placed his hand on the sigil on his skin and summoned his instrument. Lifting it high, he smashed it against the ground with all his strength.

        CLANG! The instrument—just like the bond between them—shattered into pieces.

        “YOU—” His father’s shock quickly turned into rage. “How could you destroy your instrument? HOW are you going to perform tomorrow?”

        “I won’t perform then,” Tchaikovsky shrugged. “I’m done being a melodist. Honestly, I hate music. I hate the Orchestra. I HATE it so much I wish it would all just disappear!”

        Before his father could react, Tchaikovsky turned and bolted out of the house, the place that now gave him nothing but suffocation. He kept running aimlessly through the empty streets until he reached the seaside promenade. He sank into a bench and stared out at the vast, tranquil ocean, his heart filled with helplessness and confusion.

        Like a wounded child, he buried his face in his knees, trying to shut out the world and escape from reality. However, the world refused to leave him alone.

        Three figures silently approached him. By the time Tchaikovsky looked up in vigilance, he found himself surrounded by three masked men.

        “W-What do you want?!” he stammered.

        “You people in the Court are too arrogant!” one of them sneered as he noticed Tchaikovsky’s uniform.

        “You’re the rebels who oppose the Court!” Tchaikovsky immediately realized.

        Born from the seed of music, the Consonias held music in the highest regard, and they revered the Court of Music, a governing body formed by orchestras that commanded enormous power, even greater than administrative institutions.

        A significant portion of social resources was allocated to supporting the operations of the Court of Music, which bred resentment among those outside the organization. The social discontent gave rise to radical factions that secretly formed anti-Court organizations. Some even plotted extreme actions—including ambushing lone melodists and—what melodists feared the most—crippling their ability to play music.

        “You all think you’re so great when all you do is play instruments! Where do think you get the money and resources to squander if it weren’t for us working quietly in the shadows?” Another man clicked his tongue.

        “Enough talk. Let’s take out his hands!” 

        The men lunged at Tchaikovsky and pinned him down. While the other two gripped his hands tightly, the last one pulled out a hammer, ready to strike—

        ‘No! I need my hands to play music!’ The imminent danger of losing his hands forced Tchaikovsky to face his true desires. Despite his hatred for music and his resentment over his father’s twisted obsession, he could not bear the thought of never playing a song again. Summoning every ounce of strength, he broke free from their grip and shielded his hands with his body.

        “Fine! If your hands mean that much to you, I’ll just kill you instead!” The man shouted as he raised his weapon. However, just as he swung it, a mournful melody reached his ear, freezing him in place with a haunting tune.

        “Damn it… it’s someone from the Court!” The paralyzed man bitterly gritted his teeth. The melody shifted into a gentle lullaby, and one by one, the attackers succumbed to its power and drifted into a deep sleep.

        Meanwhile, Tchaikovsky, as a melodist who had a higher resistance to music, remained unaffected by the music. He raised his head only to see a figure emerge from the shadows—a girl holding a violin. She had such an unmistakably commanding and charismatic presence that Tchaikovsky recognized her immediately.

        “It’s you—Mozart of the Rhapsody Orchestra!” Tchaikovsky gasped in surprise.

        Mozart frowned slightly at his rather impolite shout, but she quickly composed herself and said, “You’re… Tchaikovsky, a melodist of the Nocturne Orchestra… As I recall, shouldn’t you be preparing for tomorrow’s concert? Why are you wandering the streets at this early hour?”

        “I…” Tchaikovsky hesitated, but he then thought, ‘Mozart is one of the most talented melodists of our generation. Maybe… maybe she has the answer to my question.’

        Instead of explaining himself, he asked, “Why did you become a melodist?”

        Mozart looked surprised but she soon realized when she saw the confusion in his eyes. She let out a soft sigh before answering his question, “Because I want to play my own music. What about you?”

        “I… I don’t know. I became a melodist because of my father’s expectations… I hate music… I hate performing…”

        “Yet you were willing to risk your life to protect your hands. If you truly hated music that much, why would you do that?” Mozart asked.

        “But music has only brought me pain. My father forced me to become the melodist he once was… And now I don’t even know why I’m playing anymore…”

        “That’s because you’ve never played for yourself. How can you feel the beautiful essence of music when you’re burdened by someone else’s expectations and dreams?”

        “Then… what should I do?” Tchaikovsky looked at Mozart, his eyes filled with confusion.

        “Resist. Fight. Overthrow who’s in your way—” Mozart looked at him straight in the eye, her eyes burning with conviction as she said the most powerful words, “—with your own music.”

        “With my own music...”  Tchaikovsky repeated the words. His gloomy expression gradually brightened as if he had found a guiding star in the dark.

        [i]‘I don’t hate music itself; what I truly hate is being forced to be someone I’m not. I used to love playing music. I was free, unconfined by anyone’s expectations, and that allowed me to play as who I truly was. Now I know. I won’t let family ties hold me back anymore. I’m going to rediscover music and create my own melodies!’[/i]
STORY_10881:
‘The brilliance of a genius should never be buried—it must shine in all its glory.’

        This thought came into Liszt’s mind as he looked around the Melodists seated around him—or perhaps this idea had long taken root in his mind since the day he became a Melodist of the Nocturne Orchestra, quietly growing into an inescapable yearning that constantly tickled him.

        ‘It’s the Maestro Bach.’ From the corner of his eye, Liszt caught sight of an austere middle-aged man—Bach, the principal conductor of the Court of Music. He silently brushed his fingers against the musical sigil on his body to summon his musical instrument.

        ‘Or perhaps today is the perfect opportunity for the genius to finally be recognized.’

        Like a butterfly breaking free from its cocoon, the restless yearning became an unstoppable force as the opportunity came. Ignoring the rehearsed dynamics, Liszt chose to play his section in his own flamboyant style, adding a cascade of virtuosic techniques to showcase his talent. At the same time, he remained mindful of the overall harmony and elevated the performance to an even higher level with his improv.

        When the performance ended, all Melodists erupted into applause for Liszt, their compliments filling him with a glow of pride. So, when Bach summoned him, he could not help but tremble with excitement as he walked over, certain he was about to receive praise. However, the reality was far from what he expected.

        “Liszt,” Bach said in a low voice, “You are stripped of your role as a Melodist. I’m reassigning you to the workshop and you shall work as an instrument maker starting today.”

        “WHAT? WHY?”  Bach’s words utterly shocked Liszt. His disbelief quickly gave way to a tidal wave of rage that washed away all his sense of decorum. He raised his voice and demanded, “Was there something wrong with my performance?”

        “Nothing,” Bach replied, “It was flawless. Outstanding, even. But the Orchestra has no need for a Melodist who acts on his own whims.”

        “This-this is ABSURD! I—” Liszt stepped forward to defend himself, but a girl held him back, wrapping her arms around him so that he would not offend the principal conductor.

        “Don’t! Liszt! Calm down!” Mendelssohn, a fellow Melodist of the Nocturn Orchestra, pleaded, knowing all too well that Liszt’s reaction would only make things worse.

        In the end, Bach departed under the escort of Chopin, the conductor of the Nocturne Orchestra, leaving Liszt burning with indignation and Mendelssohn looking at him with a worried frown. 

        “Liszt, don’t worry,” Mendelssohn said, trying to comfort him. “I believe Maestro Bach will give you a second chance and let you become a melodist again if you work hard and prove yourself.”

        However, Liszt was too proud and ambitious to accept reality. So, he stormed off with a sharp sweep of his sleeve.

        “Harmony above all else? What nonsense!” Liszt spat, his voice seething with rage. “The capable should rise to the top—that is the only truth!”

        “Exactly. I couldn’t agree more,” A sultry voice suddenly sounded from behind Liszt. He turned around only to see a woman whom he recognized immediately—Paganini, the conductor of another orchestra.

        “Maestra Paganini,” Liszt greeted her with a scowl. Despite knowing her superior position, his foul mood had left no room in his mind for social etiquette. “Sorry, but I have things to do. Excuse me.”

        “Wait,” Paganini said softly. “I can make your wish come true.”

        “...What?” Liszt asked in disbelief.

        “To play freely as you desire—to be the incomparable on the stage,” Paganini said.

        “....And the price?”

        Paganini chuckled and said, “It’s simple. Just give the devil your soul.”
STORY_10882:
Sheets of paper were scattered into the air. The icy grip of humiliation tightened around the heart of Chopin—the very composer of the sheet music—like a bitter blizzard.

        “Chopin, WHAT is this nonsense?” Bach, the man who had hurled the pages into the air, furrowed his brow and questioned.

        “...We need change,” Chopin said, raising his head to meet Bach’s gaze directly. He remained calm and composed despite the conductor’s insulting remarks. Still, his tightly clenched fists betrayed his true emotion. His voice, however, was steady as he explained, “Our music has become stagnant in its style. We will lose all our possibilities one day if we don’t make changes…”

        “We don’t need change,” Bach interjected rigidly, his voice leaving no room for negotiation. “Change is merely an excuse to disrupt harmony. Carrying forward our ancestors’ music is the essential principle of our orchestra and it should never be compromised.”

        “…I understand.” Chopin did not argue further because he knew it would only be a fruitless discussion.

        Always do the right thing at the right time in the right way, and never cross the line—this had been Chopin’s way of conducting himself. It was his philosophy of living.

        Therefore, instead of firing back with venom-laced retorts at Bach’s negation, Chopin calmly bent down to pick up the scattered pages—the sheets of music he had spent the entire spring composing—on the floor one by one.

        “My apologies for wasting your time, Conductor. I shall take my leave now.” Chopin bowed courteously to Bach before walking away. The moment he turned his back against the conductor, the mask of composure shattered, revealing an unrestrained ambition and a burning desire that distorted his attractive features.

        ‘I knew it… True reform must come with pain and upheaval…’ Chopin thought, lifting his gaze toward the darkened sky. A determined smile tugged at the corner of his mouth. ‘Then let me be the one to sound the death knell.’
STORY_10883:
In a bridal chamber, a man and a woman intertwined with a fiery passion. It was only when the woman gently pushed against the man’s arm that he released her from his embrace. His breath was ragged, thick with desire, as he asked, “What’s wrong?”

        “The ceremony is about to begin,” the woman—the exquisite bride—the conductor of the Rhapsody Orchestra, Paganini, gave a lazy smile as she pushed the man—Schumann, not the groom but a fellow melodist of hers—away.

        “You…” Schumann hesitated, unable to voice the question burning in his mind.

        “Don’t worry. This won’t be the end of us,” said Paganini, who perceptively saw through his thoughts.

        “That’s a relief!” Schumann’s face brightened. He planted a light kiss on the corner of Paganini’s eye before he sincerely wished her well, “I hope you and Haydn find happiness together.”

        “Thank you,” Paganini graciously accepted his blessing with a radiant smile.

        Not long after Schumann left, there was a knock at the door. Paganini raised an eyebrow in surprise. She opened the door only to find an elegantly dressed woman standing there. It was Wieck, Schumann’s wife, whose face bore a note of weariness.

        “Wieck?”  Paganini asked in surprise. “What are you doing here?”

        “I… I know about you and Schumann…” Wieck paused as if she was disgusted by her own words. She stared at Paganini, her eyes filled with anger and resentment as she continued, “And here you are marrying Haydn today? You don’t even love him.”

        “I don’t love Haydn you said?” Paganini chuckled, “Oh dear, no one in this world loves him more than I do.”

        “Then why did you seduce Schumann?” Wieck asked in disbelief, her question almost like a shout.

        “I did it precisely because I love Haydn,” Paganini replied firmly. “And Schumann loves you too. But at the same time, he is a sentimental man full of love. It is in his nature, and if you can’t accept this part of him, you will lose the love he has for you one day.

        “You—” Wieck was left speechless by Paganini’s reasoning. Yet, Paganini had no interest nor patience to continue the conversation. She brushed past Wieck and made her way to the wedding venue.

        There she saw Haydn standing at the end of the aisle, waiting for his bride. Clad in an immaculate suit, he looked even more charming and commanding than usual, a sight that made Paganini’s heart flutter, a mesmerizing moment even. It was not until he gently took her hand that she redirected her focus to their wedding.

        “You look stunning today,” she said.

        “And you are beautiful,” Haydn replied with a tender smile. His eyes brimmed with love as he affectionately lifted his hand to tuck a stray lock of hair behind her ear. However, his hand suddenly froze in mid-air.

        “What is it?” Paganini asked softly, sensing his hesitation. Then she remembered—Schumann had planted a kiss on her neck in the bridal chamber earlier, and she instantly understood what had caused Haydn’s pause.

        “Oh, that’s probably a mosquito bite,” Paganini said with a smile. Her tone sounded perfectly natural, so convincing that no one would doubt her words. However, she knew deeply that Haydn would not believe her—even though he hid it well, she still caught that faint flicker of anger in his eyes.

        Unfortunately, there was no time for Haydn to unleash his wrath—the ceremony was about to begin.

        Theatrical melodies filled the air as the romantic sound of strings and pipe organs echoed through the dreamlike garden. To the guests’ warm applause, Haydn walked hand in hand to stand before the officiant.

        What is love?

        “Haydn, do you take Paganini as your wife? To cherish her in wealth or poverty, in sickness or health, in sorrow or joy, to love her faithfully for the rest of your life?”

        “…I do.”

        Is it eternal faithfulness? Or selfless sacrifice?

        Who can define it?

        “Paganini, do you take Haydn as your husband? To cherish him in wealth or poverty, in sickness or health, in sorrow or joy, to love him faithfully for the rest of your life?”

        “I do.”

        [i]I know Haydn better than anyone in this world. I know what he truly desires, so I will willingly jump into the abyss for him, to fulfill his vision, even if it means destroying myself.[/i]

        [i]Perhaps no one will ever understand my love for him, but I don’t regret my decision to be the source of his inspiration—which is something far more eternal than any expression of “love.”[/i]

        “And now, I pronounce you husband and wife. You may begin your destined duet.”

        After the officiant’s declaration, Paganini and Haydn summoned their instruments. With their eyes locking on each other, they began to play in perfect unison. Their melodies intertwined, flowing in a seamless and passionate harmony.

        As Paganini watched Haydn immersed completely in their performance, the fiery love in her eyes burned even brighter.

        [i]‘And this is my one-of-a-kind love for you, Haydn.’[/i]
STORY_10884:
Severed limbs and shattered remains lay scattered across the dry grass. The dead’s eyes remained wide in eternal horror as countless grotesque, misshapen creatures feasted ravenously on their bodies.

        It was a battlefield of utter carnage. Amidst all the sprawling corpses, however, a lone boy survived, holding a bloodied instrument in his arms, his eyes wide with shock as he blankly surveyed the gruesome devastation around him.

        “How… How did we come to this…?”

        The boy was a Consonia, a young Melodist who had gone on his very first mission with the orchestra to exterminate ferocious monsters that had invaded a border planet.

        It should have been an easy assignment, one that was common to the Melodists. However, something went terribly wrong this time, and at the heart of this tragedy was none other than the conductor himself.

        The conductor had long grown weary of the orchestra’s unchanging musical style. He had petitioned the principal conductor many times, begging for reform, but his requests were repeatedly denied. Determined to prove his point, he chose to adopt a new style during this mission. The results were, of course, catastrophic.

        ‘I… I only followed the Conductor’s instructions… But why did we end up like this?’ The boy’s mind spiraled into the depths of confusion and despair. The conductor’s whimsical decision threw the entire orchestra into chaos. The sudden change of style disrupted the Melodists’ rhythm and affected their performance, which eventually weakened the magical barrier they conjured with their music. Like a swarm of bees drawn to the scent of honey, some ravenous monsters poured in through the cracks in the barrier and attacked the defenseless Melodists.

        With each Melodist’s demise, the barrier fractured further. More monsters surged through the gaps and began their hunt, chasing and slaughtering the remaining Melodists one after another. Although the conductor fought desperately, trying to turn the tide, his efforts proved futile. In the end, he sacrificed his life to protect the boy.

        With the conductor’s death, the orchestra fell apart, and the battlefield became the monsters’ feast. Miraculously, the boy lived thanks to the conductor’s dying efforts. He survived as the last member of the orchestra.

        However, miracles are ephemeral. The monsters eventually discovered the boy. They encircled him, closing in from all sides. In that moment of bleak despair, the boy closed his eyes and surrendered to his fate.

        Yet death did not come. Two summoners from the Heptara Unies—who happened to pass through this desolate planet—saved him from the clutches of death.

        He survived, but at a cost far worse than death. The terror of that day had been etched on his memory forever, festering into a fear he could never dispel.

        For years afterward, the once confident boy continued to live in terror and confusion. Eventually, he grew up and turned into a withdrawn and taciturn man who madly indulged himself in music—a desperate attempt to flee the cruel and hopeless memories haunting him.

        The tragedy of the conductor’s failed reform scarred the boy and shaped him into a stubborn and uncompromising Melodist who only obeyed tradition. After paying an immeasurable price, he became the principal conductor, entrusted with the fate of the Court of Music.

        ‘Reforms only invite catastrophe. Preserving harmony is the only and absolute principle we should follow.’

        The boy—now the principal conductor—Bach,  blinded by the fear of his haunting past, clung stubbornly to this belief. He refused to face the mistakes of history. Little did he know that his extreme rigidity would lead the Consonias into an even greater calamity…
STORY_10885:
“WHY? Was there something wrong with my performance?” A young man’s voice echoed through the side hall of the Saint Fleur Music Auditorium, silencing all the other chattering melodists, including the man’s childhood friend, Mendelssohn.

        There, at the center of everyone’s attention, Liszt stood proud as he defiantly questioned the principal conductor, Bach. His face was flushed with rage. 

        ‘This is bad,’ Mendelssohn thought. She immediately rushed to Liszt’s side, attempting to stop him from embarrassing himself in front of everyone.

        Fortunately, Chopin, the conductor of the Nocturne Orchestra, arrived just in time and stepped in to stop the confrontation. He then escorted Bach out of the hall, leaving Mendelssohn looking at the indignant Liszt with a worried frown

        “Liszt, don’t worry,” Mendelssohn said, trying to comfort him. “I believe Maestro Bach will give you a second chance and let you become a melodist again if you work hard and prove yourself.”

        “And then what? Abandon my style and play the same hollow harmony as everyone else?” Liszt retorted, his tone dripping with sarcasm.

        “What’s so wrong with that?” asked Mendelssohn out of genuine puzzlement. Yet, her question only fueled Liszt’s exasperation.

        He clicked his tongue in frustration and yelled, “Someone like you who settles for mediocrity will never understand! I HATE harmony. What is so great about that harmonized hypocrisy that everyone wants to celebrate? I did NOTHING wrong, and I have nothing to change!” 

        With a sharp sweep of his sleeve, Liszt turned on his heel and stormed off. His cold and biting words gave Mendelssohn a pang of sadness. That evening, she returned home with a heavy heart. She headed straight to her bedroom without having dinner, burying herself in her comfortable bed.

        ‘So… is harmony wrong? Is being like everyone else truly such a bad thing?’ Mendelssohn’s mind began to spin with countless questions.

        However, the more she thought about it, the harder she found it to understand Liszt’s perspective. Frustrated, she let out a long, weary sigh. Just then, a soothing melody flowed from the outside of her bedroom, and someone opened the door—

        It was her parents, playing a joyful tune with instruments in their hands. For Consonias who both had once been melodists themselves, it was their most commonly artistic way to lighten their daughter’s spirit.

        “Papa… Mama…” Mendelssohn whispered, deeply moved by her parents’ heartwarming gesture. Touching the musical sigil on her skin, she summoned her instrument and joined their ensemble number.

        The beautiful melody soothed Mendelssohn’s troubled mind. In the warm embrace of sound, she rediscovered her roots—the harmony that had nurtured her since birth and given her protection as she grew.

        Mendelssohn found her answer in the music.

        “I still don’t think anything is wrong with harmony. It’s indeed something worth celebrating. Liszt must have some kind of misunderstanding. He’d surely know the beauty of harmony if I could talk to him.”

        Optimistic and pure-hearted, Mendelssohn was truly convinced she could help her friend see the beauty of harmony. However, what she failed to realize was how unyielding and radical Liszt’s opposition to the concept of harmony could become…

STORY_10891:
In the eastern lands of Tarones, where the ancient Runedragons once thrived, the vast mountain ranges stood tall and imposing, their grandeur untouched by time. However, most of the Runedragons had relocated to the planets in the dragon territories, leaving only a few to guard their old home.

        A crimson Runedragon soared gracefully through the skies, circling above the peaks before descending slowly. The moment his claws touched the ground, his form shifted, transforming into that of a young boy.

        “It seems you’ve recovered quite a bit, Ke Hun,” said Ji Ying, a female Runedragon who approached him with a warm smile.

        “Of course, how could I not after resting for so many years?” Ke Hun replied with a slight shrug. 

        “Still, you’re not fully healed. While you might feel fine now, there’s always the risk of a relapse. It’s best to have someone by your side in case of emergencies.” Ji Ying hesitated before asking, “Where’s your Souliade? Are you two still in a fight?”

        The Runedragons were born in pairs, each bound for life to their Souliade—a partner who would protect them and share an unbreakable bond.

        “He’s the one throwing a tantrum! I don’t even know why he’s always so angry,” Ke Hun grumbled, pursing his lips. “Well, I’m not going to be the one to go looking for him. I can take care of myself just fine.”

        “That won’t do. You’re still recovering, and venturing out alone isn’t wise.” Ji Ying continued after a thoughtful pause, “Perhaps you should go to He’s clan and choose a servant to take care of you.”

        Long ago, one of the Runedragons, Qing Gui, had helped Heshi, the ancestor of the He’s clan, survive in troubled times. To repay Qing Gui’s kindness, Heshi vowed that his descendants would serve the Runedragons for generations, allowing each Runedragon to choose a member of He’s clan as their servant, someone who shall dedicate their life to aiding their master.

        However, the Runedragons were powerful beings, rarely in need of assistance. Only a few had called upon He’s clan over the centuries.

        ‘A servant…’ Ke Hun thought, his mind drifting to irreplaceable moments and the unbreakable bond he had shared with his Souliade, Hua Jin. ‘No… No one can take Hua Jin’s place. I only need one to stand by my side forever—my Souliade, not anyone else.’

        Resolute in his decision, Ke Hun refused Ji Ying’s suggestion. Unable to convince him otherwise, Ji Ying could only breathe a resigned sigh and watched as he left to embark on an adventure alone.

        Ke Hun’s journey went smoothly at first. The long-forgotten thrill of exploration filled him with joy, and he gradually let his guard down. When he came across a human town under attack by some ferocious wild beasts, he did not hesitate to step in, forgetting for a moment that his old injuries had yet fully healed.

        Taking on his human form, he hovered high in the sky to survey the town below. With swift precision, he drew a magical circle in the air to summon a staff of finely carved ebony wood. His sharp eyes scanned the rampaging wild beasts as he channeled his magic, and the tip of his staff began to glow, releasing a brilliant light.

        “Be purged by the breath of the Runedragons!” Ke Hun declared coldly as a powerful surge of magic erupted from him, transforming into a blazing plume of flames that poured down on every wild beast. In the blink of an eye, all the beasts were reduced to ashes, their remnants quietly vanishing into the air.

        “Phew… It’s been so long since I’ve used this much magic. I’m exhausted—” Ke Hun’s words halted as a searing pain tore through his body. His eyes widened in shock as he plummeted from the sky due to the sudden loss of strength. Fortunately, he landed in a soft patch of grass which spared him from serious injury.

        Still, he was far from safe.

        It turned out that the leader of the wild beasts had been observing the battle from the shadows. Seizing the vulnerable moment of its formidable opponent, it revealed itself to strike.

        Ke Hun tried to move, to fight back, but the pain rendered him powerless. He could only lie on the ground, struggling to breathe as he helplessly watched the beast close in.

        ‘Damn it… Why now…’ He gritted his teeth. His vision blurred, and his consciousness began to fade. Just as he braced himself for the end, a familiar figure—a dragon—appeared before him and shielded him from the beast’s attack, slaying it with a ferocious strike.

        Ke Hun tried to call out the dragon’s name—a name that had been echoing in his mind for days. But his voice failed him. His eyelids grew heavier as his strength continued to ebb away. In his hazy vision, he saw the dragon shift into the form of a tall, sturdy man. He walked toward him, knelt down, and gently cradled him in his arms, as though holding the most fragile and precious treasure in the world.

        “Hua… Jin…” Ke Hun finally managed to say the man’s name, his voice trembling with longing and relief, before succumbing to unconsciousness.

        It was after what seemed like an eternity that Ke Hun finally awoke, his body weak but stable. After some effort, he managed to sit up, realizing he was inside a small inn.

        On the table beside him was a cup of freshly brewed tea and a plate of his favorite snacks. Yet, the man who had prepared them was nowhere to be found.

        “...That idiot… Hua Jin, you big idiot!” Ke Hun muttered angrily. The angry frustration tempted him to knock the table over, but he held back, grabbing the tea and snacks instead.

        A sense of peace settled over him as he ate—a quiet reassurance knowing that his Souliade had never stopped protecting him even during their fight.

        From then on, Ke Hun continued his journey in solitude, but with greater caution. Eventually, through a twist of fate, he joined the Starmage and dedicated himself to the study of magic…

        “Fate works in mysterious ways. Clinging to the past will only leave me stagnant. Perhaps, in the future, new encounters will bring a more interesting life than I could ever imagine.”

STORY_10893:
A lean, athletic young man navigated the jagged mountain ravine. His nimble steps skimmed over streams of varying depths with practiced ease until he reached a secluded slope deep within the forest.

        On the fertile soil stood a towering tree, its trunk thick with a dense canopy of leaves. Its branches sagged under the weight of crimson fruits, each one glistening as if kissed by morning dew. Guarding the tree, however, was a ferocious lion-like beast. The creature sprawled lazily under the shade, its long, bushy tail flicking idly back and forth.

        ‘There it is—the Moon Lotus Fruit!’ The young man’s eyes lit up with excitement, but his expression quickly hardened as his gaze fell upon the beast. “Of course, it’s guarded by a Moonlion. But that can’t stop me.  I need that fruit… With it, I can change Bai Hu’s constitution for the better!”

        The young man was named Xuan Huang, a proud member of the Runedragons. As soon as he summoned his power, he transformed into a massive violet dragon amidst a swirl of mist. With a powerful beat of his wings, he launched himself toward the tree.

        “Roooar—!” The Moonlion leapt to its feet, its deafening roar shaking the air as it pounced toward the intruder. The dragon twisted his body in midair to avoid the attack, but the beast was relentless. It lunged again, claws bared, and Xuan Huang retaliated with his own. The two clashed in a ferocious battle, exchanging blows in a fierce dance that spanned more than a dozen rounds. Finally, Xuan Huang spotted an opening. Seizing the moment, he dodged the Moonlion’s strike and dove toward the tree.

        ‘Just a little more—I’m so close!’ Determination burned in Xuan Huang’s eyes as he reached out for the fruit. But just as his claws brushed its surface, the Moonlion swished its tail, coiling it around the dragon. With a forceful yank, it slammed him into the rocky ground, dragging him across the earth and leaving a deep gouge in his scales.

        “Argh!” Xuan Huang let out a guttural roar of pain as the Moonlion growled and tightened its grip with its tail.

        “Damn you, you overgrown cat!” he cursed, thrashing against the tail’s vice-like hold with every ounce of his strength. However, the more he struggled, the tighter it became. The pressure ground against his bones, leaving him gasping for air. A suffocating sense of helplessness crept over him, threatening to extinguish his flame.

        ‘I’m NOT going to lose!’ Xuan Huang roared inwardly. He ceased his futile struggle and began beating his unrestrained wings with all his might. With a mighty flap, he lifted both himself and the Moonlion into the air. Then, with a sudden dive, he plunged toward the ground, twisting mid-fall to hurl the beast into a massive boulder.

        The impact was devastating. The Moonlion slammed into the boulder and slumped to the ground, unconscious, its tail slackening its hold. Finally freed, Xuan Huang wasted no time in snatching the fruit from the tree.

        “Got it… Now I just need to get this back while it’s still fresh!” Ignoring the pain coursing through his body, Xuan Huang clamped the fruit in his jaws and took to the skies, heading toward the Runedragons’ stronghold. As he soared through the heavens, a massive skeletal remains of a dragon came into view—the landmark that marked their territory. Beneath its shadow, he spotted a familiar figure.

        ‘It’s Bai Hu!’ Xuan Huang’s heart leapt as he descended. Shifting back into his human form, he landed softly and approached quietly. Yet, his excitement dimmed when he saw Bai Hu chatting animatedly with a blue-haired man, Qing Gui, a fellow Runedragon whose exceptional talents had earned him the position of the next clan leader.

        The sight seared itself into Xuan Huang’s mind, stirring a bitter envy that clawed at his heart. His emotions boiled over, and before he could stop himself, his hand crushed a nearby stone. The sharp sound jarred in the quiet air, startling Bai Hu, who turned to the source of the noise. When his gaze fell on Xuan Huang, the warmth drained from his face. His smile vanished, replaced by a deep frown that sent a pang of unease through Xuan Huang’s chest.

        “Bai Hu, let’s talk another time,” Qing Gui said, sensing the tension in the air. He offered a polite farewell and left.

        Bai Hu nodded and waved him off. Once Qing Gui was out of sight, he turned to Xuan Huang, his expression stern and displeased. “So, this is why you skipped morning training? To run off and play?”

        “I wasn’t playing. I went to get this.” Xuan Huang brought out the Moon Lotus Fruit he had held behind his back and showed it to Bai Hu.

        “This is… the Moon Lotus Fruit?”

        “Yes. With this, we can improve your frail constitution.” Xuan Huang’s voice was filled with hope, his eyes searching Bai Hu’s face for a spark of joy.

        To his dismay, his gesture only made Bai Hu’s face darken further. His voice carried a hint of anger as he said, “So, you went off to fight a Moonlion by yourself without telling me?”

        “I can handle a Moonlion by myself,” Xuan Huang replied defensively, his frustration rising as he failed to understand Bai Hu’s reaction.

        “Oh, really?” Bai Hu let out a derisive laugh as he grabbed Xuan Huang’s arm, exposing the deep gash in his right arm. “And this? Is this what you call handling it?”

        He then let out a long, disappointed sigh. “Why are you always so reckless? Why can’t you be more like Qing Gui?”

        The words struck like a dagger to Xuan Huang’s heart. The frustration and hurt he had been holding back erupted all at once. “I knew it! You’ve always hated me! Fine! Why don’t you just ask Qing Gui to be your Souliade then?”

        Boiling with rage, Xuan Huang threw the fruit at Bai Hu and soared into the sky in his dragon form.

        “Xuan Huang!” Bai Hu shouted. He tried to follow, but a wave of dizziness overcame him.

        Xuan Huang glanced back from above. His heart clenched as he saw Bai Hu stumble to his knees, and for a second, he thought of turning back to help him. But then he saw Qing Gui appear, steadying Bai Hu. The sight made Xuan Huang’s heart harden once more, and with a final beat of his wings, he disappeared into the clouds.

        At the time, Xuan Huang thought the fight between him and Bai Hu would resolve itself when Bai Hu called a truce, just as all their previous arguments had. However, fate turned out to be unkind this time.

        The demons, enraged by the Runedragons’ protection of the humans, launched a full-scale assault on their clan. Armies of demons descended upon the stronghold, but the Runedragons, with their immense power and the humans’ timely reinforcements, managed to repel the invaders.

        During the chaos, however, Xuan Huang’s reckless nature got the better of him. He defied orders, charging headlong into the heart of the demon army, which led him to be nearly killed. In the direst moment, it was Bai Hu—his Souliade—who threw himself into the line of fire, taking a fatal blow to save his life.

        “Qing Gui! Help Bai Hu!” Xuan Huang cried desperately, carrying Bai Hu’s gravely wounded body back to the stronghold.

        After examining Bai Hu’s injuries, Qing Gui shook his head gravely. “His injuries are too severe. The only way to save him is to let the elements heal him over time while he rests in the form of a dragon egg.”

        “No! With the scarce elemental energy, that’ll take years—centuries even!” Xuan Huang’s voice cracked with desperation.

        “You should be grateful there’s even a chance for him to live,” Qing Gui said, placing a firm hand on Xuan Huang’s shoulder. “If Bai Hu hadn’t protected you, you wouldn’t even have lived. So, don’t waste the chance he gave you and make him worry about you again.”

        With those words said, Qing Gui turned to oversee the post-battle efforts.

        Left alone with the egg that now held Bai Hu’s soul, Xuan Huang sat in silence. His eyes burned with a fierce determination as his fingers gently traced the egg’s surface. His voice softened to a whisper, “Bai Hu, don’t worry… I’ll bring you back, I swear… I’ll find enough pure souls to wake you… This time, I’ll listen, and I won’t let you down again…”
STORY_10894:
One day, a thunderous explosion echoed through the Heavenly Kingdom, shattering the realm’s tranquility like a bolt of lightning striking a calm plain.

        A man with bronze skin stepped out from the ornate parlor, his brows furrowed in concern. Turning to the Xian stationed at the doorway, he asked, “What happened?”

        “Enlightened Master,” the Xian replied with a respectful bow, his expression calm and unruffled as if used to such occurrences, “It seems there was an explosion in the alchemy workshop.”

        “That white-bearded old man must be causing trouble again,” a boy with an impish grin approached the man, Dipankara, interjected, his tone dripping with schadenfreude.

        “Nezha, this is not how you should talk about a senior Xian!” Dipankara scolded the boy in a low voice. “Taiyi Zhenren may come across as a bit of an eccentric man, but don’t forget that it was he who fashioned your lotus body and gave you a second chance at life. You should at least show him some gratitude.”

        “Yes, yes,” Nezha brushed off the admonishment with a half-hearted reply.

        “You—ah, never mind,” Dipankara let out a resigned sigh before turning back to the Xian. “An explosion in the workshop could mean unforeseen consequences. I’ll go check on it. Would you please inform Yuanshi Tianzun if he arrives in my absence?”

        The Xian nodded in response. Dipankara, with Nezha in tow, headed toward the alchemy workshop, where they were greeted by utter devastation—the towering building now bore a gaping hole with debris littering the ground.

        “Well, this is quite the thorough destruction,” Nezha quipped with a smirk.

        “Is that you, lotus boy? Oh, come here and help an old man out, quick…” A voice called out from beneath the rubble, muffled yet audible.

        ‘Is that Taiyi Zhenren? But it doesn’t quite sound like him…’ Nezha mused, a puzzled frown crossing his face.

        “It’s him. Let’s go,”  Dipankara said with a concerned look. The two quickly landed amidst the ruins, spotting a hand protruding from the debris.

        Nezha grabbed the hand and gave it a firm pull. From the cascade of sand and shattered tiles, a man, covered head to toe in dust, rose.

        “Cough, cough!” The flying dust made the man erupt into a fit of coughing. It was not until a moment that he regained his composure and pressed his fingers together, casting a spell to cleanse his robes of dirt. He then turned to Dipankara and Nezha with a broad grin.

        “Dipankara, lotus boy, thank heavens you were here! I’d have been buried under that rubble for half a day if not for you. But alas, the pill I spent seven days and nights refining... is now gone!”  His voice trailed off in lamentation before he noticed the stunned look on the two’s faces. “Why are you two looking at me like that? Is there something on my face?”

        “Who... are you?” Dipankara asked, his composure unusually shaken.

        “WHAT? I’m your dear friend! Your confidant, and old companion, Taiyi Zhenren!” the man exclaimed indignantly. “Dipankara, how could you be so heartless? It’s only been a few months, and you’ve already forgotten me?”

        “It’s not that, old man… no, I mean, I can’t call you that now,” Nezha replied, “Taiyi Zhenren, take a look at yourself, and you’ll understand.” Merging his fingers, he drew a glowing circle in the air, which transformed into a mirror, revealing an unexpected reflection.

        “Wh-what is this? Why do I look like this?” Taiyi Zhenren cried out in shock. The once venerable elder with flowing white hair and a magnificent beard now appeared as a refined, youthful man with smooth skin and a scholarly demeanor.

        “And my beard! My beautiful beard! I spent two hours grooming it every day—WHY is it gone?”

        “Isn’t looking young usually a good thing?” Nezha remarked, crossing his arms and giving Taiyi Zhenren an appraising look before he continued, “You look much more spirited than the old man you were before.”

        “What old man? That was the dignified visage of a true Xian with wisdom! This... this immature face is humiliating!” Taiyi Zhenren shouted, clenching his fists in frustration. “No, this won’t do! I must return to my former self! Dipankara, lend me your pneuma-powered flames—I need to make a pill to fix this!”

        “I’ll lend them to you, but don’t blow up the workshop again,” Dipankara warned.

        “Of course, of course! That was just a momentary lapse. I promise it won’t happen again!” Taiyi Zhenren promised fervently.

        After much reassurance, Dipankara relented and handed over his flames. Taiyi Zhenren raised his fingers and began chanting incantations to summon the Eight-trigram Crucible from beneath the rubble, setting up in the least damaged part of the workshop where he swiftly immersed himself in the art of alchemy once more.

        Seeing that Taiyi Zhenren was fully engrossed in his work, Dipankara turned to Nezha and said, “Let’s go, Nezha.”

        “I… I’ll stay here,” Nezha replied, “I don’t understand a word that goldfish-faced Xian says anyway.”

        “Nezha, you—” As much as Dipankara wanted to reprimand Nezha, he stopped and shook his head with a sigh, “Fine. Stay here and keep an eye on Taiyi Zhenren then. Don’t let him cause any more trouble.”

        With that, Dipankara headed back to the parlor. Nezha watched as his figure retreated into the distance, his eyes glinting with obvious mischief.

        ‘Taiyi Zhenren is so desperate to return to his old self. I’ll just make sure that doesn’t happen,’ Nezha thought, his lips curling into a wicked grin. 

        Taiyi Zhenren, drained from his work for the past seven days, was dozing off beside the crucible. Seizing the opportunity, Nezha approached him with a friendly smile and said, “You look exhausted. Want me to watch the Crucible for you?”

        “You’d do that? Wonderful!” Taiyi Zhenren, trusting as ever, heartily patted Nezha on the shoulder. “I’ve got almost everything covered. Just add the goldenwood if the fire dims.”

        “Yeah, I’ve got it,”  Nezha assured him.

        “Oh, lotus boy, I’m so happy to see how much you’ve grown,” Taiyi Zhenren said, wiping away imaginary tears. “It’s truly such a relief.”

        “…Is that so?” Nezha replied through gritted teeth, suppressing his anger.

        “Yes, yes. I’m going to take a nap now. Just be careful,” Taiyi Zhenren said, paying no effort to conceal a yawn as he wandered off and found a rather intact room in the crumbling building. He began snoring blissfully soon after he threw himself onto a bed.

        ‘Humph, sleep tight now. Soon enough, you’ll find yourself in a nightmare,’ Nezha thought with a sly grin. Then, he casually grabbed a vial from the medicine chest and poured its contents into the Crucible, adding a strange hue to the mixture inside.

        It was only several hours later that Taiyi Zhenren awoke from his peaceful nap. Stretching contentedly, he returned to the Crucible and thanked Nezha for watching over it for him. The boy only responded with a mysterious smile before leaving.

        Despite how strange and puzzling Nezha’s reaction was, Taiyi Zhenren dismissed it as the whims of a teenage boy and directed his attention back to the Crucible, and the pill was finally complete by dawn.

        “Hmm? Why does this pill look a little... different from usual?” Taiyi Zhenren muttered, studying it carefully, but he soon brushed off his doubts. “Bah, I must have remembered it wrong. Once I take this pill, I’ll return to my glorious self, divine, elegant, and wise!” 

        Without hesitation, he swallowed the pill in one gulp. Almost immediately, a cloud of white smoke spread around him. It enveloped his body for a few moments before fading into the air.

        ‘Oh, it’s working! Let’s see the results,’ Taiyi Zhenren thought excitedly. Conjuring a mirror into the air with a flick of his fingers, he eagerly examined his reflection, only to see a younger man stare back at him. His smile froze.  Clutching his head in disbelief, he threw his gaze skyward and let out a desperate wail, “Wh-wh-WHY? Why didn’t it work? Not only did the pill fail to return me to my original self, but now I look even younger!” 

        Meanwhile, Nezha, who had already left the workshop, let out a triumphant laughter as if he could hear Taiyi Zhenren’s cries of despair.

STORY_10916:
