STORY_11124:
Brahmic End - Ch. 3

        On the seventh level of the Brahmic Abyss, a young boy and a girl stood back‑to‑back before the jagged cliffs. A horde of hideous monsters ringed them from all sides, snarling savagely at them,  as if itching to tear the pair apart and feast on their flesh.

        “Ugh! When will this come to an end? How many monsters did those bastards from the World Regulators dump down here?” The boy, Sakra, clicked his tongue in irritation. His tanned skin shimmered faintly as dragon scales surfaced beneath.

        “But isn’t this perfect?” The girl, Alayavijnana, let out a soft, amused laugh. Her fingertip gently brushed Sakra’s spine, sending electric shock-like shivers through his body. Amused by his reaction, she teased, “With this many targets, you can polish your new powers brought by the dragon bone in your body.”

        Not long ago, the gravely wounded Sakra had been cast into the Brahmic Abyss by the mysterious organization known as the World Regulators. Driven by the instinct to survive, he asked Alayavijnana, the ancient demon imprisoned in the depths of the abyss, for help. The demon, in need of a convenient tool, agreed and implanted a dragon’s bone into his body.

        Through agony that literally tore him apart and reforged his body, Sakra clawed his way back from the clutches of death with new powers. He then began his training with Alayavijnana, learning how to wield the dragon bone’s powers, and even defeated the monster that guarded the thirteenth level, the Bodhi Tree.

        After that, Alayavijnana and Sakra traveled side by side, climbing level after level. Though they were continuously attacked by unknown monsters along the way, they effortlessly repelled every threat with their combined might—just like this one.

        Alayavijnana stood atop a mountain of corpses. Crimson threads spread from her fingers, weaving into a web of fate that sliced through the throats and hearts of the monsters with effortless precision. Despite the bloodshed, her expression remained calm, her eyes unshaken, as if death was nothing more than a part of the natural cycle.

        Meanwhile, Sakra fought at the front, letting out a throaty roar as the dragon bone’s powers coursed through his body. With a swing of his fist, he blasted a monster’s skull apart. Blood rained down, the heat so intense it melted the rock beneath their feet.

        “Right rear.” Alayavijnana’s voice was soft, yet it struck his mind like a command branded into his soul.

        Sakra spun instantly. Lightning burst from his palm and reduced the ambusher to ash. Veins bulged at his temples as he panted and said, “I—I can keep up with you now!”

        “No,” Alayavijnana said with a slight smile on her lips. With a flick of her hand, she slit the last monster’s throat with her red threads. Blood splattered across her face. Without blinking an eye, she simply wiped it away, her tone strangely gentle as she said, “I’m the one matching your pace. But… you did well.”

        The monsters’ screams faded. Silence reclaimed the battlefield

        “Argh!” Suddenly, a stabbing pain exploded in Sakra’s chest the moment he let down his guard.

        The pain drove him to his knees. His spine bulged as the dragon bone writhed within him. Scales tore through his skin; his fingertips sharpened into claws. With his pupils turning into golden slits, his horns unleashed a blinding golden radiance.

        Alayavijnana knelt beside him. The powers within the boy surged like a tidal wave; she could feel his bones trembling, his blood boiling, as she brushed his neck with her fingers.

        “You can’t suppress the bone’s power.”

        “Yes, I can… I can do it my—agh!” His protest was cut short as streaks of lightning erupted from his back, threatening to burn him alive.

        “Don’t move.” Alayavijnana gently murmured, her voice carrying more authority than any command. Sakra froze as she cupped his face. The crimson threads dissolved into a soft glow between her palms. “Let me suppress it for you.”

        Then, she kissed him.

        Her kiss was no intimate act, but an act of domination, one that symbolized her control. Through the contact of their lips, she poured her powers into him to subjugate the rampaging dragon bone within his body.

        Only moments later did she draw back. Though the searing pain had vanished, the boy’s heart churned like a storming sea.

        His eyes widened in shock. His breath quickened as his face flushed scarlet. His voice trembled with panic: “Y-You— How could you just do that?”

        “What’s the problem? I saved your life.” Alayavijnana chuckled. Her eyes revealed a mischievous glint as she teased, “Or… are you blushing?”

        “I am NOT!” Sakra sputtered, mortified. He spun around and stormed toward the passage ahead.  “I-I’m going to check if there are more monsters!”

        “Sakra—” Suddenly, the ground began to shake violently when she had barely spoken.

        The earth beneath Sakra’s feet split open with a thunderous crack. In the next instant, a current of dark serpent-shaped shadows surged through the crack. Quiet yet incredibly swift.

        “Wha—” Sakra barely turned before a shadow coiled around his waist. In the blink of an eye,  both he and the shadows disappeared into the fissure, leaving not even a trace of his presence.

        Alayavijnana’s pupils contracted. She immediately shot her crimson threads to catch up, but the fissure had already sealed, as though it had never existed. The threads struck empty air and scattered into fading sparks.

        “Heh, the audacity to steal my person right under my nose… Interesting.” Her smile vanished, replaced by a cold, lethal glare. “Very well. I’ll show you who writes the laws of causality.”

        Crimson threads flared in her palm once again, only to be severed by another force.

        A tall, broad‑shouldered man slowly stepped out from a warped black rift. His eyes shone with a saintly yet detached clarity that seemed to see through the truths of the world.

        “Who are you?” Alayavijnana asked, her tone sharp with impatience.

        “Karuna, a follower of the World Regulators.” His voice was deep, hands pressed together in solemn prayer.

        “Oh? So you’re one of those lunatics who want to destroy the world.”

        “Ancient demon, Alayavijnana, submit to us.” Karuna’s voice brimmed with mournful compassion. “All existence is tainted. Only extinction is true salvation. And you, with your powers capable of erasing causality, are the most fitting guide for this purification.”

        “All existence is tainted?” Alayavijnana let out a mocking laugh. “That’s merely a coward’s excuse. Why would I ever want to stand beside some trash like you?”

        “You’re stubborn,” Karuna shook his head sadly. “Perhaps your karma will enlighten you.” As he began to chant, golden light burst from his palms and engulfed the entire space.

        Darkness flickered across Alayavijnana’s vision. When light returned, she was no longer in the Brahmic Abyss, but in a boundless, pitch‑black cosmos.

        Hovering before a colossal star was a flawless dragon, his wings unfurled. His eyes—no longer empty or hollow—burned with pure fury that was so vivid and alive, a proof of his unmistakable will.

        No one knew this dragon better than Alayavijnana. After all, she had created him herself and named him Paramita.

        “...I see,” She whispered, “I’m having a vision of the past…”

        “A vision?” Paramita’s voice rumbled through the cosmos. “I am no vision! I’m right here! I’m no longer the mindless dragon that had to listen to your command. I’ve learned to think—and to hate!”

        “And?” Alayavijnana asked, despite knowing she was talking to an illusion. “What are you thinking now? What do you want?”

        “I wanted freedom!” Thunder roared as Paramita bellowed. “But you stole it from me! You called me perfect, then demanded I crawl at your feet! Alayavijnana, you know nothing of life!”

        “I do. And that is exactly why I needed you to obey me.”

        “But I never wanted your control nor your command! I refuse to obey you! I’m going to tear you apart, Alayavijnana!” Paramita roared, flapping his wings as he charged at Alayavijnana, so quickly like lightning that blazed across the void.

        Amidst the golden streak, countless crimson threads materialized in the air. As Alayavijnana swept her arms, the threads joined and created an intricate web that wrapped around the dragon’s wings and head, trapping him in place.

        “Paramita, I once paid the price for underestimating your ambition. But I won’t repeat that mistake.” She drew close, stroking the dragon’s head as she whispered.

        “Why… Is this what you meant when you said you loved me?” Paramita’s voice trembled with sorrow.

        “Yes. My love is possession, and possession means dominion,” Alayavijnana said in a flat tone. “I have no hesitation in destroying my creation if they betray me. There’s no reason to keep a creature that disobeys its creator.” 

        The crimson threads abruptly tightened and slit the dragon’s skin. Blood sprayed across the cosmos. Paramita screamed, writhing in pain, but the threads held firm. Slowly, life drained from him until he collapsed upon the colossal star beneath them.

        Alayavijnana withdrew her threads and descended gracefully beside the fallen dragon and gazed upon the dragon’s flawless form.

        She still remembered the day she created Paramita, as well as the words she had whispered to him with her most gentle voice before he was awake to the world: “If you open your eyes and be my dragon, I will give you a future free from causality.”

        To her disappointment, Paramita refused to be her dragon when it awakened.

        A flicker of emotion—pain or warmth perhaps—crossed her eyes, but it soon disappeared into the crimson light that returned to silence as the crimson threads faded.

        “Don’t worry, Paramita. I will make you anew, and you can’t defy me next time,” She murmured with quiet longing as she placed her hand over the dragon’s dimmed eyes.

        “NO! I don’t want to be made anew by you!” Suddenly, countless eyes and mouths appeared on the dragon’s corpse, screaming, “I don’t want your control! I don’t want your domination!”

        Thunder exploded again. The illusory cosmos turned into an abyss of roaring dragons. Yet, Alayavijnana remained unfazed. She simply lifted her gaze and asked, “Karuna, do you really think I would falter because of this?”

        She extended a hand. From her palm, numerous threads erupted and pierced the invisible walls, ripping the illusory world apart along with Paramita’s twisted form and its shrieks. She was back to reality, where Karuna stood before her, impaled by one of her threads. Blood pooled beneath his feet.

        “I knew it… I can’t trap you… Alayavijnana… the demon of causality…”

        “I never cling to the past, nor drown in regret.” Alayavijnana stepped toward him. She gripped the thread lodged in his chest. Her lips curved as she said with unshakable conviction, “Creations that defy me die. That is my rule, the end I define.”

        She tore the thread free. Karuna couldn’t even let out a final cry before his body crumbled into dust and drifted away on the wind.

        [i]‘I’ve wasted too much time on this fool… all because I cared too much about Paramita… Now, where is my dragon…’[/i] Alayavijnana closed her eyes, quietly searching through the abyss with her senses. Soon, she sensed a familiar presence not far away—it was Sakra.

        However, his presence was terribly faint and unstable, flickering as if it might vanish at any moment.

        “Good. He’s still alive.” She said, though her furrowed brows revealed her irritation.
        “Sakra, don’t you die on me before I find you. Otherwise, I will drag your soul back even if I must tear the world apart.”

        Countless red threads erupted again. Engulfed by the threads, her form magically turned into a scarlet flutter of butterflies that flew toward the upper levels of the abyss…
STORY_11125:
Brahmic End - Ch. 4

        On the seventh level of the Brahmic Abyss, a snake woman, half-human, half-snake, hid in a secluded corner between layers of ashen stones, her tail wrapping around a tanned boy. She tightened her tail’s grip again and again, trying to throttle him. Yet, the boy held his arms wide and forced back the fatal pressure, refusing to let himself be strangled.

        His name was Sakra.

        Not long ago, Sakra, gravely wounded, had been cast into the Brahmic Abyss by the mysterious organization known as the World Regulators. Driven by the instinct to survive, he asked Alayavijnana, the ancient demon imprisoned in the depths of the abyss, for help. The demon, in need of a convenient tool, agreed and implanted a dragon’s bone into his body.

        Through agony that literally tore him apart and reforged his body, Sakra clawed his way back from the clutches of death with new powers. He then began his training with Alayavijnana, learning how to wield the dragon bone’s powers, and even defeated the monster that guarded the thirteenth level, the Bodhi Tree.

        From then on, Alayavijnana and Sakra traveled side by side, climbing level after level and slaying unknown monsters one after another. However, the snake woman, Upasama, abducted Sakra while the pair was in a moment of distraction, which left the boy in his current peril.

        To keep him subdued, Upasama dragged him through the cavern tunnels. Yet, the boy was unyielding, refusing to let her tighten the coils again. His grip on her tail had not loosened once, despite his bloodied form.

        ‘I can’t die now! I still have to avenge my sister!’ Sakra roared inside his mind, the powers of the dragon bone churned along his blood. In the next instant, he forcefully pried apart Upasama’s tail. His muscles tightened, unleashing an unexpected burst of power as he reversed their positions, slamming Upasama into a wall.

        Boom! Sakra’s ferocious strike stirred up a cloud of dust. Upasama cried out in pain, reflexively releasing her hold on him. Both of them crashed down onto the ground.

        “You wretched brat!” Upasama spat through clenched teeth and began lashing her tail again. Sakra pushed himself up in time, leaping aside to evade the strike. Lightning flared around him as he summoned his powers, coalescing into a crackling thunderbolt that shot directly toward the snake woman.

        Upasama barely had the time to evade the attack. The bolt grazed her shoulder. Some of her scales shattered, causing blood to splatter. Her pupils shrank to needles. For the first time, she felt as if she were the prey instead of the hunter.

        [i]‘How does he possess such strength… If I clash with him head-on, I may actually lose…’[/i] Panicked, she grit her teeth and drew out a ghanta, a palm-sized ritual bell. Pressing her palms together, she poured her magic into the bell. 

        The bell began to grow, expanding into a giant bell taller than a person in the blink of an eye. Despite the absence of wind, it rang, its tone deep and far-reaching.

        “This is—ugh!” Before Sakra could figure out what the bell was, a wave of overwhelming dizziness struck him. His vision blurred.

        “No… no…!” He struggled desperately. The horns on his forehead shimmered with faint light as he tried to resist the dizziness with his powers, but the knell overwhelmed him, and he could only let himself fall into a fathomless dream…

        When Sakra opened his eyes again, he saw a sky tinged with a golden hue.

        The breeze of spring brushed his face, carrying along the fragrance of flowers and the scent of rippling rice fields. At the far end of the grassland were the town’s walls, with flags fluttering above the gate. Behind the walls stood rows of brick houses. It was a sight etched into his memory. This was his homeland, the kingdom of Sumeru.

        “I… I’m back?” His head throbbed with pain. He lifted a hand to rub his brow, only to find that he was holding a bouquet of vibrant flowers. In a daze, he murmured, “Ah… that’s right. Today is the day Sister returns to the town. I came to the outskirts to pick the prettiest flowers for her…”

        Sakra had a twin sister, Shachi, who was the saintess of the kingdom. The siblings had never officially met, for the previous saintess had taken Shachi away since the moment of her birth. Still, Sakra cared deeply for this sister who shared his blood.

        Several days ago, an organization, the World Regulators, had requested a meeting with the saintess at their headquarters. The king of Sumeru, wary of the organization’s influence, had no choice but to send Shachi away for a week, and today was the day she was to return.

        Sakra had long awaited his sister’s return. Somehow, he felt an inexplicable dread that urged him to stand up and run toward the gates. And the moment his foot crossed the threshold, a somber sound of the death knell traveled through the air.

        “The saintess has fallen—” The knell echoed hollowly through the town, battering the boy’s soul like a heavy hammer.

        [i]‘No… That can’t be…’[/i] Sakra’s mind exploded with shock the moment the death knell reached his ears. Blinded by panic, he sprinted for the sanctum, shoving aside the crowd as startled cries and anguished shouts burst around him.

        The sanctum’s doors were firmly shut, guarded by two armored men blocking the entrance with their crossed blades.

        “Halt! The saintess’s remains are being prepared. No one is allowed—”

        “Move.” Sakra’s voice thundered.

        “You insolent kid! Step back—”

        “I SAID MOVE!” Sakra shattered the stone pillar before the doors with a single kick. Shards flew in all directions in a swirl of dust. A faint gold gleam lit his eyes as a terrifying aura surrounded him. The guards froze beneath the weight of his murderous intent before finally backing away and opening a way through.

        Sakra stormed into the sanctum and rushed into the quiet chamber of rites. At its center lay a white coffin.

        The warm glow of dusk fell gently upon the girl resting within. She was Shachi, both the saintess revered by the people of Sumeru, and the sister he had adored.

        She looked serene, as though peacefully asleep. However, the black stitches on her wrists, ankles, and chest suggested otherwise; she looked like a doll that had been torn apart and sewn back together.

        “No… no illness looks like this… It was them… Those bastards from the World Regulators killed you!” Sakra fell to his knees with a thud. Grief and fury churned inside him until they overflowed as tears that dripped onto the cold floor.

        Suddenly, Shachi’s fingers twitched. The girl who was supposedly dead slowly sat upright and opened her eyes. In her calm eyes was the reflection of Sakra’s surprised face.

        “Sister! You’re alive!”

        “No. I died long ago.” Shachi’s was soft as ever, yet now tinged with a chilling malice. “And it was your fault. You failed to protect me. You let them turn me into their experiment, and let them torture me in ways no one could imagine.”
 
        “I… I didn’t know they would treat you like that! If I had known, I would have stopped them even if it meant defying the king!” Sakra choked up as guilt swept over him. He prostrated himself before her with complete submission.

        “How pretty your words sound. Still, you didn’t stop them from taking me away. And you even failed to avenge me. Those bastards defeated you and threw you into the Brahmic Abyss like garbage. Sakra, you are useless.” Shachi berated her twin brother instead of accepting his apology, her tone sharp with contempt.

        “I’m sorry… Sister… It’s all my fault…” With his heart quivering with agony, all Sakra could do was to keep apologizing helplessly.

        “I knew you couldn’t accomplish anything without me.” Shachi picked up a dagger and placed its tip over Sakra’s chest. With a stiff smile, she said, “So come with me. Use your death to atone for what you’ve failed me.”

        The dagger pressed deeper. The pain was excruciating, but Sakra didn’t resist. Instead, he closed his eyes, allowing her to drive the dagger in—

        Clang! A flash of red light sliced through the air and knocked the dagger away.

        The force sent Sakra staggering back. When he looked up, he saw a beautiful girl standing before him. Her hair danced in the glow of dusk; her eyes, as deep as an endless abyss, now burned with cold anger.

        “Who gave you permission to die?” she demanded. Her voice was so familiar in a way that tugged at Sakra’s soul. However, he had no memory of her, so he asked blankly, “You… who are you?”

        “Don’t tell me you’ve forgotten about me? Oh my, you’re truly a trouble,” The girl said with a slight frown. In the next moment, a red thread wrapped around Sakra’s neck and pulled him toward her. She cupped his face with her slender fingers, leaning down as she whispered, “Then let me remind you.”

        Her lips touched his.

        Red threads streamed from her palm and disappeared into the boy’s body. As the illusion’s restraints cast on Sakra were broken and the dormant powers within him reawakened, the dragon bone unleashed a silent roar, its resonance echoing through his blood.

        Memories all came flooding back in an instant— the Brahmic Abyss, Alayavijnana, their covenant of dominion and submission.

        Embarrassed, Sakra pushed Alayavijnana away, his cheeks burning as he stuttered, “W-What… what is going on…?”

        “You’re in an illusion,” she replied flatly, her eyes turning toward the warping sanctum. “It’s one of the World Regulators’ traps. To escape, we must destroy its core.”

        “The core?”

        “Her.” Alayavijnana pointed to Shachi, who was still sitting in the white coffin.

        “But… she’s my sister.” Sakra hesitated.

        “She is merely a shadow from the past, a karmic bond you’ve yet to sever, ” Alayavijnana said coldly. “If you don’t sever that bond, the illusion will eventually devour you.”

        “I…” Sakra’s breath quickened; his fingers trembled.

        “I will do it if you can’t.”

        “…No. I’ll do it.” Sakra finally made up his mind. As he walked toward Shachi, his gaze lingered on the elegant features that mirrored his memories to the last detail. They belonged to the girl he had idolized all his life. Now, he had to destroy her with his own hand.

        [i]‘Forgive me… Sister.’[/i]

        Closing his eyes, Sakra summoned his powers. When he opened them again, her pupils had turned into golden slits. He then threw a punch. Shachi’s form shattered into countless fragments that were scattered by the wind.

        With the core destroyed, the illusory world shook violently. Within seconds, the world broke apart into a cascade of light shards, then collapsed with a resounding crash.

        “You did a good job.” Alayavijnana walked to his side, comforting him in a gentle voice while brushing his grief-stricken face.

        Before Sakra could say anything, they found themselves back into the Brahmic Abyss, where Upasama lay on the ground clutching her chest; at her feet lay her ghanta, broken in half.

        “You actually broke my illusion… Damn it!” Seeing the tables had turned, Upasama immediately thrashed her tail to flee. However, Alayavijnana’s crimson threads had already surrounded her, binding her limbs.

        “You know, taking what’s mine comes with a great price,” Alayavijnana whispered as she tightened her threads.

        “N-no—wait—please—don’t—! Aaaah!” Upasama’s shrieks split the air as the threads tore her body apart. Blood sprayed across the earth, staining the pale rock crimson.

        Sakra watched as Alayavijnana retracted her threads. He felt a storm of conflicting emotions. In the end, he lowered his head and muttered, “Thank you… for saving me again.”

        Smack!

        A stinging slap landed on his cheek. It was so sharp and merciless that it caused his face to swell instantly.

        “W-what was that for?”

        “That was your punishment.” Alayavijnana’s voice was cold. She abruptly leaned in, their faces separated by barely the width of a finger, their breaths mingling in the limited space.

        “You are my dragon. My kin. I decide whether you live or die. Don’t ever let your life end up in someone else’s hands again. Do you understand?”

        “I…”  Only a breath away, Alayavijnana’s face was so close and spellbinding that Sakra couldn’t pull his eyes away. That unnameable feeling stirred again within his chest, and finally he answered in quiet submission: “…I understand.”

        “Good.” Alayavijnana turned, her silver hair fluttering in the wind. “Come. We still have a long road ahead.”

        Sakra followed in silence. In his eyes burned a bright, fervent light. It was the light of devotion and the beginning of obedience.
STORY_11126:
Brahmic End - Ch. 5

        “Hah… Finally, we reached the third level,” a boy muttered, standing at the entrance of the third level of the Brahmic Abyss, his breath uneven, sweat still glistening on his brow.

        “Finally? This is only the third level,” said a girl in an even tone, approaching with unhurried steps.

        Her name was Alayavijnana, and the boy was Sakra.

        Not long ago, Sakra, gravely wounded, had been cast into the Brahmic Abyss by the mysterious organization known as the World Regulators. Driven by the instinct to survive, he asked Alayavijnana, the ancient demon imprisoned in the depths of the abyss, for help. The demon, in need of a convenient tool, agreed and implanted a dragon’s bone into his body.

        Through agony that literally tore him apart and reforged his body, Sakra clawed his way back from the clutches of death with new powers. He then began his training with Alayavijnana, learning how to wield the dragon bone’s powers, and even defeated the monster that guarded the thirteenth level, the Bodhi Tree.

        From then on, Alayavijnana and Sakra traveled side by side, climbing level after level. They slayed unknown monsters one after another, breaking the ambushers’ illusions, and after much struggle, they finally arrived at the third level.

        “Three more levels and we’ll reach the end!” Filled with determination, Sakra stepped forward, only to freeze as a sudden dragon’s roar shook the heavens. 

        Dozens of murky silhouettes came swooping from the shadows, their wings slicing through the air like sharp blades.

        “We’re ambushed—” Sakra had barely spoken before Alayavijnana flicked her hand.

        Countless crimson threads unfurled from her fingertips. In the blink of an eye, the threads intertwined and created a space defined by her karmic law. Light and shadows danced around her, spinning and folding, as if reality had been reshaped at her touch. With a sweep of the threads, all the ambushers—a flight of fledgling dragons—were all erased in a breath before they could even scream.

        “The audacity to ambush me. What a bunch of foolish dragons.” Alayavijnana murmured, her lips curling with quiet amusement.

        Suddenly, the entire level began to shake violently. A colossal dragon emerged through smashed rocks. With its black scales gleaming with a golden hue, its eyes glowed with an eerie light. Its aura was so raw and savage that it seemed ready to crush the whole space.

        “WHO are you?” the dragon roared. “How dare you slaughter the brood of Shadowdragons!”

        “Oh? So you’re the Shadowdragons.” A faint smile tugged at Alayavijnana’s lips as crimson threads spun above her palm. “Perfect. Today marks the extinction of your clan.”

        Her voice was terrifyingly calm, as though she were merely stating a fact.

        “Insolent brat!” The dragon, Prajna, let out a wrathful roar, its voice so powerful that it unleashed a shockwave that sent stones flying everywhere. It then spread its wings and dove, its sharp talons ripping through the air.

        Alayavijnana took a slight turn. The talons scraped past her hair, leaving only an invisible trail in the air. Unexpectedly, a murderous aura pressed against her spine before she could strike back. In that moment, her instincts took over. Crimson threads flared from her palm in a burst of light and blocked the thunderous blow just in time. Even so, the force drove her back several steps. Her breaths faltered. She lowered her gaze, face darkening as she saw her attacker—Sakra.

        However, those eyes held neither the defiant spark nor the fervor she recognized, only a pool of pure hatred and resentment, so dreadful, almost suffocating. It was something that Sakra had never had.

        The sight made Alayavijnana slightly frown. Crimson threads trembled in her hand as she demanded coldly, “You’re not Sakra. Who are you?”

        “Heh, so you noticed. Long time no see, my dear creator.” The voice—low, mocking, and soaked in malice—belonged to someone else, one that dredged up memories she had buried long ago.

        “Paramita.” Alayavijnana’s brow slightly darkened as she spoke the name with conflicted emotions. “You’re dead.”

        “I woke him,” said Prajna, landing beside Paramita. It lowered its head and stared at Alayavijnana; its gaze betrayed a cruel amusement.         “A fragment of his soul lingered within the dragon bone. He never truly died, simply asleep within the boy’s body, and I awakened his will.”

        “And?” asked Alayavijnana, tilting her head slightly. Her voice dripped with disdain: “I killed him once; I can kill him twice.”

        “You’re still as arrogant as ever, Alayavijnana.” Paramita lifted a hand, lightning crackling at his fingertips. “Let’s see whether you kill me again, or whether I end your dominion here!”

        Paramita and Prajna lunged at Alayavijnana at once. She conjured a shield with some of her threads in defense while spinning the other behind the dragons in a retaliatory strike. However, Paramita evaded it with his keen senses. Meanwhile, Prajna seized the opening and struck, but she avoided it with a simple leap.

        They clashed back and forth, each exchange more savage than the last. Their batter left the third level in ruins—rock scarred with claw marks and craters, dust rolling like a storm.

        There were moments when Alayavijnana could have ended Paramita with a single thrust, yet she pulled back each time. Paramita sensed her hesitation and turned it into an advantage, steering the flow of battle until Prajna managed to trap her with its tail.

        With a roar and a sweep of its tail, Prajna hurled her into a wall, pinning her on the surface with all his might.

        “It’s over.” Paramita walked to her side, his golden eyes lit by the thrill of a hunter who’s finally cornered his prey. “This happened because you went soft. You couldn’t bring yourself to kill this boy.”

        “Of course not. I’ve poured all my heart into crafting him. I can’t destroy my creation without a fair reason.” Even with peril pressing in, Alayavijnana remained unfazed. Instead, she smiled and said confidently, “Besides… this isn’t over.”

        She flipped her palm. Crimson threads materialized in the air and stabbed Paramita right in his brow. Then she shouted: “Sakra! Wake up!”

        “ARGH!” Paramita’s pupils trembled violently as two consciousnesses collided within the same body—

        Within a boundless ocean of golden waves, the sea of consciousness, Paramita, in his dragon form, gazed down at Sakra struggling up through the crashing surf.

        “Give my body back, you filthy thief!” Sakra glared up and shouted, his fists tightly clenched.

        “Sakra, I am not your enemy.” Paramita descended, folding his wings as a friendly gesture. He looked down at Sakra and continued, “Your true enemy is Alayavijnana.”

        “Lies! If not for her, I’d be dead! She could never be my enemy!”

        “She saved you only because she needed a puppet, an obedient pet. And you were the perfect choice. But I’m nothing like her. Work with me, and I guarantee you will get your freedom.”

        “…Freedom?” Sakra repeated.

        “Yes. Alayavijnana will only make you her slave. She will rob you of your freedom, your will—”

        “So what?” Sakra cut him off.

        Sakra recalled the first time Alayavijnana commanded him to rise, her tone frigid yet laced with a faint warmth that drew him in.

        He remembered the tingling sensation and the sense of peace when she touched his horns; he remembered that domineering kiss she gave him to stop his powers from rampaging, pulling him from the depths of untamed fury.

        Her cold discipline had shaped him between the countless brushes with death and survival; it was her gaze that kept him moving forward.

        ‘Her control holds a softness that makes one fall… and makes one hunger for more.’ Sakra concluded inwardly with enthralled devotion as he revisited every memory of her.

        To Paramita’s horror, he realized Sakra was untroubled by the idea of submission. Nevertheless, he persisted.  “You have no idea what that means. You’ll lose the right to your own heart, bound to her command, living only at her pleasure.”

        “And I ask you, what is wrong with that?” Sakra asked. “Her dominion is what keeps me alive. She gave me purpose and powers. I’d have died at the lowest level of the Brahmic Abyss if it weren’t for her.”

        Sakra lifted his gaze. His eyes held a brilliant, almost wild, fire. He spoke with devotion that Paramita could not understand, “I don’t need freedom. I don’t want to choose my own path. I just need someone to show me the right path—and Alayavijnana is the one I’m meant to follow!”

        “You—” Sakra’s reply left Paramita speechless, wide-eyed. “You’re insane! That isn’t trust! That’s imprisonment!”

        “Perhaps to you. But to me, it is home.” Sakra’s voice turned cold. “Domination or possession—whatever you call it, I accept it, and I savor it. And no one gets to be the judge of that!”

        A blinding radiance rippled through Sakra’s form. Even as he spoke, he was clawing his way back into control, reclaiming the authority that had been stolen from him.

        “So get out of my body now! You uninvited parasite!”

        Sakra’s voice boomed across the sea of consciousness. Amidst the light that swallowed everything in its wake, Paramita’s form shattered in the raging wind as he gave his final, defiant howl—

        “Sakra! One day you’ll regret this! You won’t live under her rule forev—” His voice vanished, and silence was restored to the sea of consciousness.

        Sakra opened his eyes. Lightning roared across his skin as he regained full command of his body, and Paramita’s presence had completely vanished. Prajna turned around in terror, fear flashing across its eyes as it sought to flee, but Sakra was a step ahead of it.

        “You’re not getting away,” Sakra muttered, lightning flashing over his fist as he hurled it at Prajna in a ferocious arc.

        BOOM! Sakra’s punch split the air as lightning speared through Prajna’s body, leaving nothing but blackened ash behind.

        Sakra sank to his knees, drained of strength. Alayavijnana walked toward him at an unhurried pace. She looked down at him with a faint smile. “You did well, Sakra. As your reward—”

        She paused, then bent close. Her fingers slid over one of his horns. Her eyes glinted with mischief and something far more suggestive as she whispered, “I’ll grant you one wish. Anything you want.”

        “An… anything…?” Sakra repeated blankly.

        His reaction made Alayavijnana laugh. Her fragrant breath brushed his ear as she leaned close and whispered, “Yes. Well? Feeling excited?”

        Sakra froze. His face blazed red as he denied, “W-What are you talking about? I-I-I’m not excited at all!”

        Sakra was so flustered that his voice nearly cracked at the last word, which made the moment even more humiliating. He spun around in a panic and bolted, throwing back a hasty, overwrought excuse: “I—I’ll go… go check the path ahead!”

        Alayavijnana watched as the boy ran away. Her smile faded into silence while the crimson threads slid from her fingers, melting quietly into formless light.

        “Struggle only tightens karma’s hold…” she murmured, her eyes glinting with a strange blend of compassion and quiet tenderness.

        “It is the law of causality, and it is my love.”
STORY_11127:
Brahmic End - Ch. 6

        Cold wind howled outside the Keep of Asamskrta—the entrance to the Brahmic Abyss, carrying with it a sharp scent of blood and rusted iron.

        A tall, broad-shouldered man dragged a dead monster along the ground. Blood continued to drip from the ragged stump of the monster’s neck, leaving a glaring red line over the frozen earth. Humming an unnamed tune, he walked with a spring in his step, as if the weight in his hand were not a corpse but a delightful trophy.

        “Phew—quite the haul today.”  He casually tossed the headless carcass onto the stone steps before the tower. Blood splattered as it landed with a wet thud. He looked up at the auroral sky, then grinned. “What a beautiful night. The scent of fresh blood suits it perfectly. How intoxicating.”

        Cradling the monster’s head in his arms, he jubilantly stepped inside the tower, only to hear a cold sneer the moment he entered.

        “You seem to be enjoying yourself, Nirvana.” A mocking voice came from the darkness.

        Nirvana raised a brow and followed the sound. From the shadows emerged a cloaked figure, their face hidden behind a mask, leaving only a pair of icy eyes exposed.

        “Have you forgotten our mission?” The voice was as cold as a blade made of ice; the tone carried a hint of scrutiny. 

        Nirvana snickered. He tossed the monster’s head to the floor, then wiped the blood on his hands across a wall without a care.

        “How could I?” He shrugged and spread his hands. With feigned sincerity, he began reciting the doctrine, his tone dripping with irreverence: “The World Regulators exist to restore order to the chaotic world, to erase the worldly flames that should never have existed, and return all things to supreme serenity… See? Word for word.”

        “Humph. Cut the act. Just get the job done. The High Lord cares little for what dwells in your mind.”

        “Relax. No one’s more diligent than I am.”  Nirvana’s tone held a quiet, taunting lilt. “Every level of the Brahmic Abyss is sealed by a barrier. No one escapes this cage. And that Alayavijnana you’re all so obsessed with is still staying quietly at the very bottom.” 

        “But there was infiltration a few months ago,” the cloaked figure said. “The High Lord suspects this is a sign of upheaval.”

        “Hahahahaha—” Nirvana threw his head back and let out a hearty laugh that echoed through the room. “It was just some stupid human who had no clue what he was getting into!”

        He stomped down on the monster’s head and crushed it with a sharp crack. Blood burst across the floor. As if hinting at something, he added, “You people made his sister an experimental subject. Your experiment failed, and she died miserably. That foolish lad came to avenge his sister, only to get himself killed. I cut him clean in half and threw him to the bottom level. With those starving monsters down there, there’s no way he’s coming back from that.”

        “Let’s hope you’re right,” said the cloaked figure, their voice emotionless. “The High Lord tolerates no mistakes.”

        “You’re all chickens,” Nirvana clicked his tongue in annoyance. He then took out a crimson wheel from his robe. The wheel bore faintly glowing runes that flowed like living veins, radiating an aura beyond mortal comprehension. “This is the artifact you crafted using Alayavijnana’s karmic powers. It can seal the threads of causality. With this in my hand, there’s no way Alayavijnana is ever going to escape her cage.” 

        “I will report your words truthfully to the High Lord,” the cloaked figure said in a low voice. “But do not forget—underestimating your enemy is the root of failure.”

        As the final word fell, the figure vanished into the air like mist, leaving only fragments of dimming light.

        “Tut! I’d never bother joining your bizarre little cult if it weren’t for the fact that you people make me stronger!” Irritated, Nirvana groaned as he scratched at the back of his head.  “Urgh, this is so annoying! I’m heading down to kill anoth—”

        BOOM! Suddenly, a deep, hollow sound shook the entire tower.

        “What was that?” Nirvana immediately dashed outside, only to see that the auroras in the sky had gone. The entire land had been plunged into an eerie gloom, save for the entrance, where the powerful barrier shone unsteadily, as if someone was tearing it apart.

        “No… That barrier is unbreakable!”

        However, a thunderous explosion shattered his confidence. The lightning strike, powerful enough to rattle the very ground, reduced the barrier to pieces.

        From the golden radiance stepped a boy whose youthful yet striking features were marred by several blood-seeping wounds. Still, he stood tall, like an unyielding spear. In his vertical slit pupils burned a fierce, defiant fire, one that made even Nirvana’s heart falter.

        “You… How are you still alive?” Nirvana stared in disbelief as he saw the boy he had butchered months ago return and break the barrier with new powers that froze him to the bone.

        “Because I kept him alive.” A silver-haired girl glided gracefully out from behind the boy. Crimson threads danced between her fingers like blossoms from the far shore—flowers blooming only for the sake of ruling the world.

        “Alayavijnana…” Nirvana spat out her name through clenched teeth, sending her a baleful glare.

        Sakra quickly stepped before Alayavijnana. With proud defiance, he said, “Nirvana, I’ve come to take your life.”

        “Take my life?” Nirvana gave a dark, vicious laugh. “In your dreams!”

        With a flick of his wrist, six red chains spread from the wheel and lashed straight toward Alayavijnana. She could not stop them from wrapping around her even as she summoned her crimson threads in defense, and soon she was lifted high in the air, helpless and exposed.

        Watching Sakra’s growing panic, Nirvana sneered triumphantly. “This artifact was forged from her karmic powers; even she can’t break free from it!”

        “Let her go!” Sakra roared. Lightning gathered around his fist as he lunged at Nirvana.

        More red chains appeared, forming a sturdy shield that deflected the lightning straight back at Sakra. The blow landed squarely, driving the boy back several steps as he coughed up blood.

        “It’s useless, Sakra!”Nirvana’s laughter grew even more arrogant. “You can’t overcome the power of causality!”

        “You don’t understand the true meaning of karma,” said Alayavijnana softly, bound in midair while staring coldly at Nirvana. “What you stole from me will be your undoing, and this place will be where you fall.”

        “Still got that hard mouth on you, huh?” Nirvana scoffed. A red radiance appeared in his palms as he conjured a long sword. Aiming it straight at Sakra, he shouted, “Just watch how I kill your ‘dragon’!”

        “You can’t kill me! My life belongs to Alayavijnana; no one can take it from me!” Sakra raised his head, his golden eyes blazing with fury as he unleashed his powers.

        The clash of lightning and crimson radiance lit the entrance like sudden daylight, and just like that, a brutal fight began…
STORY_11128:
Brahmic End - Ch. 1

        In the moment of instinctive madness, the origin of all things unleashed a roar so mighty that it shook the fabric of the universe. An ancient creature managed to contain such insanity and tear apart the core that birthed all powers. Yet, the impact was soul-wrecking—it denied the creature’s existence, reducing its form into ashes, which intertwined with the overflowing power of the origin. From that union, embryos took their first form—a new species was born.

        Repelled by the power of creation, the tenacious embryos drifted across light-years, cast to the far reaches of the universe. Each fell upon a different star, sinking into its heart, where they entered hypersleep for recovery.

        Among all the embryos, Alayavijnana was special. With the powers of creation and destruction blended in perfect proportion, she was born with an extraordinary ability to grasp the threads of causality.

        Such a gift allowed her to comprehend the laws embedded in all existence. Thus, she could take on a humanoid form when she finally awoke from her long and peaceful sleep.

        Her fair, flawless face held a pair of pronounced eyes so deep that they seemed to devour the very light of the universe. In their fathomless depths shimmered contempt, sacrilege, and a blasphemous disdain for the world.

        From the moment of her birth, Alayavijnana could see through the cycle of fate. Having watched the endless weave of lives, causes, and consequences, she had a higher resistance to the influence of the origin of destruction than any other ancient demon. So when her brethren, Laplace and Vorvadoss, came to invite her to join in liberating the origin of destruction at the far edge of the cosmos, she refused without hesitation.

        “Why?” Laplace asked, curious as a child.

        “Because it’s disgusting… anything steeped in the stench of others.” Surprisingly, Alayavijnana answered his question, her words carrying a hint of casual disdain. “I loathe what has been possessed. All I desire is uniqueness—something that belongs solely to me.”

        “What a pity. I hope you get what you desire then.” Laplace accepted her refusal with grace, then departed with Vorvadoss.

        Alayavijnana, once again, was left to drift alone in the vast cosmos. Yet, solitude never bothered her, for she was busy searching for the causes of the past.

        In an age long forgotten, Azathoth, the primordial dragon of destruction, had roamed around the universe, leaving traces invisible to mortal perception. Only Alayavijnana, who commanded the world’s causality, could discern his vestiges. She gathered them, kneading their latent power into a form that would be hers alone—a dragon beyond mortal comprehension.

        However, creating such an extraordinary dragon was far from simple. It was after countless failures and ages of effort that she finally wrought a perfect dragon.

        She gazed upon the beautiful dragon, a vision so sublime it stole the breath from her weary soul. A soft smile graced her lips as she caressed its gleaming and smooth scales. With tender affection, she whispered, “Paramita… your name is Paramita, my one and only, perfect dragon.

        However, Alayavijnana underestimated the arrogance of life. Paramita refused to be her dragon—he spurned her claim, denied her ownership. Their first meeting soon turned into a fierce battle, which ended with Alayavijnana slaying the dragon. She kept his corpse, intending to build herself another dragon. However, “they” came and struck when she was in her most vulnerable state.

        They called themselves the World Regulators, self-proclaimed arbiters of cosmic order, who had sworn to rectify the wrong world. In an attempt to seize Alayavijnana’s power over causality, they ensnared her in labyrinthine traps and even used Paramita’s corpse as bait. At the cost of near annihilation, they succeeded in tearing away half her power and cast her broken form into the depths of a special prison designed solely for her—the Brahmic Abyss.

        Guards were sent to keep the ancient demon from escaping. However, for the mighty Alayavijnana, even grievously wounded and stripped of half her strength, sheer resolve could still have shattered this cage. But such a victory would have come at too steep a cost—one not worth the sacrifice. 

        For an ancient demon such as Alayavijnana, time was the cheapest coin. And so she chose to lie dormant, regaining her strength in silence. During her recovery, the World Regulators kept throwing different monsters into the Brahmic Abyss from time to time, but none disturbed her slumber.

        Until one day, the Brahmic Abyss quivered with an unsettling current, as though something were about to break. The commotion stirred Alayavijnana from her long slumber. As she slowly opened her eyes, thousands of crimson threads burst from her fingertips, grinding the gray rocks around her into dust. 

        [i]‘At last, the seed I’ve waited so long for has come.’[/i] She raised her gaze to see a broken figure fall from above with a rain of blood that painted the ground scarlet.

        Moments later, the figure struck the ground before her. It was a boy, nearly grown, his body mangled, breath faint, yet his eyes still burned with unwavering defiance. He strenuously turned his head; through the crimson haze, he saw Alayavijnana’s silhouette. Driven by an instinct to survive, he struggled to speak. His words came out in weak rasps: “Hel… Help me…”

        “So, do you wish to live?” Alayavijnana asked, her lips curving in playful amusement.

        “Yes… There’s… someone I must kill…”

        “A fair reason. Your eyes hold the flames of vengeance, of obsession. Good, I love making deals with those who are driven by obsession.” She nodded, satisfied. “I can help you, but for a price.”

        “What… price…”

        “Make a covenant with me. Become my most loyal servant, and obey me.”

        “I… agree…”  The boy’s voice was resolute. His eyes blazed brighter with determination.

        “Good boy. I adore obedient children.” Alayavijnana smiled gently, her right hand pulling a massive dragon bone from the void she summoned.

        It was Paramita’s bone, one that the World Regulators had seized during their plan to ensnare the ancient demon. Alayavijnana had risked all to reclaim it, only to be ambushed and cast into the abyss with half of her powers stripped from her.

        “Let’s see if you can stay this obedient,” she murmured as she thrust the bone into the boy’s broken flesh, then took a step back—

        “AAAAAAAHHHHHHHHH—!”

        The next instant, a scream of raw agony resounded throughout the lowest level of the Brahmic Abyss. The boy writhed on the ground like a fish out of water, convulsing as his bones shattered and fused, flesh torn and remade.

        “Human blood is incompatible with the dragon bone. But if you survive, you shall be reborn,” Alayavijnana explained with a delighted smile as she watched the boy suffer. Her eyes gleamed with fascination, savoring the spectacle of pain and rebirth as though it were some kind of performance.

        [i]‘What fruit will you bear for me?’[/i] she wondered, her eyes alight with anticipation. [i]‘I can hardly wait to see.’[/i]
STORY_11129:
Brahmic End - Ch. 7

        As the afternoon sun blazed across the kingdom of Sumeru, its golden heat scorched the arena, raising the air temperature even higher. Still, the heat did not stop tens of thousands from gathering to witness the annual Warrior Trial, a tournament to determine the greatest warrior of the kingdom, a stage where strength and honor were defined. And now, at last, the final battle was about to begin.

        The iron gates swung open with a bang. A colossal man stepped out from the shadows, his muscles knotted like sculpted bronze gleaming under the sunlight. A deafening cheer rose from the stands, to which he responded by raising his mighty arms. His name was Shivaji, the Greatest Warrior of Sumeru, who had reigned over the arena for the past three years.  

        Meanwhile, a lean, almost slender, boy in plain clothing emerged from the gates that slowly opened at the opposite side. His name was Sakra. Set against Shivaji’s massive frame, he looked almost fragile, his young, unseasoned features a far cry from those of a warrior ready to fight for glory.

        “Kid, you sure you’re in the right place? The arena isn’t for fledged birds,” Shivaji laughed, crossing his arms as the audience burst into derision.

        But Sakra did not reply; in fact, he did not hear him at all.

        His gaze swept the arena, ignoring Shivaji’s scornful words, cutting through the tide of voices, across the shimmering heat and swirling dust until it settled at the highest row.

        There sat a girl dressed in white.

        Her features were as graceful as a serene painting, her eyes clear as dawnlight. She was Shachi, the Saintess of Sumeru, and Sakra’s twin sister, separated from him since birth.

        Though the two had never met, the bond of blood stretched unbroken across the years. Years ago, when Sakra was still a child, he saw Shachi parading through the city as the newly ordained Saintess. As his eyes landed on her for the first time, a strange, indescribable feeling stirred within him, as if a missing piece of his soul had returned, like fate had finally found its resting place.

        From that day on, Sakra chased his sister’s distant figure with a fervor he could not restrain.

        However, the Saintess stood far above the reach of ordinary people. All Sakra could do was edge closer in whatever humble ways left open to him.

        In such attempts, he once climbed a deadly cliff just to pick the rarest flower and place it upon the altar.

        He wished only that her eyes might fall upon it, that the bloom might bring her a heartbeat of joy, even though she would never know that it was a gift from her twin brother.

        What began as admiration and faith grew into a deep attachment, and little by little, it eventually became a desire bordering on obsession.

        ‘I want her to look at me… even if only once.’ That wish burned fervently within the boy.

        So when he learned that the greatest warrior would receive the Saintess’s blessing, he entered the competition without a second thought despite knowing that it would require brutal training, one that would drench him in blood, sweat, and tears. Each time he fell, he forced himself to rise, again and again, and pressed on through trials beyond human endurance.

        His efforts had paid off, leading him at last to the stage of the final duel, where he waited for the signal to begin.

        WHOOO—

        A horn blared through the scorching air; drums rumbled in its wake, signaling the beginning of the fight.

        With a mighty roar, Shivaji charged forward. His fist ripped through the air; the floor cracked beneath the weight of his blow. Yet, Sakra had already flickered out of his sight, reappearing behind him like a phantom. He tried to strike Shivaji’s torso with a whipping kick, but the man blocked it with his arm. He reached for Sakra’s ankle, but the boy slipped away like a fish in water, leaping back to a safe distance.

        Strike followed counter, and counter followed strike. The sheer force of exchanged blows sent waves of wind through the arena. Before long, the battle had reached its final stretch.

        Blood streaked Sakra’s body, his left arm numb and his breathing ragged.

        “You can’t dodge it this time!” Laughing loudly, Shivaji abandoned all defense and threw a broad, heavy punch. 

        Lightning wrapped around Sakra’s right hand as he gathered his powers, poised for the moment he had awaited. The moment Shivaji lunged, he crouched low and drove his fist into the man’s abdomen. The warrior convulsed with pain, letting out an agonized cry before collapsing in a cloud of dust.

        For a still moment, the arena held its breath. Then cheers crashed down like thunder as Sakra, drenched in blood, raised his fist and looked upward.

        There, in the top row, Shachi smiled softly beneath the sun, as if she shared the happiness of his victory.

        For that moment, Sakra believed all his pain had meaning, that all those years of waiting had finally been justified. Everything he had been through was all about this very moment. Yet, he could have never known how brutal the reality awaiting him would be.

        The day before the investiture ceremony, death knells tolled across the kingdom, mourning the Saintess’s death by sudden illness. But Sakra refused to believe it. Desperate to know the truth, he forced his way into the sanctum and tore open the coffin. There he saw her body, marred by unusual stitches and surgical marks—she did not die of illness; she was murdered by an organization called the World Regulators.

        Consumed by grief, Sakra hunted the murderers’ shadows, day and night, until he found their stronghold. He broke in, believing he could avenge his sister, only to learn how gravely he had misjudged his power.

        Outmatched and surrounded, he was ripped open and cast into the lowest depths of the Brahmic Abyss.

        As he fell, all he felt was endless darkness and a crushing choking feeling of helplessness.
 
        Just before his mind slipped into nothingness, he met her—Alayavijnana, the ancient demon who was imprisoned at the lowest level.

        There she stood before him, her silver hair fluttering in the wind, her skin pale as moonlight. Crimson threads coiled around her fingers. Her eyes, fathomlessly profound, seemed capable of devouring all light. 

        The gravity of her presence and a dying creature’s instinctive hunger for life compelled him to beg for her help. And she granted his wish by implanting a dragon bone that held immeasurable might within him.

        The moment the dragon bone drove through his body, a blood-curdling scream ripped itself from Sakra’s throat and quickly became a voiceless howl. His blood boiled. His bones bent and reformed. His flesh ripped apart and stitched itself anew. In that endless cycle of pain, he was remade, reborn into a new existence.

        From then on, he followed Alayavijnana, climbing level after level as they headed for the highest level of the Brahmic Abyss.

        During their climb, he faced the phantom of his sister and slain her with his own hands to break free from the illusion. He confronted the lingering will of the dragon bone and reclaimed his body. He learned to fight, and he learned to obey.

        Eventually, they reached the surface, only to find Nirvana, a guard of the World Regulators, and the very man who had butchered Sakra and threw him into the Brahmic Abyss, waiting at the exit.

        With his magical wheel, a special artifact created by the World Regulators using Alayavijnana’s karmic powers, Nirvana swept his arm, conjuring six red chains that erupted from the void to bind her in the air and suppress her powers.

        Enraged, Sakra unleashed his powers and lunged toward Nirvana head-on. But the wheel’s overwhelming power tipped the fight; Nirvana’s blade drove through his shoulder and pinned him to the ground.

        With a cruel grin, Nirvana put his foot on the boy’s wound, grinding it. The pain tore through Sakra’s body, but he bit it down, refusing to give Nirvana even a single cry.

        “Tut! Still nothing? You’re just as boring as I saw you the last time—no screams, no groan, no matter how I tortured you.” Nirvana clicked his tongue in disappointment while conjuring another sword. “Well, it doesn’t matter. Alayavijnana’s here. She should be more fun to torture.”

        “Keep your hands off her!” Sakra warned through clenched teeth.

        “Hah! Not only I’m going to touch her, I’m going to make her kneel before me and lick my feet like the most obedient dog!”

        “You— I’m going to kill you!” Sakra roared, struggling violently, but the chains held him tight.

        “You? You can’t even move,” Nirvana sneered, tapping Sakra’s cheek with his sword. “Accept it. You can’t escape fate.”

        ‘I… Am I failing again?’  His mind flashed back to the moment he saw Shachi resting in the coffin. The entire world seemed to have collapsed in that moment, leaving a gaping wound in his heart that would not stop bleeding. It was a grief that gnawed down to the bone, an experience that he refused to relive.

        The dragon bone within his body began trembling. Thunder raced through his veins.

        ‘No! I’m not accepting this! If destiny seeks to take away what’s important to me, then I will tear it down with my own hands!’

        Sakra couldn’t remember how he roared or how he struggled, only the moment when everything changed. The dragon bone melted into his flesh when he made up his mind, unleashing a searing golden radiance that coalesced into a Vajra, a weapon that symbolized his defiance of fate.

        Sakra grabbed the Vajra and swept it across his body, reducing the chains of karma into dust.

        “N-no… That’s impossible! How can you break the chains of karma?” Nirvana shrieked.

        “Because I don’t belong to the karma of this world!” Sakra roared. “I belong only to Alayavijnana!”

        With a swing of his arm, he drove the Vajra through the wheel and Nirvana’s heart. The next instant, thunder roared across the land, shaking the earth and heavens. Nirvana toppled in horror as the wheel shattered and the red chains dissolved into dust.

        Sakra dropped to one knee. As he gasped for breath, someone approached. He lifted his head to see Alayavijnana smiling softly.

        “You have surpassed causality, Sakra,” she whispered. “You are free now—free from my dominion. From this moment on, you may choose your own path.”

        But Sakra felt no joy. Instead, he panicked, terrified she would leave him. So, he reached for her hand.

        “I don’t want freedom.” His voice trembled, but it carried an unshakeable devotion, shadowed by a touch of madness. “I want your dominion. Let me be yours—command me, possess me, see me. That is the only happiness I live for.”

        “…Good boy.” Alayavijnana leaned close. She stroked his cheek with her slender fingers, her voice cold yet alluring as she whispered, “Your wish shall be granted.”

        She floated into the air. Crimson threads bloomed from her palm and coiled around Sakra’s neck, his hands, his chest. At last they reached his brow and burrowed between his eyebrows, leaving a crimson mark on his forehead.

        “From this day forward, you are my dragon, one of a kind.”

        Sakra closed his eyes. A faint smile lifted his lips as peace washed over him and softened his features. Holding Alayavijnana’s ankle, he planted a reverent kiss upon the pale arch of her foot, and vowed, “Yes. I’m yours, forever.”

        [i]‘The seed I sowed has finally borne the fruit I desired—a dragon unbound by fate, yet willing to obey me.’[/i] Alayavijnana closed her eyes, a faint, elusive smile gracing her lips as she murmured inwardly.

        With her ability to control causality, she had seen the stars shift a million times. She had watched their birth, their growth, their fall, and their rebirth. She had witnessed lives crawl from fire to the heavens, only to perish in their pride. Every world labored under the same loop; the wheel of fate kept spinning with no pause.

        For someone who knew the cycle so thoroughly, everything was nothing more than destiny repeating its lines. Every birth was foretold; every death was predetermined. Even the primordial dragons that had created the world were doomed to fall.

        “How boring… Everything is bound by the law of causality…” she muttered. She drew her fingers through the empty air. Crimson threads trembled between them, as though the destiny itself were whispering in her ear. “I want… a life unbound by the law of karma.”

        And so she set her plan into motion. Now, she had what she desired.

        Dawn broke once more over the distant plains. Sunlight poured over the devastated battlefield where a demon rested quietly beside her dragon.

        It was the end of karma, and the beginning of a new cycle.
STORY_11130:
In the wide courtyard, two people stood ten paces apart, facing one another in silent tension.

        As the morning breeze brushed past, a leaf fell from a swaying branch. The leaf hit the ground with a soft tap, a sound that broke the standoff like a quiet starting cue.

        The first to move was the slighter of the two: a young girl. She lowered her stance, then launched herself with a powerful kick, ripping through the air like a thunderbolt. The weighty claymore in her hands drew a fierce arc with a momentum that tore apart the wind as she charged straight toward the tall man before her.

        The claymore came down with unstoppable force; the air shrieked as it cut through. A hit like that could easily cripple a man or even kill him. The man, feeling the threat, immediately dropped his waist to dodge the attack, all while delivering a kick at her shin to throw her off balance.

        But the girl had seen through his move. Holding the claymore with both hands, she twisted it downward and used it as a lever to flip herself into the air. The man pressed on without pause by skillfully thrusting his sword toward her landing point—

        Clang!

        Steel struck steel, not flesh. The girl knocked the sword away by hurling her claymore mid-air. She landed cleanly, and in the same heartbeat, she took out the dagger strapped to her thigh and pressed its cold edge against the man’s neck.

        Even then, the man didn’t flinch. His hand held a jagged stone just inches away from the girl’s chest. It turned out that he had grabbed the stone and used it as a weapon the moment the girl knocked his sword away.

        For a moment, the courtyard fell completely silent, leaving nothing but the sound of their uneven breaths. The silence reigned until a hearty laugh escaped the man’s mouth, easing the tension.

        “Hahaha,” The middle-aged man laughed, tossing the stone away. He then ruffled the girl’s hair as he said with pride, “Ourea, you’ve improved quite a lot.” 

        “Father! S-stop!” The girl, Ourea, covered her head with both hands, her cheeks puffed in protest. “I’m not a child anymore!” 

        “Yes, yes. My daughter is now an exceptional summoner.” Ares withdrew his hand, his gaze full of pride and fatherly love.

        Ares and Ourea were both Holy Gods. As one of the twelve major gods, Ares was in charge of the heavy cavalry. His daughter, Ourea, however, didn’t follow in his footsteps into the army. She chose a path outside her home: becoming a summoner, working for the Heptara Unies, an international organization.

        Over the years, Ourea had shed the immaturity of her early summoner days; time had shaped her into someone more mature and composed. She had grown so exponentially that she could stand equal to her father—who had decades of battlefield experience—even without using magic or heroic spirits.

        “You’ll be leaving for Rycaza soon. Did you get everything you need?” Ares asked with genuine concern. Although he might be the stern and disciplined commander revered within the army, he was simply a caring father in front of his daughter.

        “Yes, I’m all ready,” she replied.

        “So you’ll be gone again, for who knows how long this time,” he said. “Pay your mother a visit before you leave.”

        “…Alright.” Ourea’s expression dimmed. She had struggled to deal with her strict mother, Semele, ever since she was a child; whenever they met, her nerves tightened on instinct. And after learning what had happened between her mother and elder sister as she got older, that feeling of unease deepened into something closer to resentment, one that created a lasting rift between them.

        Even so, Semele was still her mother, connected by blood. Reluctantly, she walked to the garden at the back of the courtyard, where Semele stood before a bed of lilies, watering the buds.

        “Mother,” Ourea called softly.

        Instead of looking up, Semele simply remarked with a cold voice, “Don’t get too full of yourself. Your sparring with Ares just now may be a tie, but don’t let that little taste of accomplishment get into your head. After all, he’s a commander—his strength lies in warfare, not one-on-one combat. That’s the only reason you were able to keep up.”

        “…Yes, Mother,” Ourea replied, looking hesitant. Only after a moment of silence did she finally say the news, “I-I’m going to Rycaza because I found news about Sister!”

        Semele’s hand paused for a second, but she quickly regained composure and answered emotionlessly, “I see.”

        However, her seemingly indifferent reaction only ignited the spark of resentment that had long smoldered inside Ourea. Her voice trembled as she asked the sharp question through her clenched teeth, “How could you act like you don’t care at all? Is it because you still resent Sister? Resent her for making you lose the throne?”

        Only then did Semele turn around and look at her daughter. Her expression was complicated, her voice low and tight. “Does it even matter now? She’s already dead.”

        “No! Sister is alive! And I will bring her home!” Ourea’s voice cracked as she shouted. With tears spilling down her cheeks, she spun and ran away.

        “Ourea,” Ares called. He had quietly watched the entire conversation from afar. He followed Ourea as soon as she ran.

        “Father…” Ourea’s eyes reddened. She threw herself into her father’s arms and broke into sobs. “What do Sister and I even mean to her?”

        “You’re both her beloved daughters, of course.” Ares gently stroked her back, then continued, “She never hated your sister. The only one she hates is the stubborn version of herself from the past.”

        “…Really?”

        “Of course.” He nodded firmly. “Did you know? The lilies your mother tends so carefully were actually planted by your sister.”

        “What?” Ourea lifted her head in shock.

        “Your mother has always been too proud to talk about something like love. She just doesn’t know how to show it,” Ares smiled, his gaze filled with warmth. “So please don’t question her love for you. She loves you, and your sister, more deeply than you think.”

        “...I see.” Bolstered by her father’s words, Ourea wiped her tears and straightened her posture. Clenching her fist with renewed resolve, she said, “I’ll find Sister. I’ll uncover the truth, no matter what!”

        And so, she bade her father goodbye and set off for Rycaza. Little did she know that a spaceship would crash into the Enochian Tower shortly after her arrival, and that she would discover a conspiracy far bigger than she could ever imagine…
